Track S · Statistics & probability · Module S1

Distributions & the Central Limit TheoremWhy averages go normal, how fast, and the one family of data where they don't.

Almost every statistical tool you will use — confidence intervals, t-tests, control charts, the standard error on a conversion rate — rests on one claim: the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal. That claim is true, conditionally. This bench draws real samples from five different populations so you can watch the convergence happen, measure how fast, and find the case where it fails.

Sampling distribution bench
real draws · real KS distance
left: the population you are sampling from · right: the distribution of sample means, with the normal it is supposed to approach

The statement, precisely

For i.i.d. draws from a population with finite mean μ and finite variance σ², the sample mean of n draws has expectation μ and standard deviation σ/√n, and its distribution tends to normal as n grows. Two consequences you will use constantly:

SE = σ / √n the standard error — the SD of the estimate, not of the data quadrupling n halves the error. That is the whole cost curve of "just collect more data": diminishing at a known rate. n=100 → SE = σ/10 n=400 → SE = σ/20 n=10,000 → SE = σ/100

The bench reports predicted SE next to the observed spread of the means. On the well-behaved distributions they agree to two or three decimals — that agreement is the theorem, measured rather than asserted.

How fast is "tends to"?

Convergence speed depends on the skew of the population, not on any fixed rule of thumb. Drag n and watch the KS distance — the largest gap between the empirical distribution of the means and a fitted normal:

PopulationSkewn for the means to look normalFraud analogue
Uniform0~5Random sampling weights
Exponential2~30Time between transactions
Bernoulli p=0.03~5.5~150 (need np ≳ 10)Fraud rate per batch
Log-normal> 6Several hundredTransaction values
Pareto, α < 2undefinedNeverWhale transfers, gas spikes

"n > 30 is enough" is a classroom simplification of the exponential row and nothing more. For a 3% fraud rate it is badly wrong: with n = 30 you expect 0.9 fraud events per batch, and the sampling distribution of that proportion is a lumpy staircase, not a bell. The working rule for proportions is n·p ≥ 10 and n·(1−p) ≥ 10.

The failure case

Press Show where the CLT fails. A Pareto population with tail index α < 2 has infinite variance, so σ/√n is not a small number — it is undefined, and the classical CLT simply does not apply. The distribution of means stays skewed no matter how large n gets, and the observed spread refuses to settle. Any confidence interval you build on σ/√n here is fiction, and this is not an exotic case: transaction values, gas fees, wallet balances and network degree distributions are all routinely power-law.

Interview point

"The CLT needs finite variance and i.i.d. draws — and how fast it kicks in depends on skew, not on n > 30. For a 3% fraud rate I check n·p ≥ 10 rather than n ≥ 30, and on power-law columns like transaction value I log-transform first or use bootstrap intervals, because σ/√n assumes a variance that may not exist."

The trap

The CLT says nothing about the distribution of your data — only about the distribution of an average. People routinely test their raw feature for normality and conclude their t-test is invalid, or the reverse: assume their skewed data means skewed estimates. Both miss the point. The other silent assumption is independence: transactions from one compromised card, or rows duplicated by retries, are not independent draws, and correlated observations shrink your effective sample size well below your row count while leaving the SE formula looking perfectly healthy.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State the CLT.

For i.i.d. draws with finite mean and variance, the sample mean's distribution approaches normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n as n grows.

Difference between standard deviation and standard error?

SD describes spread of the data; SE describes spread of an estimate. SE = σ/√n.

You want to halve your standard error. What does it cost?

Four times the data — SE scales with 1/√n.

Is n > 30 a valid rule?

Only for mildly skewed populations. For proportions use n·p ≥ 10 and n·(1−p) ≥ 10; for heavy tails, no fixed n works.

When does the CLT not apply at all?

Infinite variance (Pareto with α ≤ 2), or non-independent draws.

Your feature is heavily right-skewed. Does that break a t-test on its mean?

Not necessarily — what matters is the sampling distribution of the mean. With enough n it is fine; with small n and heavy tails, use bootstrap or a log transform.

Why are transaction amounts a problem?

They are power-law distributed, so the variance may be effectively undefined and interval estimates built on σ/√n understate the true uncertainty.

Track S · Statistics & probability · Module S2

Hypothesis Testing & p-valuesWhat the number means, what it does not mean, and how running twenty of them manufactures a discovery.

A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability the null is true, not the probability your result is a fluke, and not a measure of effect size. This bench runs the actual test on simulated arms so you can watch p move with sample size while the underlying effect stays fixed — and then watch twenty tests on pure noise produce a "significant" winner.

Test bench
two-proportion z-test
single test: the null distribution, the critical region and where your statistic landed · many tests: the p-values from k experiments where nothing is really different

The machinery

H₀ : p_A = p_B the null — no difference z = (p̂_B − p̂_A) / SE SE = √( p̄(1−p̄)(1/n_A + 1/n_B) ) p = 2·(1 − Φ(|z|)) two-sided reject H₀ when p < α α = 0.05 by convention, not by law Type I error = reject a true null → rate α, you choose it Type II error = miss a real effect → rate β; power = 1 − β

Power is the number people forget. A test with 30% power will miss a genuine improvement seven times out of ten, and "not significant" then tells you almost nothing. Drag n per arm with a real lift set: the effect never changes, but the p-value marches down and the power readout climbs. Statistical significance is a statement about your sample size at least as much as about the world.

The multiplicity problem

Switch to Many tests, no real effect. Every arm is drawn from the identical distribution — the true lift is zero by construction. Press New draw a few times: at k = 20 about three runs in five turn up at least one "significant" result, against the 64% the arithmetic below predicts. With k independent tests at α = 0.05:

P(at least one false positive) = 1 − (1 − α)^k k = 5 → 23% k = 20 → 64% k = 40 → 87%

This is how a segment analysis produces a finding. Slice by device, region, tenure, channel and card type, and something will look significant whether or not anything is happening. Bonferroni mode divides α by k, which restores the family-wise error rate at the price of power — and that trade is the honest one to state out loud. For large-scale screening the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, which controls the false discovery rate instead, is the usual practical choice.

Interview point

"A p-value is P(data this extreme | null true), not P(null true | data). I pair it with an effect size and a confidence interval, because with a large enough n a trivial difference becomes significant. And if I'm slicing an experiment into twenty segments I correct for multiplicity — at k = 20 there's a 64% chance of at least one false positive at α = 0.05."

The trap

"Not significant" is not "no effect" — it is "this sample was not enough to distinguish it from zero", which is a very different claim and often just a power problem. The inverse trap is worse: at n = 500,000 a 0.02% difference clears p < 0.001 and means nothing operationally. Always report the interval alongside the p-value. And note the arithmetic in this bench is a normal approximation to the binomial; it needs the same n·p ≥ 10 condition from S1, so at a 0.1% fraud rate with small arms you should be using an exact test instead.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define a p-value in one sentence.

The probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

Type I vs Type II error?

Type I: rejecting a true null (false positive, rate α). Type II: failing to reject a false null (false negative, rate β).

What is statistical power?

1 − β: the probability of detecting an effect that is genuinely there. Driven by sample size, effect size and α.

Twenty segments, α = 0.05, no real effect. Expected false positives?

One on average, and a 64% chance of at least one. Correct with Bonferroni or Benjamini–Hochberg.

Bonferroni vs Benjamini–Hochberg?

Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate (α/k) and is conservative; BH controls the false discovery rate and retains far more power for large k.

Significant but tiny. What do you say?

Report the effect size and interval — significance at large n does not imply operational relevance.

Why prefer a confidence interval to a bare p-value?

It carries the magnitude and the uncertainty, so it answers "how big, and how sure" rather than just "distinguishable from zero".

Track S · Statistics & probability · Module S3

Confidence Intervals & the BootstrapWhat 95% actually refers to, and what to do when the textbook formula has no formula.

A 95% interval does not mean the true value has a 95% chance of being inside this interval. It means the procedure traps the truth 95 times out of 100 across repeated samples. That distinction sounds pedantic until you measure it — this bench builds hundreds of intervals from fresh samples and counts how often each method actually covers the truth. Some methods miss badly.

Coverage bench
real resampling · real coverage count
coverage measured over 150 fresh samples
left: the bootstrap distribution of the statistic with both intervals marked · right: coverage across 150 repeated experiments, target 95%

Two ways to build an interval

Normal theory estimate ± 1.96 · SE needs a formula for SE and approximate normality of the estimate Percentile bootstrap for b in 1..B: resample n rows WITH replacement, recompute the statistic interval = [ 2.5th percentile , 97.5th percentile ] of those B values needs no formula at all

The bootstrap's appeal is that it works for statistics with no clean standard error: a median, a 95th percentile, a ratio of two means, an AUC, the difference in PR-AUC between two models. Switch the statistic selector to 95th percentile and watch the normal interval's coverage collapse — the sampling distribution of an extreme quantile is skewed and lumpy, so a symmetric ±1.96·SE interval is the wrong shape by construction.

What the coverage readout is doing

It reruns the entire experiment 150 times: draw a fresh sample, build both intervals, check whether each contains the population value computed analytically from the generator. The reported percentages are therefore measured coverage, not nominal coverage. A method advertising 95% and delivering 25% is not a rounding issue — it is a method that will mislead you far more often than you think. Mis-specification cuts both ways, and the bench shows both: on the 95th percentile the naive normal interval badly under-covers, while on the median the textbook 1.2533·s/√n plug-in over-covers, producing intervals so wide they are useless for deciding anything. Neither is 95%.

SituationUseWhy
Mean, large n, mild skewNormal intervalCheap, closed form, coverage is honest
Median, quantiles, ratios, AUC gapsBootstrapNo usable SE formula; sampling distribution is asymmetric
Small n, heavy tailBootstrap — cautiouslyIt can only resample what you sampled; it cannot invent the tail you missed
Grouped or time-series dataBlock / cluster bootstrapPlain resampling destroys the dependence structure and understates uncertainty

Interview point

"A 95% interval is a statement about the procedure, not about this one interval — repeat the experiment and 95% of the intervals cover the truth. For anything without a clean standard error, like a median or the gap in PR-AUC between two models, I bootstrap. And I resample at the entity level, not the row level, so retries of the same transaction don't count as independent draws."

The trap

The bootstrap resamples your sample, so it inherits every one of its defects. If your sample missed the tail, every resample misses it too, and the interval will be confidently narrow and wrong — exactly the failure mode on power-law transaction values from S1. It also assumes independent rows: on grouped or time-ordered data you need a block or cluster bootstrap, or you will produce intervals far tighter than reality. The bootstrap is a machine for propagating sampling uncertainty, not for repairing a bad sample.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Interpret a 95% confidence interval correctly.

If the experiment were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true parameter.

Describe the bootstrap in two lines.

Resample your data with replacement many times, recompute the statistic each time, and read the interval off the percentiles of that distribution.

When is the bootstrap the right tool?

When the statistic has no tractable standard error — medians, quantiles, ratios, AUC differences, complex pipeline outputs.

What does the bootstrap not fix?

Bias in the sample itself, missing tail mass, or dependence between rows.

How many resamples?

Several hundred for a standard error, one to two thousand for percentile intervals; more mainly buys smoothness, not accuracy.

Confidence interval vs prediction interval?

A confidence interval covers a parameter such as the mean; a prediction interval covers a future individual observation and is much wider.

Your data is grouped by customer. What changes?

Resample whole customers, not rows — otherwise the interval understates uncertainty.

Track S · Statistics & probability · Module S4

Bayes' Rule & the Base-Rate FallacyA 99%-accurate fraud test, fired on a 0.1% population, is wrong nine times out of ten.

This is the single most useful piece of probability in fraud work, and the one non-technical stakeholders get wrong most reliably. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. What operations actually experience is precision — and precision depends on the base rate, which the test knows nothing about. This bench does the arithmetic exactly and draws the population so the intuition lands.

Base-rate bench
exact arithmetic, per 100,000
left: PPV as prevalence moves, with your operating point marked · right: the flagged pile, split into true and false positives

The rule, in the form worth memorising

P(fraud | flagged) = P(flagged | fraud)·P(fraud) ───────────────────────────────────────────────── P(flagged|fraud)·P(fraud) + P(flagged|legit)·P(legit) = sens · prev ─────────────────────────────── sens·prev + (1−spec)·(1−prev)

Do it in natural frequencies instead and it becomes obvious. Take 100,000 transactions at 0.1% fraud: 100 are fraud, 99,900 are not. A test with 99% sensitivity catches 99 of the 100. A test with 99% specificity misflags 1% of 99,900 — that is 999 false alarms. Your queue holds 1,098 cases and 99 are real. Precision: 9%. The test is accurate; the queue is noise. Nothing is broken — that is simply what those three numbers imply.

Why specificity is the expensive parameter

Drag sensitivity from 99% down to 80%: precision barely moves. Now drag specificity from 99% to 99.9%: precision jumps roughly tenfold. At low prevalence, false positives are drawn from a population hundreds of times larger than the positive class, so a tiny change in the false-positive rate swamps any change in recall. This is the quantitative version of the point from D1 — and it is why "our model is 99% accurate" should always be answered with "at what base rate, and what is the precision".

The two-stage answer

Switch to Two-stage triage. A cheap high-recall rule runs first, and only the flagged pile — where the prevalence is now far higher than in the population — goes to a stricter second model. Because stage two operates on a pre-enriched population, the same specificity buys far more precision. Every mature fraud stack is built this way: rules, then a model, then a human, each stage handing a richer population to the next.

Interview point

"Precision is not a property of the model, it's a property of the model and the base rate together. At 0.1% prevalence a 99%/99% detector gives about 9% precision — ten false alarms per catch. That's why I raise specificity rather than recall at low prevalence, and why triage stages exist: each one enriches the population handed to the next."

The trap

The two-stage calculation here assumes the stages are conditionally independent given the true class. They rarely are — a rule engine and a model built on the same features fail on the same transactions, so the real second-stage lift is smaller than the arithmetic promises. Say so before someone else does. The same caveat applies to ensembles sold as independent votes: correlated errors do not cancel.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write Bayes' rule for a detector.

P(fraud|flag) = sens·prev / [sens·prev + (1−spec)·(1−prev)].

99% sensitivity, 99% specificity, 0.1% prevalence — precision?

About 9%. Roughly 99 true positives against 999 false ones per 100,000.

Sensitivity vs specificity vs precision?

Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN), specificity = TN/(TN+FP); both are test properties. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) and depends on prevalence.

At low prevalence, which do you improve first?

Specificity — false positives come from the much larger negative class.

What is the base-rate fallacy?

Reading P(flag|fraud) as if it were P(fraud|flag), ignoring how rare the positive class is.

Why does two-stage triage work?

Stage one raises the prevalence entering stage two, so the same specificity yields far better precision.

What assumption does stacking stages rely on?

Conditional independence of the stages' errors, which shared features routinely violate.

Track S · Statistics & probability · Module S5

Maximum Likelihood & Where Loss Functions Come FromMSE, MAE and log-loss are not three arbitrary choices. They are three assumptions about noise.

Most people learn losses as a menu. They are not a menu — each one is the negative log-likelihood of a specific noise model, and choosing a loss is choosing a claim about how your errors are distributed. Once you see that, "which loss should I use" stops being taste and becomes a question about your data. This bench fits the same dataset under three losses and shows which assumption survives contact with outliers.

Likelihood bench — recovering a known slope β = 2.000
real optimisation
left: the data with the three fitted lines · right: each loss as a function of β, with its minimum marked

The derivation, once

Assume the residuals are i.i.d. draws from some density. The likelihood of the whole dataset is the product of the densities; maximising it is the same as minimising the negative log of it, which turns the product into a sum:

Gaussian noise: p(e) ∝ exp(−e²/2σ²) → −log L = Σ e²/2σ² + c → minimise Σ e² = MSE Laplace noise: p(e) ∝ exp(−|e|/b) → −log L = Σ |e|/b + c → minimise Σ|e| = MAE Bernoulli label: p(y) = p^y (1−p)^(1−y) → −log L = −Σ[y log p + (1−y)log(1−p)] = log-loss / cross-entropy

So least squares is not "the natural way to measure error" — it is the maximum-likelihood estimator under Gaussian noise. Squaring the residual is exactly the exponent in a Gaussian density. And because the exponent is quadratic, a residual ten times larger contributes a hundred times the pull, which is why one bad row can drag an entire regression line.

LossImplied noise modelEstimatesBreaks when
MSE / L2GaussianThe conditional meanHeavy tails, outliers, contaminated labels
MAE / L1LaplaceThe conditional medianNon-differentiable at 0; slower optimisation; ignores magnitude of large errors
HuberGaussian centre, Laplace tailsA compromiseNeeds δ chosen; δ is in the units of y
Log-lossBernoulliA calibrated probabilityPunishes confident mistakes enormously — one p=0.001 on a true positive dominates
Pinball / quantileAsymmetric LaplaceA chosen quantileYou need to know which quantile the business wants

Why this matters at 3am

Select Contaminated and raise the outlier share. The MSE fit walks away from β = 2 while the MAE and Huber fits hold. Nothing about the "true" relationship changed — only the noise model did, and MSE's assumption became false. In fraud data, contaminated labels are the norm rather than the exception: chargebacks that were really customer disputes, mislabelled friendly fraud, amounts entered in the wrong units. If your loss assumes Gaussian noise and your labels contain a few percent of nonsense, the loss will faithfully fit the nonsense.

Interview point

"Every loss is the negative log-likelihood of a noise assumption — MSE assumes Gaussian errors and estimates the mean, MAE assumes Laplace and estimates the median, log-loss assumes Bernoulli and gives you a calibrated probability. So when labels are contaminated I don't 'try MAE and see', I switch because the Gaussian assumption is false, and Huber if I want the efficiency back near the centre."

The trap

Log-loss and accuracy disagree, and log-loss is the one that matters if anything downstream multiplies your score by money. A model can improve accuracy while getting worse at log-loss by becoming overconfident — and overconfidence is invisible in a confusion matrix and fatal in the expected-cost calculation from D3. Note too that switching to MAE changes what you are estimating, from the mean to the median. On a right-skewed target like transaction value those are very different numbers, and "the model got worse" may simply mean "the model now answers a different question".

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is maximum likelihood estimation?

Choosing the parameters that make the observed data most probable under an assumed distribution.

Which noise assumption gives MSE?

Gaussian — minimising squared error is the MLE under Gaussian residuals.

Which gives MAE, and what does it estimate?

Laplace noise; it estimates the conditional median rather than the mean.

Where does log-loss come from?

The Bernoulli likelihood — the negative log-likelihood of the observed labels under predicted probabilities.

Why is MSE sensitive to outliers?

The squared term makes the gradient grow linearly with the residual, so extreme rows dominate the fit.

What does Huber loss do?

Quadratic within δ of zero and linear beyond it — Gaussian efficiency near the centre, Laplace robustness in the tails.

Why prefer log-loss to accuracy for a scoring model?

It is a proper scoring rule: it rewards calibrated probabilities rather than just correct sides of a threshold.

Track S · Statistics & probability · Module S6

A/B Testing & Experiment DesignSizing the experiment before you run it, and the reason checking early results is a bug.

A new fraud model is not shipped because its PR-AUC improved offline. It is shipped because a controlled experiment showed it moves a business metric without wrecking the customer experience — and that experiment has to be sized before it starts. This bench computes the required sample size from the real power formula and then simulates the single most common way teams fool themselves: peeking.

Experiment bench
analytic sizing · simulated peeking
sizing: required n as the detectable effect shrinks · peeking: simulated null experiments and how many cross significance at least once

Sizing, from the formula

n per arm = 2 · (z1−α/2 + z1−β)² · p̄(1−p̄) / δ² α = 0.05 → z = 1.96 power 80% → z = 0.84 power 90% → z = 1.28 δ = absolute effect = baseline × relative MDE

The term that governs everything is δ² in the denominator: halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the sample you need. Drag the MDE slider from 20% down to 5% and watch the required n and the runtime explode. This is why "we'll just see if it helps" is not a plan — a 2% improvement on a 3% base rate needs a sample most teams cannot get inside a quarter, and the honest answer is to say so at design time rather than to run an underpowered test and interpret the noise.

Peeking

Switch to Peeking damage. Every simulated experiment here has no real effect — the arms are identical by construction. The test is run to its planned horizon, but the team checks significance k times along the way and stops the moment p < 0.05. The false-positive rate reported is measured, not theoretical, and it climbs far above 5%: with ten looks it typically lands in the twenties or thirties. The fixed-horizon test on the same data holds at roughly 5%, as advertised.

The mechanism is simple. The z statistic wanders as data accumulates; given enough opportunities to look, it will cross the boundary at some point purely by chance, and stopping rules that trigger on that crossing convert random walks into "wins". The legitimate fixes are sequential designs built for it — alpha spending, group-sequential boundaries, or always-valid confidence sequences — not discipline.

DecisionMade whenFailure if skipped
Primary metric, singleBefore launchYou pick the metric that won, after the fact
Guardrail metricsBefore launchFraud recall improves while decline rate and support tickets quietly double
MDE and horizonBefore launchUnderpowered test, ambiguous result, argument
Randomisation unitBefore launchSplitting by transaction when the effect is per customer leaks between arms
Stopping ruleBefore launchPeeking, and a false-positive rate several times what you claimed

Interview point

"I size the test before running it: required n scales with 1/δ², so halving the effect I want to detect quadruples the sample. I fix the horizon, the primary metric and the guardrails up front — and I don't stop early on a p-value, because with ten interim looks the false-positive rate goes from 5% to roughly 25%. If we need to stop early, that's a sequential design decision, not a judgement call."

The trap

For a fraud model the randomisation unit is almost never the transaction. Fraudsters operate per card, per device, per wallet; if the same entity can land in both arms, the treatment leaks and the measured effect shrinks toward zero. Randomise on the entity. And beware the label delay from A2: if chargebacks arrive 30–90 days later, an experiment read at day 14 is measuring an incomplete outcome, and early reads are systematically biased toward whichever arm resolves faster — which is a bias no amount of statistical rigour inside the test can fix.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
How does required sample size scale with the effect size?

As 1/δ² — halving the detectable effect quadruples the sample needed.

What is an MDE?

The minimum detectable effect: the smallest true difference the test is powered to find at your chosen α and power.

Why is peeking a problem?

Each interim look is another chance for the statistic to wander across the boundary; the realised false-positive rate rises far above α.

What legitimises early stopping?

A sequential design — alpha spending, group-sequential boundaries, or always-valid confidence sequences agreed before launch.

What is a guardrail metric?

A metric you are not trying to improve but refuse to damage — decline rate, latency, support contacts.

What is the randomisation unit for a fraud model, and why?

The entity — card, customer, wallet — because behaviour and treatment effects follow the entity, not the individual transaction.

Why can't you read a fraud experiment at day 14?

Chargeback labels lag by 30–90 days, so the outcome is incomplete and the early read is biased.

Foundations & data prep · Module A1

Bias–Variance & the Learning CurveEvery model failure is either "too simple to see it" or "memorised the noise". This bench shows you which.

You never observe bias and variance directly — you observe a train score and a test score, and the gap between them tells you which disease you have. Get that diagnosis wrong and you spend a week tuning the wrong knob. This is the first bench because every other module's failure mode is a special case of it.

Fit Complexity Bench
real least squares
true function · training sample · fitted polynomial

What is actually being computed

The true signal is f(x) = sin(1.6x) + 0.35x on x ∈ [-3, 3]. Training points are drawn uniformly and corrupted with Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ. The fit solves the ridge-regularised normal equations directly — w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹ Xᵀy — by Gaussian elimination on the Vandermonde design matrix, with columns standardised so that degree 15 doesn't collapse numerically. Test error is the expected out-of-sample MSE: mean squared deviation of the fit from the true function over a dense grid spanning the domain, plus the analytic irreducible term σ². Computing it that way rather than re-drawing a finite test set removes sampling jitter, so when the gap moves you know the model moved and not the dice.

The decomposition worth memorising

For squared loss, expected test error at a point decomposes exactly into three terms:

E[(y − f̂(x))²] = Bias[f̂(x)]² + Var[f̂(x)] + σ² wrong shape unstable fit irreducible

The third term is the noise floor. No model, no amount of data, no architecture removes it. If your test RMSE is 0.30 and σ is 0.30, you are done — further tuning is chasing noise and will only produce a model that looks better in validation and worse in production.

SymptomTrain errorTest errorDiagnosisFix
UnderfitHighHigh, close to trainBias dominatesMore capacity, better features, less regularisation
OverfitVery lowHigh, big gapVariance dominatesMore data, more regularisation, fewer features, simpler model
At the floor≈ σ≈ σ, small gapIrreducible noiseNothing. Stop. Go improve the data
Test < trainHigherLowerUsually leakage or a soft train-time regulariser (dropout)Check the split before celebrating

Reading the learning curve

Switch the bench to Learning curve and watch the two lines as n grows. They tell you whether more data is worth buying:

  • Curves converge high and flat — high bias. More rows will not help. A hundred million more labelled transactions will not save a linear model on a non-linear boundary.
  • Wide gap that is still narrowing — high variance. More data is the cheapest fix available, and it is the only fix that costs you nothing in bias.
  • Gap has flattened at a stable width — you have hit the model's ceiling for this feature set. Change the features or the model class, not the row count.

Interview point

"Before I tune anything I plot the learning curve, because it answers a question tuning can't: if train and test converge high and flat, the model is biased and more data is wasted spend — I need better features. If there's still a closing gap, it's variance and more data is the cheapest fix on the table."

The trap

The classic U-shaped complexity curve is a fixed-n phenomenon, not a law. Push degree to 15 with 12 points and the bench shows the textbook explosion — but modern over-parameterised networks routinely sit far past the interpolation threshold and generalise anyway (the "double descent" regime). Quote the U-curve for classical models; don't claim it as a universal ceiling on capacity, because a panel with a deep-learning person on it will pick that up.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define bias and variance in one line each.

Bias is error from the model being the wrong shape for the truth; variance is how much the fitted model moves if you resample the training set.

What is irreducible error?

σ² — noise in the labels themselves. No model removes it; it sets the floor your test error can never beat.

Train 0.02, test 0.48. Diagnosis?

Variance / overfitting. Regularise, simplify, or get more rows — in that order of cost.

Train 0.44, test 0.46. Diagnosis?

Bias / underfitting. More data is useless here; add capacity or better features.

Does regularisation raise or lower bias?

Raises bias, lowers variance. You accept a slightly wrong shape in exchange for a stable one.

When does more training data not help?

When the learning curves have already converged — the error is bias plus noise, and neither responds to row count.

Why can test error be lower than train error?

Leakage, an unlucky split, or train-time regularisers like dropout that are switched off at evaluation. Investigate before you celebrate.

Foundations & data prep · Module A2

Splits, Leakage & the Score That LiesThree one-line mistakes, each of which hands you a validation number your production model will never reproduce.

Leakage is the only bug in machine learning that makes your metrics better. That is what makes it lethal: nothing alerts, nobody investigates a jump from 0.83 to 0.97, and the failure surfaces months later as a fraud model that misses fraud. This bench runs the same fraud-style dataset through honest and leaky pipelines with a k-NN model — a learner that can memorise, which is exactly what makes duplicate leakage visible — and shows you both numbers side by side.

Leakage Bench — reported vs future AUC
k-NN · k=7
top: what you report · bottom: the timeline, showing which rows the model was allowed to see

The three leaks, mechanically

LeakWhat the code doesWhy the score inflatesCorrect form
Preprocessing on full dataStandardScaler().fit(X) before splittingTest-set mean and variance are baked into the training transform. Mild but real, and it compounds with imputation and PCAFit the scaler on train only, then transform test. Use a Pipeline
Near-duplicate rowsRetries, reversals, card-on-file re-auths of the same event, split randomlyThe model has effectively seen the test row. Random split scores soar; the future does notGroup-aware split on entity or event id (GroupKFold)
Target encoding without foldsMerchant mean fraud rate computed on all rows, then used as a featureEach row's own label is inside its own feature. Catastrophic; AUC approaches 1.0Out-of-fold encoding, smoothing, and computed inside the CV loop

Why fraud data is time-ordered data

Random splits assume rows are exchangeable. Transaction data is not: attack patterns evolve, merchants churn, a mixer service appears in March that did not exist in January. Push the drift slider up and watch the honest random-split AUC stay comfortable while the future-block AUC drops — the random split is silently averaging future information into the training set. A time-ordered split reproduces the deployment condition: train on the past, score the future, accept the lower number, and ship a model that behaves the way the number said it would.

# the only split that matches deployment train = df[df.ts < cutoff] test = df[df.ts >= cutoff] # plus an embargo gap if labels arrive late # ^ and every transform fitted inside a Pipeline on train only

The label-availability trap

Chargeback labels arrive 30–90 days after the transaction. If you train on rows whose labels did not exist at prediction time, you have built a model that cannot run. Add an embargo — a gap between the end of train and the start of test at least as long as your label delay — and be able to say the number out loud in an interview, because it is exactly the detail that separates people who have shipped a fraud model from people who have read about one.

Interview point

"For fraud I split on time with an embargo the length of the chargeback window, and I group by entity so retries of the same transaction can't straddle the split. If a change makes my validation AUC jump, my first assumption is leakage, not improvement."

The trap

Leakage is not always a bug in your code — it can live in the data itself. A column like investigation_opened, chargeback_amount or account_closed_reason is generated after the fraud decision and will be a near-perfect predictor of it. The test is not "is this correlated with the target" but "would this value exist, populated, at the moment I need the prediction". Ask that question of every column before it enters the feature set.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define data leakage.

Information in training that would not be available at prediction time, producing validation scores the deployed model cannot reproduce.

Why fit the scaler on train only?

The test mean and variance are future information. Fitting on everything leaks distributional detail into the transform.

When is a random split wrong?

Time-dependent data, grouped/duplicated entities, and anything where the deployment condition is "predict the future from the past".

What is an embargo?

A deliberate gap between train and test periods, sized to the label delay, so you never train on labels that did not exist at prediction time.

Why does target encoding leak?

A category's mean target includes the row's own label. Compute it out-of-fold, with smoothing, inside the CV loop.

Your AUC jumped 0.83 → 0.97 after one feature. First move?

Assume leakage. Check whether that feature is populated at decision time and whether it is derived from the outcome.

What is GroupKFold for?

Keeping all rows of the same entity — user, card, wallet — entirely on one side of the split.

Foundations & data prep · Module A3

Feature ScalingDistance-based and gradient-based models care about units. Trees genuinely do not. Know which is which and why.

"Always scale your features" is advice that is half wrong and taught as a ritual. Scaling is not hygiene — it is a fix for a specific mechanism: any model whose objective contains a distance or a shared step size is sensitive to units, and any model that splits one feature at a time is not. This bench makes that difference measurable rather than memorised.

Units Bench — same data, three model families
real fit + boundary
decision surface drawn in the model's own working space · axes: wallet age (days) vs transaction value

Why the mechanism decides, not the ritual

ModelScale-sensitive?Mechanism
k-NN, k-means, DBSCAN, SVM (RBF)Yes, severelyEuclidean distance. A feature measured in rupees dominates one measured in days by construction
Logistic / linear regression with gradient descentYes, for convergenceOne shared learning rate across coordinates of wildly different curvature — you get a ravine and zig-zag
Ridge / Lasso / any L1–L2 penaltyYes, for correctnessThe penalty is on coefficient magnitude, and magnitude depends on the feature's units. Unscaled, you penalise arbitrarily
PCA, LDAYesMaximises variance; the largest-unit feature captures PC1 regardless of information content
Neural networksYesSame gradient argument, plus saturation of bounded activations at large inputs
Decision tree, random forest, XGBoostNoSplits are ordered comparisons on one feature at a time. Any monotone rescaling gives the identical tree

Set the model to Decision tree and drag the unit mismatch from ×1 to ×1000. The accuracy readout does not move — not approximately, exactly. That is not a quirk to memorise; it is the definition of a rank-based split.

Choosing the scaler

standardise z = (x − μ) / σ default; assumes roughly symmetric spread min-max z = (x − min)/(max − min) bounded [0,1]; one outlier crushes everything else robust z = (x − med) / IQR heavy-tailed data — transaction values, gas fees log1p z = log(1 + x) right-skewed money columns, before any of the above

Push the outlier share slider with min-max selected: a handful of whale transactions compress the entire honest population into the bottom few percent of the range, and k-NN accuracy falls off. Robust scaling holds, because the median and IQR do not care about the tail. For blockchain value columns — which are famously power-law distributed — log1p then standardise is the sane default.

Interview point

"I scale when the model's objective contains a distance or a shared step size — k-NN, SVM, anything penalised, anything gradient-trained. I don't scale for tree ensembles, because axis-aligned splits are invariant to any monotone transform. On transaction values I log first and use robust statistics, since the tail would otherwise define the scale."

The trap

Scaling is a learned transform, so it is subject to the leakage rules from the previous module: fit on train, apply to test, and persist the fitted parameters with the model artifact. The most common production incident here is not statistical at all — it is a training job that standardised with one set of μ/σ and a serving path that recomputed them from the live batch. Same code, different numbers, silent accuracy loss. Put the scaler inside the model artifact, not inside the feature job.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Which models need scaling and why?

Distance-based (k-NN, k-means, RBF SVM), gradient-trained (logistic, NN), and penalised models — distance, shared step size, and magnitude-based penalties all depend on units.

Why are trees exempt?

Splits are ordered threshold comparisons on one feature; any monotone rescaling produces an identical tree.

Standardisation vs normalisation formulas?

z = (x − μ)/σ versus (x − min)/(max − min).

When does min-max fail?

With outliers — the extremes define the range and squash the bulk of the data into a narrow band.

Best treatment for transaction amounts?

log1p to tame the power-law tail, then standardise or robust-scale.

Does scaling change a model's accuracy or just its speed?

Both, depending on the model: for k-NN it changes the answer; for gradient descent it mostly changes how fast — and whether — you reach it.

Where should the fitted scaler live?

Inside the serialised model pipeline, so training and serving cannot drift apart.

Foundations & data prep · Module A4

Missing Data & ImputationThe mechanism behind the hole decides whether filling it fixes your model or biases it.

Every tutorial reaches for fillna(mean). Whether that is harmless or actively destructive depends on why the value is missing — and there are exactly three answers to that question. This bench estimates a known coefficient from data with holes punched in it under each mechanism, so you can watch the bias appear rather than take it on faith.

Imputation Bench — recovering a known coefficient
true β = 2.000
observed rows · imputed rows in gold · true line (teal dashed) vs fitted line (solid)

The three mechanisms

MechanismDefinitionBlockchain exampleCan you fix it?
MCAR — missing completely at randomMissingness independent of everything, observed or notA node dropped a random slice of RPC responsesYes. Dropping is unbiased (just wasteful); mean imputation shrinks variance but not the coefficient
MAR — missing at randomMissingness depends on observed variablesGas price is missing mostly for old blocks, and block age is a column you haveYes, conditionally — model-based imputation using the observed predictors recovers most of it
MNAR — missing not at randomMissingness depends on the unobserved value itselfWallet balance is hidden precisely when it is large; KYC fields blank exactly for the actors avoiding KYCNo, not from the data alone. It needs a model of the missingness or external information

Run MNAR at a 50% missing rate with mean imputation and read the estimated β. It is not noisy around 2.0 — it is systematically wrong, and adding rows does not help, because the bias is in the mechanism rather than the sample size. That is the whole point: more data cures variance, never bias.

Why "missing" is often the most predictive feature you have

Under MNAR the fact of absence carries signal. Select Median + missing flag and watch what happens: the coefficient is still attenuated, but the model now has an explicit indicator column it can use to separate the two populations. In fraud work this is routine — a wallet with no ENS name, no first-seen date, and no counterparty history is not a wallet with average values, it is a fresh wallet, and freshness is one of the strongest single signals in on-chain fraud.

# the pattern that survives contact with production X['gas_missing'] = X['gas_price'].isna().astype('int8') # keep the signal X['gas_price'] = X['gas_price'].fillna(train_median) # fitted on TRAIN only # tree ensembles: consider skipping imputation entirely — # LightGBM and XGBoost learn a default direction for NaN at each split

Interview point

"I ask what generated the hole before I fill it. MCAR is a nuisance, MAR is fixable with model-based imputation, and MNAR is a bias you can't remove from inside the dataset — there I keep a missingness indicator, because absence is itself the feature. On tree ensembles I often don't impute at all and let the learner choose a default direction."

The trap

Mean imputation understates variance by construction: you are piling mass on a single point, which shrinks the standard error and makes coefficients look more significant than they are. If anyone downstream reads a p-value or a confidence interval off that model — and in a regulated bank someone will — the numbers are wrong in the direction that gets a model approved. Multiple imputation exists precisely to restore that uncertainty; single-value imputation never does.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
MCAR, MAR, MNAR in one line each.

MCAR: missingness unrelated to anything. MAR: related to observed columns. MNAR: related to the missing value itself.

When is dropping rows safe?

Under MCAR, and only if you can afford the rows — it is unbiased but throws away information.

Why add a missing-indicator column?

Because absence often carries signal, especially under MNAR, and the flag lets the model use it explicitly.

What is wrong with mean imputation statistically?

It biases the variance downward, distorting standard errors and any inference built on them.

Where must the imputation statistic be fitted?

On the training split only, then applied to validation and test — otherwise it is leakage.

Do XGBoost or LightGBM need imputation?

No — they learn a default branch direction for missing values at each split, which is often better than a fabricated value.

Give an MNAR example from fraud.

Balance or KYC fields that are systematically absent for the very accounts trying not to be measured.

Foundations & data prep · Module A5

Encoding Categorical VariablesOne-hot explodes, ordinal invents an order that isn't there, and target encoding leaks unless you build it inside the fold.

Categoricals are where feature engineering quietly decides your model's ceiling. Merchant id, chain, token contract, counterparty label — high-cardinality columns carrying most of the fraud signal, and every encoding of them trades dimensionality against leakage against information loss. This bench measures all three at once on the same data.

Encoding Bench — features, honest AUC, leaked AUC
real fit, held-out test
per-category fraud rate: raw estimate vs smoothed estimate · bar width ∝ category count

The encodings, and what each one costs

EncodingColumns producedCostsUse when
One-hotk (or k−1)Dimension explosion, sparse matrices, slow trees, memoryLow cardinality (< ~15) and linear models
Ordinal / label1Invents a false ordering — catastrophic for linear and distance models, tolerable for treesGenuinely ordered categories, or tree ensembles
Frequency / count1Collides categories that share a count; loses identityHigh cardinality where popularity is itself the signal
Target / mean encoding1Leaks the label unless computed out-of-fold; unstable for rare categoriesHigh cardinality with real per-category signal — merchant, wallet, contract
Hashingfixed dCollisions, no interpretabilityUnbounded / streaming vocabularies

Push the categories slider to 250 with one-hot selected and read the two numbers that matter: 251 columns against roughly a thousand training rows, and most categories seen fewer than ten times. Each of those columns is a parameter estimated from a handful of observations. Whether that instability shows up as a wider train–test gap depends on how much genuine per-category signal exists — in this generator the extra categories also carry extra signal, which partly masks it. The dimensional cost, though, is unconditional, and it is what kills you on real merchant ids.

Target encoding done properly

Two things make it safe. First, smoothing — a category seen three times should not be trusted at its raw mean:

enc(c) = ( n_c · ȳ_c + m · ȳ_global ) / ( n_c + m ) ^ category mean ^ prior, weighted by m # m large → everything shrinks to the global rate (safe, uninformative) # m = 0 → raw category mean (informative, wildly unstable for rare categories)

Drag the smoothing slider and watch the chart: rare categories snap toward the global rate while frequent ones keep their own estimate. That is exactly the behaviour you want when a merchant has four transactions.

Second, out-of-fold computation. Encode each fold's rows using statistics from the other folds only, so no row ever contributes to its own feature. Switch between Target (whole data) and Target (out-of-fold): the leaked version reports a beautiful number and the honest one reports the truth, and the gap between them is the size of the lie you would have shipped.

Interview point

"For high-cardinality columns like merchant or counterparty wallet I use smoothed target encoding computed out-of-fold, so a category's own rows never contribute to its own feature. Smoothing towards the global rate is what stops a merchant with four transactions from getting a 100% fraud score, and the out-of-fold part is what stops the validation number from being fiction."

The trap

Unseen categories at serving time. Your encoder was fitted on a training vocabulary; production will hand it a merchant that did not exist last month, and a naive lookup either crashes or silently returns NaN. Decide the fallback explicitly — global prior for target encoding, a reserved "unknown" bucket for one-hot — and test it, because on a fresh-wallet-heavy fraud stream the unseen-category rate is not a rounding error, it is a large share of exactly the rows you care about most.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why avoid label encoding for linear models?

It imposes an arbitrary numeric order and spacing on unordered categories, which the model then takes literally.

What breaks with one-hot at high cardinality?

Dimensionality and sparsity — memory, training time, and weak per-column signal; trees in particular split poorly on thousands of sparse binaries.

Write the smoothed target-encoding formula.

(n_c·ȳ_c + m·ȳ_global)/(n_c + m), where m controls shrinkage toward the prior.

How do you stop target encoding leaking?

Compute it out-of-fold inside the CV loop, and refit on the full training set only for the final model.

What is the drop-first / k−1 column convention for?

Avoiding perfect multicollinearity with the intercept in linear models. Trees don't need it.

When would you hash instead?

Streaming or unbounded vocabularies where you cannot hold a fitted mapping and can tolerate collisions.

Serving sees an unknown category. What happens?

Whatever you specified — global prior or an explicit unknown bucket. If you didn't specify it, you have a production incident waiting.

Foundations & data prep · Module A6

The Curse of DimensionalityIn high dimensions everything is far away, everything is equally far away, and "nearest neighbour" stops meaning anything.

This is the reason k-NN dies, RBF kernels need tuning, clustering gets unstable, and adding "just a few more features" makes a model worse. It is not folklore — the distance concentration is a measurable geometric fact, and this bench measures it on real sampled points.

Distance Concentration Bench
sampled, not simulated
left: distribution of pairwise distances · right: contrast ratio and k-NN accuracy as d grows

The three facts that make high dimensions hostile

1. Distances concentrate

For many distributions the ratio of the farthest to the nearest neighbour distance tends to 1 as d grows. The bench reports it live as contrast. At d = 2 it is comfortably above 3; by d = 100 it is close to 1, meaning every point is roughly the same distance from every other point. "Nearest" survives as an arithmetic result but stops carrying information — and every distance-based algorithm you own is built on the assumption that it does.

2. Volume flees to the shell

The fraction of a unit ball's volume lying within the outer 10% of its radius is 1 − 0.9^d: 19% at d = 2, 65% at d = 10, over 99.99% at d = 100. Nearly all your data sits near the boundary of the space, and the "centre" — where your intuition puts the typical point — is empty.

3. Sample density collapses exponentially

To keep the same average number of points per unit hypercube, n must grow like b^d. Ten points per axis in one dimension is 10; in ten dimensions it is 1010. This is why "just add features" quietly stops working: each new feature multiplies the volume the same fixed sample has to cover.

Where it bites, and what actually helps

Affected by itLargely resistant
k-NN, k-means, DBSCAN, RBF SVM, any Euclidean methodTree ensembles — they select features rather than measuring across all of them
Density estimation, kernel methods, Gaussian mixturesLinear models with strong L1 regularisation, which zero out noise dimensions
Naive distance-based anomaly detectionLearned representations that project to a low-dimensional manifold

Select 2-D signal + noise dims: the label depends only on the first two coordinates and every extra dimension is pure noise. Watch k-NN accuracy slide from the mid-nineties at d = 2 into the low sixties by d = 200 — most of the way to the 50% chance line — while the information content of the data has not changed by a single bit. That is the mechanism behind "feature selection improved my model" — you did not add signal, you removed the noise that was diluting the metric.

Now compare it with Uniform cube at the same d, where the label depends on every coordinate. Accuracy there is no better — in this bench it is slightly worse. That is the result people get wrong: informative dimensions do not rescue a distance-based model, because what k-NN needs is a neighbourhood, and at d = 200 there isn't one. The saving grace is that real data rarely fills its ambient dimension. Images, text embeddings, and transaction feature vectors lie on much lower-dimensional manifolds, which is exactly why PCA, autoencoders and embedding methods work at all. High ambient dimension is survivable; high intrinsic dimension is not.

Interview point

"In high dimensions the ratio between the farthest and nearest neighbour tends to one, so distance-based methods lose their discriminative power — that's why k-NN and RBF kernels degrade while tree ensembles hold up. The practical answer is intrinsic dimension: real data lives on a manifold, so I reduce or embed before I let anything measure a distance."

The trap

"Curse of dimensionality" gets used as a blanket argument against adding features. It is not. Adding an informative feature is almost always positive; the curse applies to adding uninformative ones, and to distance-based methods specifically. Notice also that this module runs on i.i.d. sampled points — the concentration result is a property of the sampling distribution, and correlated features have a lower intrinsic dimension than their column count suggests, so the effect arrives later than the raw d would predict.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State the curse of dimensionality in one sentence.

As dimensions grow, data becomes sparse and pairwise distances concentrate, so distance-based methods lose discriminative power and the sample size needed grows exponentially.

What happens to the nearest/farthest distance ratio?

It tends toward 1 — every point becomes approximately equidistant from every other.

Which models are least affected?

Tree ensembles and strongly L1-regularised linear models, because they select features rather than aggregating distance across all of them.

What fraction of a unit ball is in the outer 10% shell at d=100?

1 − 0.9¹⁰⁰, which is above 99.99% — essentially all of it.

Ambient vs intrinsic dimension?

Ambient is the number of columns; intrinsic is the dimension of the manifold the data actually occupies. Only the second one hurts.

Three practical mitigations?

Feature selection, dimensionality reduction or learned embeddings, and switching to models that are not distance-based.

Why does adding noise features hurt k-NN so much?

Each noise dimension contributes variance to every distance, diluting the contribution of the informative dimensions until the ranking of neighbours is essentially random.

Track B · Regression · Module B1

OLS & the Normal EquationsThe closed form, what it assumes, and the single point that can rotate the whole line.

Linear regression is the only model in this bench with an exact answer — no iterations, no learning rate, one matrix inversion. That makes it the right place to see what a fit is: a projection of y onto the space your columns can reach. It is also the model whose failure modes are easiest to see, which is why every diagnostic you will use later was invented here.

Least squares bench
closed-form solve
fit view: data, the fitted line and every residual · diagnostics: residuals against fitted values, where structure becomes visible

The closed form

minimise ‖y − Xβ‖² → Xᵀ(y − Xβ) = 0 → β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy ŷ = X β̂ = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ y = H y H is the hat matrix: a projection residuals e = y − ŷ are orthogonal to every column of X — by construction

That orthogonality is the entire idea. The fit is the point in the column space of X closest to y, so whatever is left over carries no linear information about your features. It also explains why residual plots are the diagnostic of choice: if you can still see structure in the residuals, your columns did not span it.

The five assumptions, and which ones matter

AssumptionBroken byWhat actually breaks
Linearity in the parametersCurvature in the true relationshipThe fit itself — this is the one that matters most
Independent errorsTime series, grouped rows, retriesStandard errors, not the coefficients
Constant error varianceHeteroscedasticity (spread grows with x)Standard errors and prediction intervals
No perfect collinearityDuplicate or derived columnsXᵀX becomes singular; coefficients are undefined (module B3)
Normal errorsSkew, outliersOnly small-sample inference — the point estimate is still BLUE

Notice how few of them damage the predictions. Independence and normality mostly affect the uncertainty you report, which matters enormously in a model-risk review and not at all in a ranking task.

Leverage: one point, one lever

Push the leverage slider out to x = 12 and give it a y offset. A point far out along x has high leverage — the hat matrix gives it a large diagonal element, meaning the fitted line is heavily obliged to pass near it. Combine high leverage with a large residual and you get an influential point: it does not just sit badly, it rotates the entire line. Watch R² while you do it: a high-leverage point that happens to follow the trend inflates R² (0.48 → 0.61 in the default configuration) without the model having learned anything, while one with a large residual craters it. In neither case is R² telling you what you want to know. Leverage is about x alone; influence is leverage times residual, which is what Cook's distance measures.

Interview point

"OLS has a closed form, β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, and it's a projection — residuals are orthogonal to the columns by construction, which is why residual plots are the first diagnostic I run. The assumption I actually worry about is linearity; independence and normality mostly affect the standard errors, not the point estimate. And I check leverage separately from residual size, because influence is the product of the two."

The trap

Nobody inverts XᵀX in production, and you should not say you do. Numerically the inverse is unstable when columns are near-collinear; real implementations use a QR or SVD decomposition, which is why scikit-learn's LinearRegression quietly returns an answer on rank-deficient data instead of failing — it takes the minimum-norm solution via the pseudo-inverse. Also: R² never decreases when you add a column, even a column of pure noise. Quote adjusted R² or an out-of-sample score, never R² on training data as evidence a feature helped.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write the OLS solution.

β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, the minimiser of the squared residual norm.

Why are residuals orthogonal to the features?

Because the fit is the projection of y onto the column space of X — anything correlated with a column would have been absorbed into the fit.

Which OLS assumption matters most for prediction?

Linearity in the parameters. Independence and normality mainly affect inference.

Leverage vs influence?

Leverage depends only on how extreme x is; influence combines leverage with the size of the residual — Cook's distance measures it.

What is heteroscedasticity and what does it break?

Non-constant error variance; it invalidates standard errors and prediction intervals while leaving the coefficients unbiased.

Why does R² never go down when you add a feature?

The extra column can only expand the space being projected onto. Use adjusted R² or a held-out score.

How is OLS actually solved in a library?

By QR or SVD decomposition, not by forming an explicit inverse — it is numerically far more stable.

Track B · Regression · Module B2

Gradient DescentWhy the learning rate has a hard ceiling, why unscaled features zig-zag, and what momentum is actually doing.

Once a model has no closed form — and everything after this module does — you are optimising. Gradient descent is the whole family in one idea: step downhill, repeatedly. Its three failure modes are so consistent that recognising them from a loss curve alone is a genuine interview skill. This bench runs real descent on a real quadratic surface and draws the path.

Descent bench
real steps on a real surface
left: the loss surface in coefficient space with the descent path · right: loss against step number, log scale

The update, and the ceiling on η

β ← β − η ∇L(β) ∇L = −(2/n) Xᵀ(y − Xβ) for squared loss For a quadratic loss the iteration is stable only while η < 2 / λ_max(∇²L) λ_max = largest curvature Above that the step overshoots further than it descends and the loss grows.

The bench prints the curvature and the implied maximum learning rate. Push η past it and the loss curve turns upward within a handful of steps — not slowly, exponentially. This is why "the loss went to NaN" is nearly always a learning-rate problem and almost never a data problem.

Conditioning: the zig-zag

Drag feature scale ratio up so one column is a hundred times larger than the other. The loss surface stops being a bowl and becomes a ravine: curvature along one axis is enormous, along the other almost flat. A single shared η must be small enough for the steep direction, which makes it hopelessly slow in the flat one — so the path oscillates across the valley while barely advancing along it. The governing quantity is the condition number κ = λ_max/λ_min, and the number of steps to converge scales roughly with it.

That is the real reason to standardise features before gradient-based training, and it is a better answer than "because the library says so". It is also why Adam and friends exist: per-parameter step sizes are an attempt to fix conditioning without knowing the Hessian.

Symptom on the loss curveCauseFix
Rises, then explodes to NaNη above the stability ceilingLower η; add gradient clipping
Falls fast, then flat and highBad conditioning, or a real local floorStandardise features; try momentum or Adam
Noisy but trending downMini-batch sampling noiseNormal — larger batch or decayed η near the end
Flat from step oneη far too small, or dead gradientsRaise η; check for saturated activations (H4)

Interview point

"Batch GD is exact but O(n) per step; SGD is noisy but cheap, and the noise itself helps escape saddle points. The learning rate is bounded above by 2/λ_max — past it you diverge — and how many steps you need scales with the condition number, which is precisely why I standardise features before any gradient-trained model."

The trap

For squared loss on a linear model the surface is convex, so there are no local minima to get stuck in — if someone says their linear regression converged to a local optimum, something else is wrong. Non-convexity arrives with neural networks, and even there the practical obstacle is saddle points and plateaus rather than bad local minima. Second trap: mini-batch loss curves look worse than batch curves at equal step counts, which tempts people to "fix" the noise. Compare on wall-clock or epochs, not on steps, or you will conclude the slower method is better.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write the gradient descent update.

β ← β − η∇L(β): step against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate.

What bounds the learning rate?

Stability requires η < 2/λ_max, where λ_max is the largest curvature of the loss.

Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch?

Batch uses all rows per step (exact, expensive); SGD uses one (noisy, cheap); mini-batch is the practical compromise and vectorises well.

Why does scaling speed up convergence?

It lowers the condition number, so a single shared step size suits every direction instead of being throttled by the steepest one.

What does momentum do?

Accumulates an exponentially weighted average of past gradients, damping oscillation across a ravine and accelerating along it.

Is linear regression's loss convex?

Yes — squared loss on a linear model is convex, so any minimum is global.

Loss went to NaN. First check?

Learning rate, then unscaled features, then exploding gradients — in that order.

Track B · Regression · Module B3

Multicollinearity & VIFCorrelated features destroy your coefficients while leaving your predictions untouched. Know which of the two you were selling.

Add amount and amount_usd to the same regression and something strange happens: the fit is fine, R² is fine, and the coefficients are nonsense — huge, unstable, occasionally the wrong sign. This bench resamples the same population two hundred times and plots where the coefficients land, so you can watch the instability directly rather than infer it from a VIF table.

Collinearity bench
200 bootstrap refits
left: where β₁ and β₂ land across 200 resamples, with the true value marked · right: VIF and prediction R² as ρ rises

What VIF measures

VIF_j = 1 / (1 − R²_j) R²_j from regressing feature j on all the OTHERS VIF 1 → orthogonal VIF 5 → ρ ≈ 0.89 VIF 10 → ρ ≈ 0.95 the usual alarm threshold VIF 100 → ρ ≈ 0.995 — the coefficient standard error is 10× inflated

The name is literal: VIF is the factor by which the variance of a coefficient estimate is multiplied. It says nothing about bias — OLS stays unbiased under collinearity — and nothing about prediction. It is purely a statement about how much your coefficient will move if you had collected a slightly different sample.

The distinction that matters

Watch the two panels as you raise ρ. The coefficient cloud stretches into a long diagonal ridge — β₁ and β₂ trade off almost one-for-one, because only their sum is identified by the data — while prediction R² barely moves. That is the whole lesson:

  • If you are predicting, collinearity is close to harmless. The model does not care which of two redundant columns carries the weight.
  • If you are explaining — a credit model that must produce reason codes, a risk model facing a validation team, any coefficient you plan to quote — collinearity is fatal. "Transaction count reduces fraud risk" is the kind of sign flip it manufactures, and it will not survive a model-risk review.

Raise ridge λ and the cloud contracts toward the truth. That is regularisation buying stability with a little bias, and it is the cleanest illustration of the bias–variance trade from A1 you will see in a linear model.

Interview point

"Collinearity inflates coefficient variance without biasing predictions — VIF = 1/(1−R²_j) tells you the inflation factor, and I act above about 5 to 10. Whether I care at all depends on the job: for a pure ranking model I usually don't; for anything that has to produce an explanation or a reason code, unstable coefficients mean unstable explanations, so I drop, combine, or ridge them."

The trap

Two common misreadings. First, a high VIF is not automatically a problem to fix — dummy variables from one categorical are collinear by construction, and polynomial terms always are; that is structural, not pathological. Second, dropping the "redundant" column changes the meaning of the one you kept: it now absorbs the effect of both, so its coefficient is no longer the partial effect you were trying to report. And centring features before creating interaction or squared terms removes a large part of the collinearity for free — it is the cheapest fix on the list.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define VIF.

1/(1−R²_j), where R²_j comes from regressing feature j on all the other features. It is the inflation factor on that coefficient's variance.

Does collinearity bias OLS?

No — estimates stay unbiased. It inflates their variance.

Does it hurt predictions?

Barely, as long as the correlation structure holds at serving time. It hurts interpretation.

Typical VIF threshold?

5 to 10, depending on the field — but the decision should be driven by whether you need to interpret the coefficients.

Three fixes.

Drop or combine the redundant columns, centre before forming interactions, or regularise with ridge.

Why does ridge help here?

The penalty makes XᵀX + λI well conditioned, shrinking the ridge of near-equivalent solutions to a single stable point.

Perfect collinearity — what happens?

XᵀX is singular and the coefficients are not identified; libraries fall back to a pseudo-inverse and return an arbitrary minimum-norm solution.

Track B · Regression · Module B4

Polynomial Regression & Basis ExpansionLinear models can fit curves. What they cannot do is leave the range they were trained on.

"Linear regression" means linear in the parameters, not in the features — square a column and you have a curve while keeping the closed form from B1 intact. That is the cheapest capacity upgrade in machine learning. It also imports two problems that A1's bias–variance view does not show you: catastrophic extrapolation, and a design matrix whose condition number explodes with degree.

Basis bench
polynomial vs spline · in-range and beyond
shaded band is the training range · everything outside it is extrapolation, and the fit was never asked to behave there

In-range fit versus out-of-range behaviour

The two RMSE readouts are computed on different regions: inside the training range, and in the extrapolation band beyond it. Raise the degree and watch them diverge — in-range error falls while out-of-range error rises by orders of magnitude. A degree-12 polynomial is a perfectly good interpolator and a catastrophic extrapolator, because outside the data the highest-order term dominates and drives the curve to ±∞.

Switch the basis to piecewise linear. The in-range fit is comparable, and beyond the data the fit continues along the last segment's slope instead of exploding. This is why splines, and natural splines in particular — which are constrained to be linear beyond the boundary knots — are the standard choice in statistics for exactly this job.

Conditioning

design columns [1, x, x², x³, …] on x ∈ [0,10]: column ranges 1 … 10 … 100 … 1000 … → XᵀX condition number grows explosively with degree → coefficients become huge and cancel each other to produce a small fit

The bench prints the condition number of XᵀX. The fix is standard and worth naming: orthogonal polynomials (numpy's Polynomial.fit, R's poly()) construct an equivalent basis whose columns are uncorrelated, giving the identical fitted curve with stable coefficients. If you must use raw powers, centre and scale x first.

MethodExtrapolates asUse when
Raw polynomial, low degreeExplodes with the leading termYou genuinely believe the relationship is polynomial
Natural cubic splineLinearly beyond the boundary knotsSmooth non-linearity, safe boundaries — the sensible default
Binning / step functionsFlatYou want monotone, auditable buckets — common in credit scoring
Tree ensemblesFlat, at the boundary leaf valueSee B7 — the same limitation, less obvious

Interview point

"Polynomial regression is still a linear model — linear in the parameters — so it keeps the closed form. What I watch is extrapolation: outside the training range the highest-order term takes over and the prediction is meaningless, so I prefer natural splines, which are constrained to stay linear past the boundary knots. And I use an orthogonal basis, because raw powers make XᵀX badly conditioned."

The trap

The dangerous version of this is not a chart that looks silly — it is a production model quietly extrapolating. Fraud features drift: transaction values inflate, gas fees spike, a new merchant category arrives with volumes outside anything in training. Nothing raises an alarm, the model returns a number, and that number came from a region the fit never constrained. Monitor feature ranges at serving time as well as feature distributions, and consider clipping inputs to the training range and flagging the rows where you had to.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Is polynomial regression a linear model?

Yes — linear in the parameters. The non-linearity lives in the features.

Why is extrapolation dangerous with polynomials?

Beyond the data the highest-power term dominates and drives predictions toward ±∞.

What is a natural spline?

A piecewise cubic constrained to be linear beyond the boundary knots, which makes its extrapolation behave.

Why use orthogonal polynomials?

Raw powers are highly collinear and make XᵀX ill-conditioned; an orthogonal basis gives the same fit with stable coefficients.

How do you choose the degree or the knots?

Cross-validation, not the in-sample fit — and prefer knots at quantiles of x rather than evenly spaced.

What happens to a tree ensemble outside the training range?

It predicts a constant — the boundary leaf value. Safer than a polynomial, still not informative.

How do you detect extrapolation in production?

Monitor the range and distribution of incoming features against training, and flag or clip rows that fall outside.

Track B · Regression · Module B5

Ridge, Lasso & ElasticNetTwo penalties, two completely different behaviours, and one geometric reason why.

Regularisation is the standard answer to variance, but ridge and lasso are not interchangeable strengths of the same idea. One shrinks every coefficient toward zero; the other sets some of them exactly to zero and performs feature selection as a side effect. This bench runs real coordinate descent across a grid of λ and draws the coefficient paths, so you can watch selection happen.

Penalty bench
coordinate descent · 24 features, 5 real
left: coefficient paths as λ grows — true features in teal, noise features in grey · right: held-out RMSE against λ

Why L1 selects and L2 does not

ridge minimise ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖² constraint region = a circle lasso minimise ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖₁ constraint region = a diamond

The elliptical contours of the squared-error loss expand until they first touch the constraint region. A diamond has corners, and its corners sit on the axes — so the touch point lands on an axis, which means some coordinate is exactly zero. A circle has no corners, so the touch point is generically off-axis and every coefficient stays non-zero, merely smaller. That is the entire explanation, and it is worth being able to draw.

The same shows up in the update rule: the lasso's coordinate step is a soft threshold, sign(ρ)·max(|ρ|−λ, 0), which literally clips small correlations to zero. Ridge divides by (1+λ), which never reaches zero however large λ gets.

Reading the paths

Slide λ from left to right on the lasso. Noise features drop out first — their marginal correlation with y cannot pay the penalty — while the five real features survive until λ becomes large. The readouts count true and false selections, so you can find the λ where selection is cleanest and compare it to the λ that minimises held-out error. They are usually not the same point, which is the practical reason the 1-SE rule exists: pick the simplest model within one standard error of the best.

Now press Make the real features near-duplicates. Lasso arbitrarily keeps one of each correlated pair and zeroes the other, and which one it keeps changes with the sample. ElasticNet, which adds a little L2 to the L1, keeps them together — the "grouping effect" — and that stability is normally worth more than the extra sparsity.

RidgeLassoElasticNet
Coefficients hit exactly zeroNoYesYes
Correlated predictorsShares weight between themPicks one arbitrarilyKeeps the group
p ≫ nWorks, keeps all pSelects at most n featuresCan exceed n
Closed formYes — (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹XᵀyNo — coordinate descent or LARSNo

Interview point

"L1 has corners on the axes, so the solution lands on them and coefficients go exactly to zero — that's the geometry behind lasso doing feature selection while ridge only shrinks. With correlated features lasso picks one at random and the choice flips between samples, so when I need stable selection I use ElasticNet for the grouping effect. And both penalties require standardised features, or you're penalising units rather than importance."

The trap

Never penalise the intercept, and never regularise unstandardised features — the penalty is on coefficient magnitude, and magnitude depends on the units of the column, so a feature measured in rupees gets shrunk harder than the same feature measured in lakhs. Second: lasso is a selection heuristic, not a significance test. Selected does not mean causal, and post-selection inference on lasso-chosen features is invalid unless you use methods designed for it. Quoting a p-value on a coefficient the lasso just picked is one of the most common ways a model fails a validation review.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why does L1 produce exact zeros and L2 not?

The L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes, so the loss contours touch it at a corner. The L2 region is a circle with no corners.

Ridge's closed form?

β̂ = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy — always invertible for λ > 0, which is why ridge also fixes collinearity.

What does lasso do with two near-identical features?

Keeps one, zeroes the other, and the choice is unstable across samples.

When do you reach for ElasticNet?

Correlated predictors, or p ≫ n where lasso can select at most n features.

How do you choose λ?

Cross-validation, often with the 1-SE rule: the simplest model within one standard error of the best.

Must features be standardised?

Yes — otherwise the penalty depends on units rather than on the strength of the relationship.

Does regularisation raise or lower bias?

Raises bias, lowers variance — the same trade as A1, bought deliberately.

Track B · Regression · Module B6

Support Vector RegressionA loss function with a dead zone: errors smaller than ε cost nothing at all.

SVR inverts the usual idea. Instead of minimising every residual, it draws a tube of width ε around the fit and charges nothing for points inside it — only the points that escape the tube contribute anything, and those are the support vectors.
