That single change buys sparsity, robustness to small noise, and a natural way to plug in kernels.

ε-tube bench
subgradient descent · 40 random Fourier features
the ε-tube is shaded · points outside it are support vectors and are the only rows with a non-zero gradient · both losses are scored against the noiseless truth, not against the contaminated y

The loss

ε-insensitive loss: L(e) = max(0, |e| − ε) |e| ≤ ε → zero loss, zero gradient — the point is invisible to the fit |e| > ε → linear in the excess — not squared, so outliers pull, but only linearly objective: ½‖w‖² + C · Σ max(0, |eᵢ| − ε) ^ flatness ^ tolerance for the points that escape

Compare that with OLS from B1, where every point contributes and the contribution grows quadratically. Two consequences follow immediately. Small noise costs nothing, so the fit is not dragged around by rows that are already "close enough". And large errors are charged linearly rather than quadratically, so a single outlier has far less leverage than it does under squared loss — the same robustness argument as MAE in S5, with a dead zone added.

The trade, measured

Run the RBF basis with no outliers and read the two error columns: least squares wins, 0.057 against 0.098. That is not a bug — under clean Gaussian noise least squares is the maximum-likelihood estimator (S5), so nothing should beat it. Now push the outlier share to 12%: least squares degrades to 0.316 while the ε-tube holds at 0.124, roughly two and a half times better. Both numbers are measured against the noiseless truth on the same basis, so the only thing that changed is the loss. That is the entire case for SVR in one comparison — you give up efficiency on clean data to buy resistance to contamination.

ε and C, and what they trade

Drag ε up: the tube widens, the support-vector count falls, and the fit becomes flatter and less responsive. Drag C up: escaping the tube becomes expensive, so the fit contorts to pull points back inside — that is the regularisation knob, and C is inversely related to the λ from B5. The readouts count support vectors, so you can watch sparsity appear and disappear.

KnobRaise it and…Failure at the extreme
εFewer support vectors, flatter fit, more biasTube swallows the signal; the model predicts a constant
CTighter fit to escaping points, less regularisationOverfits noise and outliers
γ (RBF)Narrower kernel, more local wiggleEach point gets its own bump — memorisation

The kernel option here uses 40 random Fourier features, which approximates an RBF kernel rather than solving the exact dual — that is labelled in the panel because it matters: a real SVR solves a quadratic program and gets exact sparsity in the dual, while this approximation gets the shape and the intuition at a fraction of the cost.

Interview point

"SVR uses an ε-insensitive loss, so residuals inside the tube contribute nothing and the solution depends only on the support vectors outside it. That gives sparsity and robustness — errors are charged linearly, not squared. In practice I rarely reach for it on tabular data because gradient boosting is stronger and scales better; SVR is O(n²)–O(n³) in the number of rows."

The trap

SVR needs scaled features and scaled targets, for two separate reasons: the kernel measures distance in feature space, and ε is measured in the units of y. An ε of 0.1 means something completely different on a target in rupees than on a standardised one, so a default ε with an unscaled target is either a dead zone that swallows everything or one that does nothing. And be honest about the cost: kernel SVR does not scale past tens of thousands of rows, which for a transaction stream rules it out of the hot path regardless of accuracy.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is the ε-insensitive loss?

max(0, |e| − ε): zero cost for residuals inside the tube, linear cost outside it.

What is a support vector in SVR?

A training point lying on or outside the tube — the only rows that influence the solution.

What do ε and C control?

ε sets tube width and therefore sparsity and bias; C sets how expensive it is to sit outside the tube — it is the inverse of a regularisation strength.

Why is SVR more robust than OLS?

Errors are penalised linearly beyond the tube instead of quadratically, so extreme points exert far less leverage.

Why scale the target?

ε lives in the units of y, so an unscaled target makes the default ε meaningless.

What is the kernel trick, in one line?

Replace inner products with a kernel function so the model fits in a high-dimensional feature space without ever computing the coordinates.

Why is SVR uncommon on large tabular data?

Training cost scales quadratically to cubically in rows, and boosted trees usually beat it anyway.

Track B · Regression · Module B7

Tree & Forest RegressionA staircase, not a line — and averaging many bad staircases into one good surface.

A regression tree predicts the mean of a leaf, so its output is piecewise constant: a staircase. That buys non-linearity and interactions for free, with no scaling and no functional form to specify, and it costs you smoothness and extrapolation entirely. A forest fixes the variance by averaging decorrelated trees — this bench grows them one at a time so you can watch the test error fall and then stop falling.

Tree & forest bench
real CART splits · real bagging
left: the fitted step function against the true curve, with the extrapolation region shaded · right: test RMSE as trees are added

How a split is chosen

for every feature, for every candidate threshold: SSE = Σ_left (y − ȳ_left)² + Σ_right (y − ȳ_right)² choose the split with the lowest SSE variance reduction, greedily recurse until max_depth / min_samples_leaf / no improvement predict the mean of the leaf

Greedy is the operative word: each split is chosen without regard to what a later split might have made possible, which is why trees are unstable — a small change in the data can flip the top split and rewrite the entire structure below it. That instability is a defect in a single tree and the raw material for a forest.

What bagging actually buys

Switch to Random forest and pull the tree count up from 1. Test RMSE drops steeply and then flattens. The mechanism is variance averaging: if each tree has error variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ between trees, the average has variance

Var(average of T trees) = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/T ^ this term never goes away, no matter how many trees

More trees only shrink the second term — which is why a forest cannot overfit by adding trees, and also why it plateaus. To do better you must lower ρ, and that is exactly what random feature selection at each split is for: it forces trees to disagree. Bagging alone (bootstrap rows only) leaves the trees far too similar, because they all find the same dominant split first.

KnobEffectOverfit risk
max_depth ↑Finer staircase, lower biasHigh — the main overfit control
min_samples_leaf ↑Smoother, fewer leavesLowers it; often more effective than capping depth
n_estimators ↑Lower variance, plateausNone — only compute
max_features ↓Trees decorrelateLowers variance, raises individual-tree bias

Interview point

"Trees split greedily on variance reduction and predict the leaf mean, so the output is piecewise constant — no scaling needed, interactions for free, and no extrapolation at all. A forest reduces variance by averaging decorrelated trees; the residual variance term is ρσ², so past a certain point extra trees buy nothing and the lever is decorrelation, which is what max_features controls."

The trap

Trees cannot extrapolate — beyond the training range every prediction is the boundary leaf's mean, a flat line. The shaded region in the bench makes this visible, and in production it is invisible: a forest trained on last year's transaction values will simply cap its predictions when values inflate, with no error and no warning. Second trap: default impurity-based feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features, and it is computed on training data. Use permutation importance on a held-out set, or SHAP (module G5), before you show anyone a ranked feature list.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What criterion does a regression tree split on?

Reduction in sum of squared error — equivalently, variance reduction — chosen greedily.

Why is a single deep tree high-variance?

Greedy splits mean a small change in the sample can change the top split and restructure everything beneath it.

What does bagging reduce, bias or variance?

Variance. Bias is roughly unchanged, since each tree is grown deep.

Why does random feature selection help?

It decorrelates the trees, shrinking the ρσ² floor that averaging alone cannot touch.

Can a random forest overfit by adding trees?

No — more trees only reduce variance. Overfitting comes from depth and leaf size.

What happens outside the training range?

The prediction is constant at the boundary leaf value; trees do not extrapolate.

What is out-of-bag error?

Each tree's error on the roughly one third of rows its bootstrap sample omitted — a free validation estimate.

Track B · Regression · Module B8

Regression MetricsTwo models, five metrics, and a ranking that flips depending on which one you quote.

Every regression metric is a summary of the same residuals, so it is tempting to assume they broadly agree. They do not. This bench scores two genuinely different models — one that tracks the bulk of the data and one that chases the tail — and shows the leaderboard reordering as you switch metrics. Choosing the metric is choosing the winner.

Metric bench
same residuals, five scores
left: both models against the truth · right: each metric, normalised so the better model is the shorter bar

What each one is really asking

MetricFormulaAnswersBreaks on
RMSE√(mean e²)Typical error, with big misses punished hardOutliers dominate it; same units as y
MAEmean |e|Typical error, all misses equalIndifferent to a catastrophic single miss
MAPEmean |e/y|Relative errorExplodes near y = 0; asymmetric — over-prediction is unbounded, under-prediction caps at 100%
R²1 − SSE/SSTShare of variance explained vs predicting the meanCan be negative; rises with any added feature; depends on the spread of your test set
RMSLE√(mean (log1p ŷ − log1p y)²)Relative error, symmetric in ratioNeeds non-negative y; penalises under-prediction more

Switch the data to Near-zero values present and watch MAPE. It does not degrade gracefully — a handful of rows with y near zero send it to absurd values, and any leaderboard built on it is then decided by those few rows. That is not a rare edge case in fraud work: transaction counts, exposure amounts and loss values legitimately sit at or near zero.

The ranking flip

The two models here are deliberately different animals. Model A is a bulk specialist: near-exact on ordinary rows, and increasingly wrong on the top 5% of the target. Model B is a generalist: a little wrong on every row, unbiased on the tail. Push the tail miss slider and A's rare large errors grow. RMSE — which squares residuals — starts preferring B, while MAE, which weights every unit of error alike, still prefers A because A is better on 95% of the rows. Neither metric is wrong; they encode different beliefs about what a miss costs. The honest move is to state that belief before scoring: if a ₹500,000 miss is a hundred times worse than a ₹5,000 miss, say so and use a metric that agrees, rather than picking whichever number makes the new model look good.

R² deserves one specific warning: it is relative to the variance of your test set, so the same model scores differently on a homogeneous population than on a diverse one. Comparing R² across datasets, teams or time periods is meaningless unless the target spread is the same.

Interview point

"RMSE and MAE encode different cost assumptions — RMSE squares, so it cares disproportionately about big misses, and it will rank models differently from MAE. I avoid MAPE anywhere the target can approach zero, since it blows up and is asymmetric between over- and under-prediction. And I don't compare R² across datasets, because it's measured against that dataset's own variance."

The trap

The metric you optimise and the metric you report should be the same one, and both should be the one the business feels. A model trained on MSE and reported on MAE has been tuned for a cost structure nobody agreed to. Worse, in a fraud setting the quantity that matters is usually neither — it is expected loss in currency, weighted by exposure, which means the right evaluation is often a cost-weighted error or the threshold analysis from D3 rather than any of the five metrics above. Always ask what a unit of error costs before choosing how to measure it.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
RMSE vs MAE — when do they disagree?

When the error distribution has a heavy tail: RMSE squares residuals, so a few large misses dominate it, while MAE treats every unit of error alike.

Why avoid MAPE?

It is undefined at y = 0, explodes nearby, and is asymmetric — under-prediction is capped at 100% while over-prediction is unbounded.

Can R² be negative?

Yes — it means the model is worse than predicting the mean of the target.

Why can't you compare R² across datasets?

It is normalised by that dataset's own variance, so a wider target spread inflates it for the same absolute error.

What is adjusted R² for?

Penalising extra features, since plain R² never decreases when you add one.

When is RMSLE appropriate?

Non-negative, right-skewed targets where relative error matters and under-prediction is the costlier direction.

Which metric for a fraud-loss model?

Usually none of the standard five — a cost-weighted error in currency, since a unit of error on a large exposure is not worth the same as on a small one.

Track C · Classification · Module C1

Logistic Regression & Log-LossThe workhorse of regulated credit and fraud scoring — because it produces a probability you can defend.

Logistic regression survives in banking not because it is the most accurate model available but because every coefficient is a log-odds you can quote, the output is a calibrated probability by construction, and the loss it minimises is the Bernoulli likelihood from S5. This bench fits it by real gradient descent and shows you the one input that breaks it completely.

Logistic bench
batch GD · log-loss
feature space: data and the p = 0.5 boundary · calibration: predicted probability against observed frequency, in deciles

From linear score to probability

z = β₀ + β·x the log-odds, unbounded p = σ(z) = 1/(1+e^−z) squashed into (0,1) log-loss = −(1/n) Σ [ y log p + (1−y) log(1−p) ] = the Bernoulli NLL (S5) odds ratio for feature j = e^βⱼ the number a risk committee will ask for

A coefficient of 0.7 means the odds of fraud multiply by e^0.7 ≈ 2.0 for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding the others fixed. That sentence is why the model persists: it converts directly into a reason code, and the whole apparatus of adverse-action notices and model documentation is built around being able to say it.

Log-loss is a proper scoring rule — it is minimised only by reporting your true belief. Accuracy is not: a model can improve accuracy by becoming more confident on the cases it already got right, which is exactly the pathology that ruins expected-cost calculations (D3). Switch to the calibration view and watch the decile points sit on the diagonal; that alignment is the property you are paying for.

Perfect separation: the failure nobody warns you about

Press Perfectly separable data. The classes no longer overlap, so likelihood keeps increasing as the coefficients grow — pushing every predicted probability toward 0 or 1 buys a little more likelihood forever. The maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist; the coefficients diverge and the standard errors explode. The bench prints the coefficient norm so you can watch it climb with the step count.

In practice you meet this with a leaked feature, a near-duplicate of the label, or a rare category that happens to be pure in your sample. The fix is regularisation — raise the L2 penalty and the norm settles immediately — which is why scikit-learn's LogisticRegression applies L2 by default, a decision that surprises people who expect an unpenalised fit.

PropertyLogistic regressionGradient boosting
Calibrated out of the boxYes — it minimises the Bernoulli NLLNo — needs Platt or isotonic (D6)
Coefficient interpretationLog-odds, directly quotableSHAP or partial dependence only
Non-linearity & interactionsMust be engineered in by handLearned automatically
Monotonicity constraintsTrivial — sign of the coefficientSupported, but a configuration step
Typical fraud AUCGood baselineUsually several points better

Interview point

"Logistic regression optimises the Bernoulli likelihood, so log-loss isn't an arbitrary metric — it's the negative log-likelihood, and it's a proper scoring rule, which is why the outputs are calibrated without post-processing. In a regulated setting that matters more than a point of AUC: e^β is an odds ratio I can put in a reason code, and I can impose monotonicity by constraining the sign."

The trap

Two things get said wrongly. First, logistic regression is a linear model — linear in the log-odds — so it cannot represent an interaction or a U-shape unless you build the term yourself; if fraud risk rises for very small and very large amounts, a single amount coefficient will find nothing. Second, the coefficients are only interpretable when the features are not collinear (B3): with two near-duplicate columns the signs flip between refits, and a reason code built on an unstable coefficient is worse than no reason code at all.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does logistic regression model linearly?

The log-odds of the positive class, not the probability.

Interpret a coefficient of 0.7.

A one-unit increase multiplies the odds by e^0.7 ≈ 2, holding other features fixed.

Where does log-loss come from?

It is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model — the same derivation as S5.

What is a proper scoring rule?

One minimised only by reporting your true probability; log-loss and Brier are proper, accuracy is not.

What is perfect separation and what does it do?

Classes separable by a hyperplane; the MLE does not exist and coefficients diverge. Regularisation fixes it.

Why is logistic regression still used in banking?

Calibrated probabilities, interpretable odds ratios, easy monotonicity constraints, and a documentation trail a validator accepts.

Does it need feature scaling?

For convergence speed and for the L2 penalty to be meaningful, yes — the fit itself is scale-equivariant.

Track C · Classification · Module C2

k-Nearest NeighboursNo training, all inference — and every problem from A3 and A6 arrives at once.

k-NN has no parameters and no training step: it memorises the data and answers by vote. That makes it the cleanest instrument for seeing what a decision boundary is, and the clearest demonstration of why scaling and dimensionality matter, because with k-NN they are not abstractions — they change the answer.

Neighbour bench
real distance search
left: the decision surface in the two informative dimensions · right: train and test accuracy as k grows

k is the bias–variance dial

At k = 1 the training accuracy is 100% by definition — every point is its own nearest neighbour — and the boundary is a jagged shape wrapped around individual points. That is pure variance. At k = n every query returns the majority class and the boundary disappears entirely: pure bias. The right k sits where the test curve bottoms out, and the bench draws that curve as you drag.

k small → low bias, high variance, boundary follows noise k large → high bias, low variance, boundary over-smoothed rule of thumb: start at √n, then cross-validate; use odd k for two classes to avoid ties

Three ways it breaks

ProblemSymptomFix
Unscaled features (A3)One column dominates every distanceStandardise — non-negotiable for k-NN
Irrelevant dimensions (A6)Accuracy collapses as noise columns are addedFeature selection or a learned embedding
Class imbalanceThe minority never wins a voteDistance weighting, class-weighted votes, or resampling (D2)

Push noise dimensions up and watch accuracy fall while the informative content of the data is unchanged — that is A6's curse arriving in a concrete model. Then push class imbalance to 1:20: with k = 5 a minority point needs three of its five neighbours to be minority, and in a region where minority points are outnumbered twenty to one that almost never happens. The predicted class becomes constant. Distance weighting helps a little, because a very close minority neighbour outweighs distant majority ones, but the honest fix is at the sampling or threshold level.

The cost you pay at serving time

Training is free; every prediction is a search over the whole training set — O(n·d) naively, and the tree indexes that fix it (KD-tree, ball tree) degrade toward brute force above roughly twenty dimensions, again because of A6. For a fraud stream that scores thousands of transactions a second against millions of historical rows, plain k-NN is not a serving option. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF) exist precisely for this, and they are the same machinery underneath a vector database.

Interview point

"k-NN has no training cost and all its cost at inference — O(n·d) per query — and k is a direct bias–variance dial: k=1 memorises, k=n predicts the majority. It's the model most sensitive to scaling and to irrelevant dimensions, so it's a good diagnostic and a poor production choice at fraud volumes. If I need neighbour search at scale I reach for an approximate index, not exact k-NN."

The trap

k-NN's probability output is votes/k, so with k = 5 the only possible probabilities are 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1. That is not a calibrated score, it is a five-step staircase, and feeding it into a cost-optimal threshold (D3) or an expected-loss calculation is meaningless. If you need probabilities from k-NN, raise k substantially and calibrate — or use a model that produces them natively.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What happens at k = 1 and at k = n?

k=1 memorises the training set (100% train accuracy, high variance); k=n always predicts the majority class (maximum bias).

Why must features be scaled?

The vote depends on Euclidean distance, so a large-unit feature dominates the neighbour search.

Complexity of a prediction?

O(n·d) per query with brute force; tree indexes help in low dimensions and degrade above roughly 20.

Why does k-NN struggle with imbalance?

Majority points dominate any neighbourhood, so the minority rarely wins a vote regardless of how distinctive it is.

What does distance weighting change?

Closer neighbours count more, which softens both over-smoothing and imbalance without changing the metric.

Is k-NN parametric?

No — it is non-parametric and instance-based; the model is the data.

How do you pick k?

Cross-validation, starting near √n, and odd values for two classes to avoid ties.

Track C · Classification · Module C3

SVM & the MarginNot any separating line — the one with the most clearance, and the handful of points that decide it.

When two classes are separable there are infinitely many lines that split them. Logistic regression picks one by likelihood; the SVM picks the one that sits as far as possible from both classes. That single criterion — maximise the margin — produces sparsity, a clean generalisation story, and the hinge loss you will meet again in every ranking model.

Margin bench
hinge loss · subgradient descent
the margin band is shaded · circled points are support vectors — the only rows that determine the boundary

The objective

margin width = 2/‖w‖ so maximising the margin = minimising ‖w‖ soft-margin SVM: min ½‖w‖² + C · Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b)) ^ wide margin ^ hinge loss — zero once a point is correctly classified beyond the margin C large → few violations tolerated, narrow margin, fits noise C small → violations cheap, wide margin, more bias

The hinge is the mechanism behind the sparsity. A point sitting correctly outside the margin contributes exactly zero loss and zero gradient — it is invisible. Only points on the margin or violating it exert any pull, and those are the support vectors. Drag C down and watch the count rise as the margin widens to swallow more points; drag it up and the boundary is decided by a handful of rows.

Why maximising clearance generalises

The intuition is that a boundary crammed against the training points has no room for a slightly different sample, while one with clearance survives perturbation. Formally, generalisation bounds for SVMs depend on the margin rather than on the number of features, which is why the method still works when the feature count exceeds the row count. That property is worth knowing: it is the reason SVMs dominated text classification before deep learning, where the vocabulary is far larger than the corpus.

Now raise label noise. With a large C the boundary contorts to accommodate mislabelled points and the margin collapses; with a small C it ignores them. This is the same robustness dial as ε and C in B6, and it is the reason "hard margin" is a theoretical object rather than a production setting — real labels have noise, especially fraud labels.

SVM (hinge)Logistic (log-loss)
Loss beyond the marginExactly zeroSmall but never zero
Depends onSupport vectors onlyEvery row
OutputA signed distance, not a probabilityA calibrated probability
Outliers far from the boundaryIgnoredSlight pull
Multi-classOne-vs-rest or one-vs-oneNative via softmax

Interview point

"The SVM maximises the margin, which is equivalent to minimising ‖w‖ subject to the hinge constraints. Points correctly outside the margin have zero loss and zero gradient, so the solution depends only on the support vectors — that's the sparsity. C trades margin width against violations, and because real labels are noisy I'm always in the soft-margin regime."

The trap

An SVM's decision function is a signed distance to the hyperplane, not a probability. SVC(probability=True) does not change that — it runs Platt scaling, an internal cross-validated logistic fit on the margins, which costs extra training time and can disagree with decision_function's own ordering at the boundary. If you need probabilities for a cost-optimal threshold, calibrate deliberately (D6) rather than flipping a flag. And scale your features: like k-NN, the margin is measured in feature units.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does an SVM maximise?

The margin, 2/‖w‖ — equivalently it minimises ‖w‖² subject to correct classification with slack.

What is a support vector?

A training point on or inside the margin; only these determine the boundary.

Write the hinge loss.

max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) — zero once a point is correctly classified beyond the margin.

What does C control?

The cost of margin violations: large C means a narrow, noise-sensitive margin; small C means a wide, more biased one.

Hard vs soft margin?

Hard requires perfect separation and does not exist for noisy data; soft allows slack and is what you always use.

Does an SVM output probabilities?

No — a signed distance. Probabilities require Platt scaling or isotonic calibration on top.

Why do SVMs handle p > n well?

Their generalisation depends on the margin rather than the feature count.

Track C · Classification · Module C4

Kernel SVMCurved boundaries from a linear model, by never computing the coordinates you are working in.

A linear separator fails on concentric classes — and lifting the data into a higher-dimensional space where it becomes linearly separable is both the fix and, done naively, impossibly expensive. The kernel trick makes it free: the SVM only ever needs inner products between points, so replacing the inner product with a kernel function fits in that space without visiting it.

Kernel bench
RBF via 200 random Fourier features · closed-form solve
the decision surface · at high γ it fragments into islands around individual training points

The trick, stated once

linear SVM needs only ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩ kernel SVM replaces it with K(xᵢ, xⱼ) = ⟨φ(xᵢ), φ(xⱼ)⟩ RBF K(a,b) = exp(−γ‖a−b‖²) φ is infinite-dimensional — never computed polynomial K(a,b) = (⟨a,b⟩ + c)^d linear K(a,b) = ⟨a,b⟩

Nothing about the optimisation changes; only the inner product does. The RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map, which is exactly why you cannot write φ down and exactly why you do not need to. This bench approximates it with 200 random Fourier features — an explicit, finite map whose inner products converge to the RBF kernel — and fits them with regularised least squares rather than the hinge, because that has a closed form and therefore converges exactly in a browser. The kernel geometry is identical; what changes is the sparsity story from C3, since squared loss gives every point a non-zero gradient. Treat the boundary shapes here as real and the support-vector count as belonging to C3.

γ is the memorisation dial

γ sets how far a single training point's influence reaches. Small γ means a wide, smooth bump — the boundary is still curved but under-resolved, and fine structure is lost; large γ means each point influences only its immediate vicinity. Press γ far too large and the surface fragments into islands, one around each training point — the model has memorised, and training accuracy hits 100% while test accuracy falls off. It is the same failure as k = 1 in C2, arrived at from a different direction.

γ too smallγ about rightγ too large
BoundaryVery smooth, under-resolvedFollows the true shapeIslands around points
Train / test gapSmall, both poorSmall, both goodLarge
DiagnosisUnderfit / bias—Overfit / variance

γ and C interact, which is why they are tuned together on a 2-D grid rather than one at a time: a large C can partly compensate for a small γ and vice versa, so the CV surface has a diagonal valley rather than a single well.

Interview point

"The kernel trick works because the SVM only depends on inner products, so you swap in a kernel and fit in a high-dimensional space without ever computing the coordinates. For RBF that space is infinite-dimensional. γ controls how local each point's influence is — too large and the boundary becomes islands around individual points, which is memorisation — and because γ and C interact I tune them jointly."

The trap

Kernel SVMs do not scale. Training is roughly O(n²) to O(n³) and the kernel matrix is n×n — at a million transactions that matrix alone is terabytes. Everything in this module is worth knowing for the concepts and for small problems; for a fraud dataset the answer is gradient boosting, or a linear SVM on explicit random features, which is precisely the approximation this bench uses. Say that unprompted and you have shown you know where the method's limit is rather than just how it works.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State the kernel trick.

Algorithms depending only on inner products can replace them with a kernel, implicitly fitting in a higher-dimensional space without computing the mapping.

Write the RBF kernel.

K(a,b) = exp(−γ‖a−b‖²), corresponding to an infinite-dimensional feature map.

What does γ control?

The reach of each training point's influence — large γ means very local, which leads to memorisation.

How do γ and C interact?

They partly compensate for each other, so the cross-validation surface has a diagonal valley and they must be tuned jointly.

What must a valid kernel satisfy?

Mercer's condition — the kernel matrix must be symmetric positive semi-definite.

Why don't kernel SVMs scale?

Training is O(n²)–O(n³) and the kernel matrix is n×n.

What is a random-features approximation?

An explicit finite feature map whose inner products approximate the kernel, letting you use a fast linear solver.

Track C · Classification · Module C5

Naive BayesAn assumption everyone knows is false, in a model that keeps working anyway. This bench shows why.

Naive Bayes assumes every feature is conditionally independent given the class. In transaction data that is plainly untrue — amount and merchant category are correlated, velocity and device age are correlated. And yet it classifies well while producing probabilities that are badly wrong. Both halves of that sentence are measurable, and this bench measures them.

Independence bench
Gaussian NB · exact posterior
left: the NB boundary against the exact Bayes-optimal one · right: calibration — predicted probability vs observed frequency

The model

P(y | x) ∝ P(y) · Πj P(xⱼ | y) the "naive" step is that product Gaussian NB: P(xⱼ|y) = N(μ_{j,y}, σ²_{j,y}) Multinomial NB: word counts — the classic spam / text model Bernoulli NB: binary presence features work in logs: log P(y) + Σⱼ log P(xⱼ|y) — sums, not products, or you underflow

Because the parameters are just per-class means and variances, training is a single pass over the data: O(n·d) with no optimisation. That is why Naive Bayes remains the standard baseline for text, and why it is often the first thing you run on a new dataset — thirty seconds of work for a number that tells you whether anything is learnable at all.

What correlation actually breaks

Drag ρ from 0 to 0.95 and watch the two readouts diverge. AUC — a ranking metric — holds up remarkably well, while log-loss and the calibration plot fall apart. The reason is precise: correlated features carry the same evidence, and the product treats each copy as independent confirmation, so the posterior is driven toward 0 or 1 far harder than the evidence justifies. The ordering of scores survives because every point is over-confident in the same direction; the probabilities do not.

Push duplicated copies up to make it stark: adding an exact copy of a feature does not add information, but Naive Bayes counts its log-likelihood twice. Six copies and the model is certain about everything, right or wrong.

Use Naive Bayes whenAvoid it when
You need a fast, dependable baselineYou need calibrated probabilities for a cost decision
Very high-dimensional sparse textFeatures are strongly correlated or duplicated
Tiny training sets — few parameters to estimateInteractions carry the signal, since NB cannot represent them
You only need a rankingYou need the score itself to mean something

Interview point

"Naive Bayes assumes conditional independence, which is essentially always false — but it often still ranks well, because correlated features push every score in the same direction and the ordering survives. What doesn't survive is calibration: duplicated evidence gets counted twice, so the posteriors are wildly over-confident. I use it as a baseline and never as a probability source."

The trap

Zero-frequency: if a category never appears with a class in training, its conditional probability is zero and the whole product collapses to zero regardless of the other features. Laplace (add-one) smoothing exists for exactly this, and it is not optional on sparse categorical data — a single unseen merchant would otherwise veto every other piece of evidence. Related: Gaussian NB assumes each feature is normal within each class, so heavily skewed columns like transaction value need a log transform before it means anything.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State the naive assumption.

Features are conditionally independent given the class, so the joint likelihood factorises into a product.

Why does it still classify well?

Ranking only needs the ordering of scores, and correlated features distort every score in the same direction.

What does correlation break?

Calibration — duplicated evidence is counted repeatedly, producing over-confident posteriors.

What is Laplace smoothing for?

Preventing a zero conditional probability from annihilating the entire product for unseen categories.

Which variant for text counts?

Multinomial Naive Bayes; Bernoulli for binary presence features.

Why work in log space?

Multiplying hundreds of small probabilities underflows; sums of logs do not.

Training complexity?

A single pass, O(n·d) — just per-class means and variances, or counts.

Track C · Classification · Module C6

Decision Trees: Gini & EntropyHow a split is chosen, why the two criteria almost never disagree, and where the greed costs you.

A classification tree asks one question at a time and picks each question by whichever split makes the children purest. Two impurity measures dominate the textbooks and the interview questions — and this bench evaluates every candidate threshold under both, so you can see how rarely they choose differently and how the greedy search misses structure a human would spot instantly.

Split bench
exhaustive threshold search
left: the axis-aligned decision regions · right: impurity of the root split across every candidate threshold, under both criteria

The two criteria

Gini G = 1 − Σ pₖ² max 0.5 for two classes Entropy H = − Σ pₖ log₂ pₖ max 1.0 for two classes split quality = weighted impurity of the children, minimised information gain = H(parent) − Σ (nₖ/n)·H(childₖ)

The right-hand panel plots both curves over every candidate threshold. They have the same shape, peak at the same place, and pick the same split the overwhelming majority of the time — entropy is very slightly more willing to isolate a small pure group because the log punishes impurity harder near the extremes. Gini is the scikit-learn default because it avoids the logarithm and is marginally faster; the choice is not one worth spending tuning budget on, and saying so is a better answer than reciting the formulas.

Axis-aligned greed

Push the diagonal boundary slider. The true boundary rotates away from the axes, and the tree can only answer it with a staircase of horizontal and vertical cuts — needing many splits to approximate what one rotated line would do. That is the structural limitation: trees cannot express a linear combination of features, so anything diagonal costs depth, and depth costs variance.

The greed matters too. Each split is chosen to minimise impurity now, with no lookahead, so a pair of features that only helps jointly may never get selected — the XOR pattern is the classic case where no single split improves purity at all and the tree needs two levels to find anything. This is a real limitation and also the reason boosting works so well: a sequence of shallow greedy trees, each correcting the last, recovers structure a single greedy tree misses.

ControlEffectNotes
max_depthHard cap on interaction orderDepth d can express interactions of order d
min_samples_leafStatistical floor per predictionOften more effective than depth for controlling variance
min_impurity_decreaseRefuses splits that barely helpCheap pre-pruning
ccp_alphaCost-complexity post-pruningGrow fully, then prune back by cross-validated α

Interview point

"Splits are chosen by weighted impurity reduction — Gini or entropy, and they pick the same split almost always, so it's not a tuning priority. The real limitations are structural: splits are axis-aligned, so a diagonal boundary costs a staircase of cuts, and the search is greedy with no lookahead, so jointly-informative feature pairs can be missed. Boosting exists partly because a sequence of shallow greedy trees recovers what one greedy tree cannot."

The trap

Trees are unstable in a specific way worth naming: resample the data slightly and the top split can change, which rewrites every branch beneath it. That means a single tree is a poor explanation artifact even though it looks like the most interpretable model in the room — the story it tells changes between refits. If someone asks for an interpretable model, a shallow tree is defensible only if you also show that its structure is stable across bootstrap samples. Otherwise you are presenting one draw from a distribution of trees as though it were the truth.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write Gini and entropy.

Gini = 1 − Σpₖ²; entropy = −Σpₖlog₂pₖ. Both measure node impurity.

Do they choose different splits?

Rarely. Entropy is slightly more inclined to isolate small pure groups; Gini is cheaper and is the common default.

What is information gain?

Parent impurity minus the weighted impurity of the children.

Why can't a tree fit a diagonal boundary cleanly?

Splits are axis-aligned, so a rotated boundary must be approximated by a staircase.

What does greedy mean here, and what does it cost?

Each split is locally optimal with no lookahead, so jointly-informative feature pairs — XOR being the extreme — can be missed.

How does max_depth relate to interactions?

A tree of depth d can express interactions of order at most d.

Pre-pruning vs post-pruning?

Pre-pruning stops growth by depth or minimum gain; post-pruning grows fully then removes branches by cost-complexity α.

Track C · Classification · Module C7

Random Forest & BaggingMany unstable models, deliberately made to disagree, then averaged.

C6 ended on instability: change the sample slightly and a tree rewrites itself. Bagging turns that defect into the mechanism — average many high-variance, low-bias trees and the variance falls while the bias does not. The essential detail, and the one interviews probe, is that averaging only helps to the extent the trees disagree.

Ensemble bench
real bootstrap · real feature subsampling
left: test accuracy as trees accumulate, for this configuration · right: pairwise disagreement between trees — the quantity averaging actually consumes

Why decorrelation is the whole game

Var(average of T trees) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/T ↑ irreducible while trees agree more trees shrink only the second term → the curve plateaus lowering ρ shrinks the first → that is what feature subsampling buys

Switch between Bagging only and Random forest with a good number of noise features present. Bagging bootstraps the rows but every tree still sees every column, so they all find the same dominant split first and remain highly similar — the disagreement readout stays low and the accuracy curve plateaus early. Restricting each split to a random √p subset — resampled at every node, not once per tree — forces trees onto different features and disagreement rises sharply. Read the numbers carefully, though: in this configuration the forest's individual trees are markedly worse (around 74% against 79%) and the ensemble still lands level with bagging. Decorrelation is not free — it buys a lower ρσ² floor at the cost of weaker members, and whether that trade nets out depends on how much redundancy the feature set actually has. The mechanism is what the bench proves; the accuracy win is conditional.

That is the counter-intuitive sentence worth having ready: a random forest deliberately handicaps its members, because the ensemble's error depends on their correlation as well as their individual quality. The classic decisive win arrives when one feature dominates every tree's first split — real fraud feature sets, where a handful of velocity features crowd out everything else, are exactly that case.

Out-of-bag error, free

Each bootstrap sample omits about 1 − (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e ≈ 36.8% of rows. Every tree can be scored on the rows it never saw, and averaging those gives a validation estimate without a held-out split — useful when data is scarce, and a good thing to know the derivation of rather than just the number.

BaggingRandom forestBoosting (G-track)
Trees are builtIndependently, in parallelIndependently, in parallelSequentially, each fixing the last
AttacksVarianceVariance, harderBias, then variance
Base learnerDeep treesDeep treesShallow stumps
Overfits with more trees?NoNoYes — rounds are a tuning parameter

Interview point

"Bagging averages away variance, but the residual term is ρσ² — the trees' correlation — so past a point extra trees do nothing. A random forest attacks ρ directly by restricting each split to a random feature subset, which makes each tree worse and the ensemble better. And out-of-bag error gives me a validation estimate for free, since each bootstrap leaves out about 37% of rows."

The trap

Random forests are the default answer to "which model" and often the wrong one for extreme imbalance. With a 0.3% fraud rate, a deep tree's leaves fill with majority rows and the votes are majority long before you reach a threshold — you need class weights, balanced bootstrap sampling, or a threshold chosen from cost (D3), not the default 0.5 vote. Second trap: feature_importances_ is impurity-based, computed on training data, and biased toward high-cardinality features. Use permutation importance on held-out data before showing anyone a ranked list.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does bagging reduce?

Variance. Bias stays roughly the same because each tree is grown deep.

Write the variance of an average of correlated trees.

ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/T — only the second term shrinks with more trees.

What does a random forest add to bagging?

Random feature subsampling at each split, which lowers ρ and so lowers the floor that averaging cannot reach.

Why does making each tree worse help?

Ensemble error depends on correlation as much as on individual accuracy; decorrelation buys more than individual quality costs.

What fraction of rows is out-of-bag?

About 36.8% — the limit of (1 − 1/n)ⁿ.

Can a forest overfit by adding trees?

No. Boosting can, because its rounds reduce bias sequentially.

Default problem on imbalanced data?

Majority votes dominate; use class weights, balanced sampling, or a cost-chosen threshold instead of 0.5.

Classification · Module C8

Confusion Matrix, Thresholds & the Accuracy ParadoxA 99.7%-accurate fraud model that catches zero fraud is not a hypothetical — it is the default outcome.

Classifiers do not output classes. They output scores, and a human chooses a cut. Every metric you quote is a property of that cut, not of the model — which means "my model is 94% accurate" is an incomplete sentence. This bench lets you slide the cut and watch four numbers move in different directions at once.

Threshold Bench — 0.3% fraud base rate
real score distributions
left: score distributions with the cut · right: the confusion matrix, area ∝ count

The matrix and everything derived from it

predicted fraud predicted legit actual fraud TP FN ← recall = TP/(TP+FN) actual legit FP TN ← specificity = TN/(TN+FP) ↑ precision = TP/(TP+FP) accuracy = (TP+TN)/N useless when one class is 99.7% of N F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) harmonic mean — punishes the weaker of the two FPR = FP/(FP+TN) the x-axis of the ROC curve
MetricQuestion it answersWho cares in a bank
PrecisionOf the transactions I blocked, how many were actually fraud?Operations — every false positive is a support ticket and an annoyed customer
RecallOf the actual fraud, how much did I catch?Risk and loss teams — this is money out the door
SpecificityOf the legitimate transactions, how many did I let through cleanly?Customer experience, and the regulator asking about de-risking
F1Balanced summary when you refuse to state a cost ratioNobody, really — it is a modelling convenience, not a business objective

The paradox, with numbers

Press Show the accuracy paradox. The bench sets prevalence to roughly 0.3% and pushes the threshold high. Accuracy reads about 99.7%, which is higher than any model you will ship — and it is achieved by a classifier that flags nothing at all. The constant predictor "everything is legitimate" is the strongest accuracy baseline in the room, and it is worth exactly zero.

Now drag the threshold down. Recall rises, precision falls, and accuracy barely moves for most of the range because it is dominated by the true negatives you were never at risk of getting wrong. That insensitivity is the entire problem: accuracy cannot see the class you care about.

Precision and recall trade against each other by construction

Lowering the threshold can only add predicted-positives. Every added positive is either a TP (recall up) or an FP (precision down). There is no threshold that improves both — the only way to move the whole curve is a better model or better features. Say that out loud in an interview and you have demonstrated you understand what a threshold is.

Interview point

"Accuracy is meaningless at a 0.3% base rate — predicting 'no fraud' every time scores 99.7%. I report precision and recall at an operating point chosen from the cost of a false positive versus a missed fraud, and I quote PR-AUC rather than accuracy for the model as a whole."

The trap

model.predict() silently applies a 0.5 threshold. That default is only meaningful if the model is calibrated and false positives and false negatives cost the same — which is essentially never true in fraud. Use predict_proba, choose the cut deliberately, and store it with the model. And when you report precision and recall, always state the threshold they were measured at; a bare pair of numbers with no operating point is not a result.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define precision and recall.

Precision = TP/(TP+FP), of what I flagged how much was real. Recall = TP/(TP+FN), of what was real how much I flagged.

What is the accuracy paradox?

With a rare positive class, a model that never predicts the positive achieves near-perfect accuracy while being worthless.

Why is F1 harmonic rather than arithmetic?

The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value, so it refuses to reward a model that is excellent on one and terrible on the other.

Lower the threshold — which metrics move which way?

Recall up, precision typically down, FPR up, specificity down.

When do you optimise recall over precision?

When a miss costs far more than a review — fraud losses, disease screening, safety alerts with a human in the loop.

What does predict() assume?

A 0.5 cut on the score, which is a business decision the library made for you.

Can you improve precision and recall simultaneously by tuning the threshold?

No. Only a better model or better features moves the whole trade-off curve.

Track D · Evaluation & imbalance · Module D4

Cross-Validation SchemesFour ways to split the same data, three of which lie to you about this dataset.

A2 showed that a careless split inflates a score. This module is the constructive half: given time ordering, entity groups and a rare positive class all present at once — which is every fraud dataset — which CV scheme reproduces deployment? The bench runs all four on identical data and compares each estimate against the future performance you actually get.

CV bench — estimate vs reality
5 folds · logistic model
left: per-fold scores with the CV mean and the true future score · right: optimism — CV estimate minus reality — for all four schemes on this data

What each scheme protects against

SchemeProtects againstStill vulnerable to
Random k-foldNothing structural — only sampling varianceTime drift, grouped rows, empty folds at low prevalence
Stratified k-foldFolds with too few positivesTime drift, grouped rows
Group k-foldThe same entity straddling the splitTime drift
Time-series (expanding window)Training on the futureGroup leakage within a period, and it uses less data per fold

They compose: for fraud you generally want time-ordered folds, grouped by entity, with an embargo. Nothing in scikit-learn does all three, which is why production teams write their own splitter — a good detail to mention, because it signals you have done it rather than read about it.

Reading the optimism panel

The right-hand chart is the number that matters: CV estimate minus the score on a genuinely future block. Random k-fold is optimistic whenever drift or grouping is present, and the bench lets you separate the two causes — set rows per entity to 1 and the group effect vanishes while the drift effect remains; set drift to 0 and the reverse.

Time-series CV usually shows the smallest optimism and the largest fold-to-fold variance, because early folds train on very little data. That variance is honest: it is telling you the model's performance depends on how much history it has, which is a real operational fact about retraining cadence.

How many folds?

k = 5 or k = 10 standard; 10 has lower bias, higher variance and 2× the cost k = n leave-one-out nearly unbiased, high variance, and n model fits — rarely worth it repeated k-fold different random partitions, averaged: better variance estimate

Report the standard deviation across folds alongside the mean. A model scoring 0.82 ± 0.01 and one scoring 0.83 ± 0.06 are not ranked by their means, and a single-number CV score hides exactly that.

Interview point

"The split has to reproduce the deployment condition. For transactions that means time-ordered folds with an embargo the length of the label delay, and grouping by entity so retries of the same event can't straddle a fold. Random k-fold is optimistic under either drift or grouping, and I can show which by turning each one off. I also report the fold standard deviation, because a mean alone hides an unstable model."

The trap

Everything fitted must live inside the fold — scaler, imputer, target encoder, feature selector, resampler. The most common version of this bug is selecting features on the full dataset and then cross-validating the model: the folds all share knowledge of which features won, and the estimate is optimistic in a way no amount of fold discipline recovers. Put the whole thing in a Pipeline and pass that to cross_val_score, or you are cross-validating half a model.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
When is stratified k-fold necessary?

Whenever the positive class is rare enough that random folds could contain very few positives, making per-fold estimates unstable.

What does GroupKFold prevent?

Rows from the same entity — card, customer, wallet — appearing on both sides of a split.

Describe expanding-window CV.

Train on everything up to time t, validate on the next block, roll forward. It never trains on the future.

Why is random k-fold wrong for fraud?

It trains on future transactions and lets duplicated entities straddle folds, both of which inflate the estimate.

5 folds or 10?

10 has slightly less bias and more variance at double the cost; 5 is the usual default. Repeated k-fold gives a better variance estimate.

What must go inside the fold?

Every fitted transform — scaling, imputation, encoding, feature selection, resampling — via a pipeline.

Why report fold standard deviation?

Because two models with the same mean can differ wildly in stability, and the mean alone hides it.

Track D · Evaluation & imbalance · Module D5

Hyperparameter SearchWhy random search beats grid search on the same budget, and why your best CV score is a biased estimate.

Two results here are worth more than any tuning recipe. First, when only some hyperparameters matter — which is nearly always — random search finds better configurations than grid search at equal cost, for a reason that is easy to state. Second, the best score from a search is optimistically biased, and the size of that bias grows with how hard you searched.

Search bench
real search over a real surface
left: the true score surface with this search's evaluated points · right: best-found score against budget, averaged over repeated searches — each repeat places the optimum somewhere different, so no fixed grid can be lucky

Why random wins

This bench searches four hyperparameters — a modest number for a boosting model. A grid at a budget of 25 therefore manages only two distinct values per axis, because 2⁴ = 16 already nearly exhausts it. If the first parameter is the one that matters and the rest are nearly irrelevant, you have sampled the important dimension twice and spent everything else confirming that the others do not matter. Twenty-five random points try 25 distinct values of every parameter. Drag the other parameters' importance down toward 0 and watch the curves separate — that is Bergstra and Bengio's result, and it gets stronger as you add irrelevant dimensions.

grid, d parameters, k values each → k^d evaluations, k distinct values per axis random, n evaluations → n distinct values per axis, any d

Sequential search — the coarse-to-fine strategy here, and the same principle as Bayesian optimisation with a surrogate model — concentrates its later evaluations near where the early ones scored well. It wins at moderate budgets and is the honest description of what Optuna and Hyperopt do: fit a cheap model of the score surface, sample where that model is both promising and uncertain.

The optimism you introduce by searching

Each CV score is a noisy measurement. Taking the maximum over many noisy measurements selects partly for genuine quality and partly for lucky noise — so the winning score is biased upward, and the bias grows with the number of configurations tried. The bench reports the gap between the best CV score and that configuration's true score.

The fix is nested cross-validation: an inner loop chooses hyperparameters, an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure on data the inner loop never saw. It costs k_outer × k_inner fits, and for a hiring conversation the important thing is knowing why it exists — the number you report should measure the pipeline including its tuning, not the winner of a lottery.

MethodCostGood when
Gridk^d — explodesTwo or three parameters, all mattering, cheap fits
RandomAny budgetThe default. Especially with many parameters of unequal importance
Bayesian / TPEAny budget, plus surrogate overheadExpensive fits where each evaluation must count
Successive halving / HyperbandCheap early roundsWhen partial training predicts final quality — deep nets, boosting rounds

Interview point

"I default to random search because a k×k grid only tries k distinct values per axis regardless of budget, while n random draws try n distinct values of every parameter — so when only some parameters matter, random dominates at equal cost. And I don't report the best CV score as the model's performance: maximising over noisy estimates is biased upward, which is what nested CV is for."

The trap

Searching on a log scale matters more than the search strategy. Learning rate, regularisation strength and γ live on multiplicative scales — sampling η uniformly in [0.0001, 0.1] puts 99.9% of your draws above 0.0001 and effectively never explores the small end. Use log-uniform ranges for anything that spans orders of magnitude. And set a budget before you start: an unbounded search on a validation set is just slow overfitting, with the fold structure providing false reassurance.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why does random search beat grid search?

A grid tries only k distinct values per axis; n random draws try n distinct values on every axis, so budget is not wasted on unimportant parameters.

What does Bayesian optimisation add?

A surrogate model of the score surface plus an acquisition rule, so evaluations concentrate where the score is promising or uncertain.

Why is the best CV score biased?

Taking a maximum over noisy estimates selects for favourable noise as well as for quality.

What is nested cross-validation?

An inner loop that tunes and an outer loop that scores the entire tuning procedure on unseen data.

Which parameters need log-scale sampling?

Anything multiplicative — learning rate, regularisation strength, γ, tree counts across orders of magnitude.

What is successive halving?

Train many configurations briefly, keep the best fraction, train those longer — repeat. Hyperband wraps it with several bracket sizes.

How does the fold count interact with search?

Noisier folds mean noisier scores, which means more selection bias — so fewer, better-estimated candidates often beat many noisy ones.

Track D · Evaluation & imbalance · Module D6

Probability CalibrationA model can rank perfectly and still be wrong about every probability. D3's threshold formula needs the second thing.

AUC only cares about ordering. The moment you multiply a score by money — expected loss, cost-optimal thresholds, capital models, reason codes — the score has to be a probability, meaning that among all transactions scored 0.07, about 7% really are fraud. Boosted trees and SVMs are not calibrated out of the box, and anything trained on resampled data is calibrated to the wrong prior. This bench measures the damage and fixes it.

Calibration bench
Platt & isotonic, fitted on a held-out split
left: reliability diagram before and after calibration · right: expected cost across thresholds, showing what miscalibration costs when you use D3's formula

Two methods

Platt scaling fit p = σ(a·s + b) on held-out (score, label) pairs 2 parameters · monotone · needs little data · assumes a sigmoid shape Isotonic fit any non-decreasing step function minimising squared error non-parametric · fixes arbitrary distortions · overfits on small sets

Both are monotone, which has an important consequence you should be able to state: calibration does not change the ranking, so AUC is unchanged while log-loss, Brier score and ECE improve. The bench reports AUC before and after so you can see it hold — with isotonic, tiny differences appear only where the step function flattens and creates ties.

Where the money is

The right-hand panel connects this to D3. The cost-optimal threshold is p* = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN), and that formula assumes the scores are probabilities. Feed it an uncalibrated score and you get a confidently wrong operating point: the bench computes the cost you incur by applying p* to the raw scores versus applying it to the calibrated ones, on the same model with the same ranking. The gap is pure miscalibration, and it exists even though AUC never moved.

Select Trained on balanced data to see the case people meet most often. Resampling to 50/50 (D2) leaves the model calibrated to a 50% prior, so a transaction at a true 3% risk is scored near 0.5. Ranking is fine; every probability is roughly an order of magnitude too high. The correction is either recalibration on a set with the true prevalence, or an analytic intercept shift back to the real base rate.

ModelTypical calibrationWhy
Logistic regressionGoodIt optimises the Bernoulli likelihood directly (C1)
Gradient boostingUsually over-confidentOptimises a margin-like objective; probabilities pushed toward the extremes
SVMNot probabilities at allOutputs a signed distance; needs Platt (C3)
Random forestUnder-confident at the extremesAveraging votes pulls predictions toward the middle
Naive BayesBadly over-confidentCorrelated evidence counted repeatedly (C5)

Interview point

"Calibration and discrimination are different properties: AUC measures ranking, calibration measures whether a 0.07 means 7%. Platt and isotonic are both monotone, so they fix calibration without touching AUC. I calibrate whenever a score gets multiplied by money — cost-optimal thresholds, expected loss — and always on a held-out set, with Platt when that set is small and isotonic when it's large."

The trap

Calibrating on the training set is worthless: the model is already over-fit there, so the mapping it learns is the identity plus noise. Use a dedicated split or cross-validated calibration (CalibratedClassifierCV with cv, not cv='prefit' on training data). Second: calibration is a property of a population, so a model calibrated on last quarter drifts out of calibration when prevalence moves — which makes ECE a monitoring metric, not a one-time fix. Third: at a 0.3% base rate almost every score sits in the lowest bin, so a ten-bin reliability diagram tells you nothing. Use quantile bins, or plot on a log scale.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Calibration vs discrimination?

Discrimination is ranking quality (AUC); calibration is whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.

Does calibration change AUC?

No — Platt and isotonic are monotone, so the ordering and therefore the AUC are preserved.

Platt vs isotonic?

Platt fits a two-parameter sigmoid and needs little data; isotonic fits any monotone step function and needs a lot or it overfits.

What is ECE?

Expected calibration error: the average absolute gap between predicted probability and observed frequency, weighted by bin size.

Why are boosted trees over-confident?

Their objective pushes margins, driving predictions toward 0 and 1 rather than toward true frequencies.

What does resampling do to calibration?

It shifts the implied prior, so probabilities reflect the resampled base rate rather than the real one.

Where must the calibrator be fitted?

On held-out data — cross-validated if data is scarce — never on the model's own training set.

Track D · Evaluation & imbalance · Module D7

Drift Detection: PSI & KSYour inputs moved. Whether that matters is a separate question, and confusing the two is how monitoring becomes noise.

Fraud models decay because the world adapts to them — that is the arms race, and it makes drift monitoring non-optional. But the alert everyone builds first, "this feature's distribution changed", fires constantly and often means nothing. This bench separates covariate shift from concept drift and shows that only one of them reliably destroys your AUC.

Drift bench
real PSI · real KS · real AUC decay
left: reference vs current distribution of the monitored feature · right: PSI, KS and AUC as drift magnitude grows

The two statistics

PSI Σ (actual% − expected%) · ln(actual% / expected%) over fixed bins < 0.10 no meaningful change 0.10–0.25 moderate shift — investigate > 0.25 major shift — act (these thresholds are industry convention from credit scoring, not a theorem) KS max |F_ref(x) − F_cur(x)| the largest CDF gap distribution-free, no binning choice, but less sensitive in the tails

PSI's bins are a decision, and the bench exposes it: raise PSI bins and the statistic changes for identical data, because empty or sparse bins inflate the log ratio. Bin on reference quantiles, keep the edges fixed once chosen, and set a floor for empty bins — otherwise your monitoring alerts on binning artefacts.

The distinction that makes monitoring useful

TypeWhat changedEffect on AUCResponse
Covariate shiftP(x) — inputs moveOften none, if P(y|x) holdsWatch; check for extrapolation (B4)
Concept driftP(y|x) — the relationship changesDirect decayRetrain, and investigate the adversary
Prior shiftP(y) — base rate movesRanking survives; calibration breaksRecalibrate (D6), re-derive the threshold (D3)
Upstream data bugA pipeline brokeAnything, often catastrophicFix the pipeline — this is the most common cause in practice

Run Covariate shift only and push the magnitude to 3: PSI screams while AUC barely moves. Then run Concept drift only: PSI stays near zero — the inputs look identical — while AUC falls off a cliff. That is the case that should frighten you, because input monitoring cannot see it at all. Detecting concept drift requires labels, and in fraud labels arrive 30–90 days late, so the honest architecture is: input monitoring for fast alerts, delayed performance monitoring for truth, and a retraining cadence that does not wait for either.

Interview point

"PSI and KS monitor the inputs, and inputs can move without the model degrading — that's covariate shift, and P(y|x) may be unchanged. What kills a fraud model is concept drift, where the relationship changes while the inputs look the same, and no input-distribution test can see it. So I pair PSI alerts with delayed performance monitoring against the chargeback window, and I treat prior shift separately because it breaks calibration rather than ranking."

The trap

PSI thresholds of 0.1 and 0.25 are credit-scoring convention, not statistics — they have no confidence level attached, and their meaning depends on your bin count and window size. A large enough monitoring window makes any test significant; a small one makes PSI unstable. Fix the bin edges from a reference period, fix the window size, and calibrate your own alert thresholds against what historically preceded a real degradation. Otherwise you build a monitor that alerts weekly and gets muted by month two — which is worse than no monitor, because everyone believes it is watching.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write the PSI formula.

Σ (actual% − expected%)·ln(actual%/expected%) across fixed bins.

Conventional PSI thresholds?

Below 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, above 0.25 major — industry convention, not a statistical test.

Covariate shift vs concept drift?

Covariate shift moves P(x) with P(y|x) unchanged; concept drift changes P(y|x) itself and is what actually degrades the model.

Why can't PSI detect concept drift?

It only looks at input distributions; the relationship can change while the inputs are identical.

What does the KS statistic measure?

The maximum gap between two cumulative distributions — distribution-free and binning-free.

What does prior shift break?

Calibration and your chosen threshold, not the ranking.

What do you monitor when labels are delayed?

Input drift and score distribution for fast signals; performance against labels as they mature; plus proxy outcomes like analyst confirmation rates.

Track G · Ensembles & boosting · Module G1

Bagging vs BoostingTwo ensembles that look similar and attack opposite halves of the error.

Both average many trees. That is where the resemblance ends. Bagging grows deep trees in parallel to kill variance; boosting grows shallow trees in sequence, each fitting what the last one got wrong, to kill bias. The consequences follow mechanically — including the one that matters operationally: a forest cannot overfit by adding trees and a booster absolutely can.

Ensemble bench
real trees · real sequential fitting
left: the fitted function against the truth · right: train and test error as members are added — the shapes are the whole lesson

The mechanics side by side

Bagging / random forestBoosting
Members builtIndependently — parallelisableSequentially — each depends on the last
Base learnerDeep, low bias, high varianceShallow stumps, high bias, low variance
CombinationSimple average / voteWeighted sum, each scaled by the learning rate
AttacksVarianceBias first, then variance
Adding membersNever hurts — plateausEventually overfits — rounds are a hyperparameter
Sensitivity to noisy labelsLow — averaging dilutes themHigh — later rounds chase exactly those rows

Read the two curves

Switch to Compare both and watch the right-hand panel. Bagging's test error drops steeply then flattens: the members are already low-bias, so averaging removes what it can and stops. Boosting's test error keeps falling past the point where bagging plateaued — it is still reducing bias — and then, given enough rounds and a large enough learning rate, turns back upward. That upturn is the model beginning to fit noise, and it is why every boosting library has early stopping and why the round count is tuned rather than set high "to be safe".

bagging F(x) = (1/T) Σ f_t(x) f_t fitted on a bootstrap sample boosting F_t(x) = F_{t−1}(x) + η · h_t(x) h_t fitted to what F_{t−1} got wrong η is shrinkage: smaller η needs more rounds and generalises better

Why shrinkage works

Press Overfit the booster — a large learning rate with many rounds — then Shrink and re-run. The second configuration takes far more rounds to reach the same training error and ends up with a lower test error. Each step commits less, so the sequence explores a smoother path and no single tree can dominate. The standard practical setting is a small η (0.01–0.1) with the round count chosen by early stopping on a validation fold; that pair is the single most important hyperparameter decision in gradient boosting.

Interview point

"Bagging builds deep trees in parallel and attacks variance; boosting builds shallow trees sequentially on the previous model's errors and attacks bias. That's why a forest can't overfit by adding trees while a booster can — rounds are a hyperparameter, controlled with a small learning rate and early stopping. It's also why boosting is more sensitive to label noise: later rounds are specifically fitting the rows everything else got wrong."

The trap

The label-noise sensitivity is not academic in fraud work. Chargebacks include disputes that were never fraud, and boosting will spend its later rounds learning those rows in detail. If your labels contain a few percent of noise, a shallower depth, a smaller learning rate and aggressive early stopping matter more than any accuracy trick — and comparing against a bagged baseline is a cheap way to detect the problem, because a forest degrading far less than a booster on the same data is a strong hint your labels are dirty.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does bagging reduce, and boosting?

Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias first and can then reduce variance with shrinkage.

Why are boosting base learners shallow?

Each round only needs to capture a little remaining structure; deep learners would overfit the residuals immediately.

Can adding trees overfit a random forest? A booster?

No for the forest; yes for the booster — rounds must be tuned, usually by early stopping.

What does the learning rate do in boosting?

Shrinks each round's contribution, so more rounds are needed and generalisation improves.

Which is more sensitive to noisy labels?

Boosting — later rounds concentrate on the hardest, often mislabelled, rows.

Which parallelises?

Bagging across trees; boosting only within a tree's split search.

Typical learning rate and round count?

η between 0.01 and 0.1 with hundreds to thousands of rounds, stopped early on a validation fold.

Track G · Ensembles & boosting · Module G2

AdaBoostThe original boosting algorithm: reweight the rows you got wrong, fit again, repeat.

AdaBoost is worth understanding not because you will deploy it — you will deploy XGBoost — but because it makes the boosting idea concrete in a way gradient boosting hides. Each round reweights the training rows, so you can literally watch the algorithm's attention move to the points it keeps getting wrong. This bench draws that attention as point size.

AdaBoost bench
real stumps · real weight updates
left: point size is that row's current weight — watch it concentrate · right: training and test error by round, with each stump's α

The algorithm, in four lines

initialise w_i = 1/n for t in 1..T: fit stump h_t minimising the weighted error ε_t = Σ w_i · 1[h_t(x_i) ≠ y_i] α_t = ½ · ln((1 − ε_t) / ε_t) a stump's vote weight w_i ← w_i · exp(−α_t · y_i · h_t(x_i)) then renormalise final: F(x) = sign( Σ α_t h_t(x) )

Two things fall out of α's formula. A stump with ε = 0.5 gets α = 0 — a coin flip earns no vote. A stump better than chance gets positive α, and one worse than chance gets negative α, meaning AdaBoost happily inverts a bad learner and uses it. That is why the requirement is only "weak learner: better than random", not "good".

Watching the weights

Run a few rounds and watch the point sizes. Correctly classified rows shrink, misclassified rows grow, and the concentration is measurable: after 40 rounds the heaviest single row carries roughly twelve times its starting weight, and the top 5% of rows hold about a third of the total mass against a uniform share of 5%. That focusing is the mechanism, and it is also the vulnerability: press Add mislabelled points and the weight moves onto rows whose labels are simply wrong. Note what the concentration readout does: with 18% of labels flipped it falls, because the mass now spreads across every mislabelled row rather than a few boundary cases. AdaBoost cannot distinguish "hard" from "wrong", so it spends its capacity on them, and test error rises past its optimum while training error keeps falling.

AdaBoost minimises exponential loss, Σ exp(−y·F(x)), which penalises confident mistakes far more aggressively than log-loss does. That is exactly why it is more noise-sensitive than gradient boosting with a logistic loss — a single mislabelled point with a large negative margin contributes an exponentially large penalty.

Interview point

"AdaBoost reweights misclassified rows each round and weights each stump by α = ½·ln((1−ε)/ε), so a learner at chance gets zero vote. It's minimising exponential loss, which is why it's fragile to mislabelled data — a confident mistake costs exponentially. Gradient boosting generalises the idea to any differentiable loss, which is how you get logistic loss and the robustness that comes with it."

The trap

"AdaBoost cannot overfit" was a real claim in the 1990s, based on the observation that test error often keeps falling after training error hits zero — explained later by the margin continuing to grow. It is not true in general, and it is decidedly false with label noise, which the bench demonstrates in a few slider drags. If asked, give the nuanced version: margins keep improving for a while after training error reaches zero, which delays overfitting, but noise breaks it and the algorithm has no mechanism to resist.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does AdaBoost do between rounds?

Increases the weight of misclassified rows and decreases the weight of correct ones, then refits.

Write the stump weight α.

α = ½·ln((1−ε)/ε), where ε is the weighted error rate.

What happens at ε = 0.5?

α = 0 — a learner at chance contributes nothing.

Which loss does AdaBoost minimise?

Exponential loss, Σexp(−y·F(x)).

Why is it noise-sensitive?

Exponential loss explodes on confident mistakes, so mislabelled rows accumulate enormous weight.

What is a weak learner?

Any model performing better than chance; AdaBoost can even invert one performing worse.

How does gradient boosting generalise it?

By fitting each round to the negative gradient of any differentiable loss, rather than to reweighted misclassification.

Track G · Ensembles & boosting · Module G3

Gradient Boosting From ScratchEach tree fits the gradient of the loss. Once you see that, every variant is a choice of loss.

Gradient boosting is not "fit the residuals" — that is a special case. The general statement is that each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction, which for squared error happens to equal the residual. Say the general version and the whole family opens up: change the loss and you get regression, classification, ranking or quantile prediction from the same machinery.

Boosting bench — round by round
real trees fitted to real gradients
left: the ensemble's fit and the gradients the next tree will be fitted to · right: train and validation loss by round, with the early-stopping point marked

The algorithm

F₀(x) = argmin_c Σ L(yᵢ, c) the best constant — mean for MSE, median for MAE for t in 1..T: gᵢ = −∂L(yᵢ, F(xᵢ)) / ∂F(xᵢ) pseudo-residuals fit a shallow tree h_t to (xᵢ, gᵢ) F_t(x) = F_{t−1}(x) + η · h_t(x) L = ½(y−F)² → g = y − F the ordinary residual L = |y−F| → g = sign(y − F) only the direction — magnitude ignored L = logloss → g = y − p the residual in probability space

Switch the loss selector and look at the gradient panel. Under squared loss the gradients are the residuals, so a far-away outlier produces a huge gradient and the next tree lunges at it. Under absolute loss every gradient is ±1: the tree learns which direction to move each region but not how far, so outliers pull no harder than anything else. Raise the outlier share and watch which fit stays sane — this is S5's argument arriving inside the boosting loop.

Rounds, learning rate, and early stopping

The right-hand panel is the one to internalise. Training loss falls monotonically forever — a boosted ensemble can always add another tree that helps on the training set.
