Validation loss falls, bottoms out, and then rises. That minimum is the model you want, and finding it is what early_stopping_rounds automates.

η and T trade against each other almost exactly: halve the learning rate and you need roughly twice the rounds for the same fit, but the result generalises slightly better because each step commits less. Press Small η, many rounds and compare the validation minimum with the default. The practical recipe is fixed and worth stating plainly: set η small, set T large, and let early stopping choose T.

KnobRaise it and…Interacts with
Learning rate ηFaster fit, worse generalisation, earlier overfitNumber of rounds, inversely
Rounds TLower train loss always; validation loss eventually risesη and early stopping
DepthHigher-order interactions per tree, faster overfitRounds — deeper trees need fewer
SubsampleStochastic gradient boosting: less overfit, more variance per roundEverything; a cheap regulariser

Interview point

"Each tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss, not to the residual — the residual is just what that gradient is for squared error. That's why the same algorithm covers regression, classification and quantile prediction: you change the loss, the pseudo-residuals change, everything else is identical. In practice I use a small learning rate with a large round cap and let early stopping on a validation fold pick the round count."

The trap

Early stopping needs a validation set the model never trains on, and with time-ordered fraud data that set must be the future, not a random slice — otherwise you are choosing your round count on leaked information (A2, D4). The subtler version: if you tune η, depth and rounds against the same validation fold repeatedly, that fold has become training data and its optimism is real (D5). Keep a final untouched holdout for the number you actually report.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does each tree in gradient boosting fit?

The negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction — the pseudo-residuals.

Why is that the residual for MSE?

Because ∂/∂F of ½(y−F)² is −(y−F), so the negative gradient is exactly y−F.

What are MAE's pseudo-residuals?

sign(y−F): direction only, which is what makes it robust to outliers.

How do η and T relate?

Roughly inversely — halving η needs about twice the rounds, with slightly better generalisation.

How do you choose the number of rounds?

Early stopping on a validation set that reproduces the deployment condition.

What is stochastic gradient boosting?

Fitting each round on a random subsample of rows, which regularises and speeds up training.

Does training loss ever rise?

No — it falls monotonically. Only validation loss reveals overfitting.

Track G · Ensembles & boosting · Module G4

XGBoost MechanicsWhat the library adds to G3: a second-order split gain with regularisation built into the objective.

"It's gradient boosting but faster" is the answer that stalls an interview. XGBoost's real contribution is analytic: it takes a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, which yields a closed-form optimal leaf value and a closed-form split gain with the regularisation terms sitting inside them. This bench computes that gain for every candidate split so you can watch λ and γ change which splits survive.

Split-gain bench
real gradients & hessians
left: split gain across every candidate threshold, with the γ floor drawn · right: train and validation log-loss by round

The derivation that matters

expand the loss to second order at the current prediction: obj ≈ Σ [ gᵢ·w + ½·hᵢ·w² ] + ½λw² + γT g = first derivative, h = second for a leaf holding set I, minimise over its weight w: w* = − Σg / (Σh + λ) the optimal leaf value, closed form obj* = − ½ · (Σg)² / (Σh + λ) so splitting a node into L and R gains: Gain = ½ [ (ΣgL)²/(ΣhL+λ) + (ΣgR)²/(ΣhR+λ) − (Σg)²/(Σh+λ) ] − γ for log-loss: g = p − y, h = p(1 − p) h is largest at p = 0.5

Every hyperparameter people memorise is visible in those two lines. λ sits in the denominator, shrinking leaf values and damping gains from small nodes. γ is subtracted from the gain, so a split must earn at least γ to happen — pure pre-pruning. min_child_weight is a floor on Σh in a child, which for log-loss means a floor on Σp(1−p): a node full of confidently-classified rows has tiny hessian mass and gets blocked from splitting further, which is a far smarter brake than counting rows.

Watch the gain curve

The left panel plots the gain for every threshold at the current node. Raise γ and the floor rises through the curve — splits below it stop existing, and the tree gets shallower without you touching max_depth. Raise λ and the entire curve compresses, because the denominators grow. Set both to zero and the split search reduces to ordinary variance reduction.

Also in the libraryWhat it does
Sparsity-aware split findingLearns a default direction for missing values — no imputation needed (A4)
Weighted quantile sketchApproximate split candidates, hessian-weighted, so histograms scale to billions of rows
Column and row subsamplingRegularisation borrowed from random forests
Monotonic constraintsForces a feature's effect to be non-decreasing — often required in credit models
Cache-aware, blocked, out-of-coreThe engineering that made it dominate competitions

Interview point

"XGBoost takes a second-order expansion of the loss, so the optimal leaf weight is −Σg/(Σh+λ) and the split gain is the closed form built from those terms minus γ. That's why λ, γ and min_child_weight aren't bolt-ons — they're inside the objective. min_child_weight is a floor on hessian mass, which for log-loss means a node of confidently-classified rows can't keep splitting, and that's a better regulariser than a raw row count."

The trap

The defaults are not neutral for imbalanced data. scale_pos_weight reweights the positive class and will change your probability calibration — after using it you must recalibrate before applying a cost threshold (D6, D3). And on a 0.3% fraud rate, min_child_weight = 1 combined with deep trees produces leaves holding a handful of positives, which is memorisation dressed as capacity. Tune depth, min_child_weight and subsampling together; tuning them one at a time finds a poor corner of the space because they all control the same thing.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does XGBoost add over plain gradient boosting?

A second-order Taylor expansion giving closed-form leaf weights and split gains, with L2 and split-penalty regularisation inside the objective.

Write the optimal leaf weight.

w* = −Σg/(Σh + λ).

What does γ do?

Sets a minimum gain for a split to be made — direct pre-pruning.

What is min_child_weight really?

A minimum sum of hessians in a child; for log-loss that is Σp(1−p), not a row count.

g and h for log-loss?

g = p − y and h = p(1−p).

How does it handle missing values?

Sparsity-aware split finding learns a default branch direction from the data.

What does scale_pos_weight break?

Calibration — the output probabilities reflect the reweighted prior and must be corrected before a cost-based threshold.

Track G · Ensembles & boosting · Module G5

Feature Importance & SHAPThree methods, three different rankings of the same model, and only one of them answers a per-decision question.

"Which features matter" is four different questions wearing one name. This bench builds a model on data where the truth is known — some features genuinely drive the label, one is a high-cardinality decoy, two are near-duplicates — and then ranks them three ways. The rankings disagree, and knowing why is the difference between quoting a chart and explaining a decision.

Attribution bench
impurity proxy · permutation · exact Shapley
left: importance by the selected method, with truly useless features marked · right: all three methods side by side on the same model

What each method measures

MethodQuestion it answersKnown failure
Impurity / gainHow much did this column reduce training impurity? (this bench uses a depth-weighted split-usage proxy, which behaves the same way)Biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features; computed on training data, so noise features that enabled overfitting score highly
PermutationHow much does held-out performance drop if I shuffle this column?With correlated features, shuffling one leaves the model a perfect substitute — both look unimportant
SHAPFor this prediction, how much did each feature contribute relative to the base rate?Expensive; "importance" is then the mean absolute attribution, which is a different quantity from a drop in accuracy

Push decoy cardinality up. The decoy is pure noise with many distinct values, and impurity importance climbs steadily — it offers many split points, each of which reduces training impurity a little by carving out noise. Permutation importance, measured on held-out data, correctly leaves it near zero. That single comparison is why the scikit-learn documentation warns against the default.

Now push duplicate correlation to 0.99. Two near-identical informative features split the credit, and under permutation both fall toward zero, because shuffling one leaves the model able to read the other. The features are important; the measurement says they are not. Grouped permutation — shuffling correlated columns together — is the standard fix, and knowing that the problem exists is what an interviewer is checking.

The result that should unsettle you

Read the three-method panel with the decoy cardinality at 110. Permutation puts the decoy at 0.0% — correctly, since shuffling it costs the model no held-out AUC. The impurity proxy gives it 4.5%. And Shapley gives it 14.4% — the highest of the three. That is not a bug in the Shapley computation. Mean absolute SHAP measures how much the model's output moves with a feature, and a model that has partly overfitted a high-cardinality decoy genuinely does move with it. SHAP is describing the model faithfully, including its mistakes; permutation is describing the model's usefulness. They answer different questions, and only one of them tells you whether a feature is earning its place.

Why SHAP is a different kind of answer

φⱼ = Σ over subsets S ⊆ F\{j} |S|!(|F|−|S|−1)!/|F|! · [ f(S ∪ {j}) − f(S) ] average marginal contribution of feature j over every ordering local accuracy f(x) = base value + Σⱼ φⱼ(x) the attributions add up to the prediction consistency if a model relies more on a feature, its φ cannot decrease

The other two methods produce one number per feature per model. SHAP produces one number per feature per prediction, summing exactly to that prediction. That is what a reason code needs: not "amount matters in general" but "this transaction scored 0.71, and the amount contributed +0.22 of it". TreeSHAP computes this exactly for tree ensembles in polynomial time; this bench uses exact Shapley values over a small feature set, which is the definition rather than an approximation.

Interview point

"Default impurity importance is computed on training data and biased toward high-cardinality features, so I use permutation importance on a held-out set — and group correlated features when I permute, or they mask each other. When I need to explain an individual decision rather than the model, I use SHAP, because the attributions sum exactly to the prediction, which is what a reason code requires."

The trap

None of these are causal. A feature with high SHAP importance is one the model leans on, which may be a proxy — postcode standing in for something you are not allowed to use, device age standing in for account age. In a regulated setting that distinction is the whole review: a model can produce beautifully consistent attributions for a decision process that is nonetheless discriminatory, and SHAP will describe it faithfully without flagging anything. Attribution answers "what did the model do", never "what would happen if we changed it".

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is wrong with default impurity importance?

It is computed on training data and biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features.

How does permutation importance work?

Shuffle one column in held-out data and measure the drop in performance.

What breaks permutation importance?

Correlated features — the model reads the substitute, so both appear unimportant. Permute them as a group.

What does a SHAP value represent?

A feature's average marginal contribution to a specific prediction, over all orderings of the features.

What is local accuracy?

The base value plus all SHAP values equals the model's prediction for that row, exactly.

Global vs local importance?

Global ranks features for the model; local explains one decision. Mean absolute SHAP bridges them but is not a performance drop.

Is feature importance causal?

No — it describes what the model uses, not what would happen under intervention.

Track M · Anomaly detection · Module M1

Isolation ForestDon't model normality and measure distance from it — just count how few random cuts it takes to isolate a point.

Every other detector in this track builds a description of "normal" and scores distance from it. Isolation Forest inverts the problem: anomalies are few and different, so random axis-aligned splits isolate them in fewer cuts than they need for a point buried in a dense cluster. That inversion makes it linear in n, indifferent to distance metrics, and the default choice at fraud scale.

Isolation bench
real random trees · real path lengths
left: the anomaly surface with true anomalies circled · right: path-length distributions for normal and anomalous points — the entire mechanism, drawn

How the score is built

grow t trees on a subsample of ψ points: pick a random feature, pick a random split value between its min and max recurse until the point is alone or depth exceeds ceil(log₂ ψ) h(x) = path length to isolate x, averaged over trees c(ψ) = 2·H(ψ−1) − 2(ψ−1)/ψ expected path length in a random tree s(x) = 2^( −h(x) / c(ψ) ) → near 1 = anomalous, near 0.5 = ordinary

The right-hand panel plots the two path-length distributions. Anomalies sit left — isolated in three or four cuts — and normal points sit right, requiring eight or ten. The gap between those distributions is the detector's discriminative power, and when it closes the AUC readout falls with it.

Two design details are worth knowing. The subsample ψ defaults to 256 and smaller is often better: large samples let dense regions swamp small anomaly clusters, a problem the paper calls swamping. And the depth cap at log₂ψ costs nothing, because any point still unisolated by then is deep inside a dense region and its exact depth does not matter.

Where it fails

Select A small dense anomaly cluster. Isolation Forest is built on "anomalies are few and isolated" — a tight cluster of thirty fraudulent transactions that resemble each other is neither. They protect one another from isolation, path lengths lengthen, and the AUC drops. That is exactly the fraud-ring case, and it is the honest limitation to raise before someone else does.

Then select Correlated normal data. Splits are axis-aligned, so a diagonal band of perfectly normal points looks sparse along both axes individually, and points at the extremes of the band get flagged despite lying on the manifold. Rotating the data with PCA first (F1) removes most of that.

Interview point

"Isolation Forest scores by how few random cuts isolate a point, so it's O(n) and needs no distance metric — that's why it scales to transaction volumes. Its assumption is that anomalies are few and different, which breaks precisely on fraud rings: a tight cluster of similar fraudulent transactions isolates about as slowly as normal data. And because splits are axis-aligned it's sensitive to correlated features, so I decorrelate first."

The trap

contamination is not a property of your data — it is your assumption about it, and it does nothing but choose where to cut the score distribution. Setting it to 5% guarantees that exactly 5% of rows are labelled anomalous whether the true rate is 0.1% or 20%. The scores are the model's output; the label is your operating point, and it belongs to the same cost conversation as D3. Notice the bench reports AUC — which is contamination-free — separately from precision at the chosen cut, which is entirely determined by it.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is the core assumption?

Anomalies are few and different, so random partitioning isolates them in fewer splits.

How is the anomaly score computed?

s = 2^(−h(x)/c(ψ)), where h is the average isolation path length and c(ψ) normalises for subsample size.

Why subsample rather than use all rows?

Smaller subsamples reduce swamping and masking, and make training linear and cheap. 256 is the usual default.

What does the contamination parameter do?

Nothing to the model — it only picks the threshold on the score distribution.

When does Isolation Forest fail?

Clustered anomalies (fraud rings), correlated features because splits are axis-aligned, and very high dimensions with many irrelevant columns.

Complexity?

Training O(t·ψ·log ψ), scoring O(t·log ψ) per point — effectively linear and parallel.

Does it need scaling?

No — splits are per-feature and rank-based, like any tree.

Track M · Anomaly detection · Module M2

LOF & Distance-Based Detection"Far from everything" and "in a sparser place than its neighbours" are different questions. Only one of them survives varying density.

The simplest detector scores each point by its distance to its k-th nearest neighbour. It works until your data has regions of genuinely different density — which transaction data always does, because a high-street merchant and a niche crypto exchange have completely different normal volumes. Local Outlier Factor asks the relative question instead, and this bench shows exactly when that matters.

Density bench
real k-NN densities · real LOF
left: points sized by LOF score, true anomalies circled · right: AUC for both detectors as the density ratio grows

The two scores

k-distance score(x) = distance to the k-th nearest neighbour one global scale for the whole dataset LOF lrd(x) = 1 / mean reachability-distance to x's k neighbours LOF(x) = mean( lrd(neighbour) ) / lrd(x) LOF ≈ 1 → as dense as its neighbourhood LOF ≫ 1 → locally sparse — an outlier relative to its own region

Switch to Two very different densities and raise the ratio. The global k-distance detector starts flagging ordinary points in the sparse cluster — they really are far from their neighbours, in absolute terms — while missing genuine anomalies sitting close to the dense cluster. LOF, which divides by the local density, keeps both straight. The right-hand panel plots both AUCs against the ratio, and the curves separate exactly where the assumption breaks.

On a single-density dataset the two are close, and the global detector is cheaper. That is the honest framing: LOF is not better in general, it is better when density varies — and knowing which situation you are in is the actual skill.

k, and the two failure modes

k too smallk about rightk too large
A tight pair of anomalies looks like a dense neighbourhood to itself — they mask each otherLOF ≈ 1 for normal points, ≫ 1 for anomaliesNeighbourhoods span multiple clusters; the local question becomes global again

Push noise dimensions up and watch both detectors decay. Everything in A6 applies with full force here: LOF is a distance method, and in high dimensions distances concentrate until the density ratio it computes is meaningless. LOF on a hundred raw features is not a detector, it is a random number generator with good documentation — reduce dimensions first, or use a method that does not measure distance at all (M1).

Interview point

"k-distance asks whether a point is far from everything; LOF asks whether it's in a sparser place than its own neighbours are. That ratio is what makes LOF work when density varies across the dataset — different merchant segments, for instance. The cost is O(n²) without an index and full sensitivity to the curse of dimensionality, so I reduce dimensions first or use Isolation Forest at scale."

The trap

LOF is transductive by construction: the score depends on the neighbourhood inside the dataset you fitted, so there is no natural "predict on a new row". scikit-learn's novelty=True mode exists to bolt one on, and it changes the semantics — you can no longer call fit_predict on the training data. For a streaming fraud system this matters more than the accuracy: a detector that must re-examine the whole reference set for every incoming transaction is an architectural commitment, not just a modelling choice.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does LOF compare?

A point's local reachability density against the average density of its k neighbours.

What does LOF ≈ 1 mean?

The point is about as dense as its neighbourhood — ordinary.

When does a global distance detector fail?

When density varies across the data: sparse-region normals get flagged and dense-region anomalies get missed.

Effect of k too small or too large?

Too small and nearby anomalies mask each other; too large and the neighbourhood spans clusters, losing locality.

Complexity?

O(n²) naively, better with a spatial index in low dimensions — which degrades above roughly 20.

Why does high dimensionality hurt LOF specifically?

It is built on distance ratios, and distances concentrate as dimension grows.

Can LOF score unseen points?

Not natively — it is transductive; novelty mode adds that capability with different semantics.

Track M · Anomaly detection · Module M3

One-Class SVM & Elliptic EnvelopeTwo boundary methods with opposite assumptions: one insists normality is an ellipse, the other lets it be any shape at all.

M1 counted cuts and M2 compared densities. The third family draws a boundary around normal data and calls everything outside it anomalous. Which of the two you pick is entirely a bet about the shape of "normal" — and this bench lets you change that shape and watch one method hold while the other collapses.

Boundary bench
Mahalanobis · RBF one-class, 80 random features
left: the elliptic envelope's contour · right: the one-class RBF boundary · true anomalies circled in both

Elliptic envelope

fit μ and Σ, then score by Mahalanobis distance: d²(x) = (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ) d² ~ χ²(p) if the data really is Gaussian so a threshold comes from a χ² quantile — a rare case where the cut has a principled default

This is the most assumption-heavy detector in the track and, on data that satisfies the assumption, the best. Select Single Gaussian blob: it is close to optimal, because it is fitting exactly the right model. Then select Two clusters and watch it fail in the most instructive way possible. The fitted ellipse spans both clusters, so the empty space between them — where the anomalies are — sits at the ellipse's centre and scores as the most normal region in the dataset. The AUC readout drops to about 0.10: not merely useless but inverted, ranking the anomalies as safer than genuine normal points. Any transaction landing in that gap is worse than invisible.

Robustness matters here: the plain covariance estimate is dragged by the very outliers you are hunting, so real implementations use the Minimum Covariance Determinant, which fits Σ on the tightest subset of points. Raise contaminated training data and watch the plain envelope inflate to swallow the anomalies it should be flagging — the masking effect, in one slider.

One-class SVM

The one-class SVM finds a boundary that separates the data from the origin in kernel space with maximum margin, keeping at most a ν fraction outside. Two things fall out of that: ν is both an upper bound on the outlier fraction and a lower bound on the support-vector fraction, which is a genuinely useful fact, and the RBF kernel means the boundary can take any shape — so the two-cluster and curved cases that destroy the envelope are handled.

The cost is γ. Too small and the boundary becomes a blob resembling the envelope; too large and it shrink-wraps every training point, so a slightly unusual but perfectly legitimate transaction falls outside. Push γ up and watch the anomaly region fragment — the same memorisation failure as C4, in an unsupervised setting where you have no validation labels to catch it.

Elliptic envelopeOne-class SVMIsolation Forest
Shape assumptionA single ellipseAny, via the kernelNone
ThresholdPrincipled (χ²)νcontamination
Scales to millions of rowsYesNo — O(n²)+Yes
Tolerates contaminated training dataOnly with MCDSomewhat, via νReasonably
Needs scalingNo — Σ⁻¹ handles itYesNo

Interview point

"Elliptic envelope assumes normal data is a single Gaussian and scores Mahalanobis distance, which gives it a principled χ² threshold — and makes it fail badly on multi-modal data, where the gap between two clusters scores as normal. One-class SVM drops the shape assumption via the kernel and uses ν, which bounds both the outlier fraction and the support-vector fraction. Neither scales like Isolation Forest, so at transaction volume I use them for analysis rather than serving."

The trap

Both methods are usually described as trained on "clean" normal data, and you will not have any. Fraud labels are incomplete by construction — you only ever learn about the frauds someone caught — so your "normal" training set contains undetected fraud. That contamination is what MCD and ν exist to absorb, and it is worth stating explicitly in an interview, because it distinguishes semi-supervised novelty detection (clean training data, a luxury) from unsupervised outlier detection (contaminated data, the reality). The bench's contamination slider is the honest version of your situation, not an edge case.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does Mahalanobis distance measure?

Distance from the mean scaled by the covariance — a χ²-distributed quantity if the data is Gaussian.

Why does elliptic envelope fail on two clusters?

One ellipse spans both, so the empty region between them scores as normal.

What does ν control in a one-class SVM?

It upper-bounds the fraction of training points outside the boundary and lower-bounds the support-vector fraction.

What does γ do?

Sets boundary locality — too large and it shrink-wraps individual training points.

Why use Minimum Covariance Determinant?

The plain covariance estimate is inflated by the outliers being hunted; MCD fits on the tightest subset instead.

Novelty detection vs outlier detection?

Novelty assumes clean training data and scores new points; outlier detection assumes the training data is already contaminated.

Which of the three scales to millions of rows?

Isolation Forest and the envelope; kernel one-class SVM does not.

Track M · Anomaly detection · Module M4

Evaluating Detectors Without LabelsThe question every anomaly-detection project actually fails on, and the one no tutorial answers.

M1 to M3 gave you three detectors. Now choose between them with no labels — which is the real condition, because if you had reliable anomaly labels you would be training a classifier. This bench holds a hidden ground truth, lets you use only the tools you would genuinely have, and then reveals how badly each of those tools estimated the answer.

Evaluation bench
ground truth hidden until scored
left: each detector's true AUC against the proxy estimate you could actually have computed · right: what the label budget buys, by detector

Three things you can do, and what each is worth

1. Inject synthetic anomalies

Generate points from a different distribution, add them, and measure how well each detector ranks them. Cheap, fully automatic, and biased by exactly how you generated them. Drag injected spread: wide-spread injections are easy for every detector, so the proxy ranks them as roughly equal and tells you nothing; injections that resemble your real anomalies give a proxy AUC close to the truth. The catch is circular — you would need to know what your anomalies look like to generate good ones, which is the thing you were trying to find out.

2. Spend a label budget

You can usually get some labels: send k cases to an analyst. The rational allocation is the detectors' top-ranked cases, which measures precision@k — the metric that matches how the system is actually consumed, since a review queue only ever sees the top of the ranking. What it cannot tell you is recall: the frauds no detector ranked highly are never labelled, so they are invisible to your evaluation and to your model forever. That asymmetry is the structural problem with fraud evaluation and it is worth naming explicitly.

3. Compare detectors to each other

Rank correlation between detectors is free and genuinely informative — but about agreement, not correctness. Two detectors that both assume "anomalies are isolated" will agree beautifully and both miss a fraud ring. The useful version is the inverse: disagreement is a shortlist. Cases one detector ranks first and another ignores are the highest-information rows to spend labels on, which turns method 3 into a smarter version of method 2.

MethodEstimatesFails when
Injected anomaliesRanking of a distribution you choseYour injections don't resemble real anomalies
Precision@k on a budgetTop-of-queue quality — what operations feelAlways silent about recall
Detector agreementShared assumptionsCorrelated blind spots look like consensus
Delayed real labelsThe truth, eventually30–90 days late, and only for cases someone reviewed

Interview point

"Without labels I don't pretend to measure AUC. I measure precision@k on an analyst budget, because that's what a review queue consumes, and I spend that budget where detectors disagree rather than where they agree — agreement usually means shared assumptions, not correctness. Injected anomalies are a sanity check, not an evaluation, because the result depends on how I generated them. The only real answer is delayed labels, and the architecture has to be built around that lag."

The trap

Every case reviewed was reviewed because a model ranked it highly, so your labelled set is a sample of the model's own beliefs — the feedback loop from V3. Precision@k measured on that set is optimistic, and worse, the next model trains on it and inherits the blind spot. The standard countermeasure is a small randomly-sampled review quota alongside the ranked queue: deliberately spend a slice of scarce analyst time on cases the model thinks are boring. It looks wasteful on a dashboard and it is the only thing that measures what you are missing.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why can't you just use AUC for anomaly detection?

It needs labels; if you had reliable ones you would train a supervised classifier instead.

What does precision@k measure and why is it the right metric?

Hit rate among the top k ranked cases — it matches a review queue's finite capacity.

What can precision@k never tell you?

Recall — the anomalies nothing ranked highly are never labelled.

What is the risk of evaluating on injected anomalies?

The result reflects your injection distribution, not the real one.

Does high agreement between detectors mean they are right?

No — it usually means they share assumptions and therefore share blind spots.

Best use of a small label budget?

Cases where detectors disagree, plus a random sample to estimate what you're missing.

Why is a reviewed-case dataset biased?

Cases were reviewed because a model flagged them, so the labels reflect the model's beliefs and reinforce its blind spots.

Track X · Graph ML for fraud · Module X1

Wallet Graphs & CentralityFraud is a shape in a network before it is a row in a table. Centrality is how you turn the shape into a feature.

Every model so far treated a transaction as an independent row. On-chain, it is an edge — and the fraud patterns that matter are structural: many mules paying into one collector, one source fanning out to many, a long peeling chain moving value in small hops. This bench builds a synthetic wallet graph containing all three motifs and measures which centrality measure actually finds each one.

Centrality bench
real graph · real Brandes betweenness
left: the graph, fraud wallets in gold, node size by the selected metric · right: AUC of every metric on the same graph

The features, and what each one sees

FeatureDefinitionCatchesMisses
DegreeNumber of distinct counterpartiesCollectors and distributors — hubs by constructionPeeling chains, where every node has degree 2
In-degree / out-degree ratioIncoming vs outgoing counterpartiesDirection: collectors have high in, distributors high outAnything symmetric
BetweennessShare of shortest paths passing through the nodeIntermediaries — chain hops, bridges between clustersEndpoints; costly to compute exactly
Clustering coefficientHow many of my neighbours are connected to each otherTight rings, where everyone transacts with everyoneStar and chain motifs, which have zero clustering

The right-hand panel scores all four on the same graph, and the point of the module is that no single one wins. Degree finds the stars and is blind to the chains; betweenness does the reverse. In production you compute all of them and let a gradient booster decide — which is exactly how graph features enter a fraud model in practice: not as a graph algorithm making the decision, but as columns feeding the tabular model from G4.

The cost that decides your architecture

degree O(E) trivial, streaming-friendly clustering coefficient O(Σ deg²) fine until a hub has a million neighbours betweenness O(V·E) infeasible above ~10⁵ nodes — sample sources instead PageRank O(E) per iter the practical choice at scale (X2)

Drag betweenness samples down to 10 and watch its AUC become unstable: the sampled estimate is noisy, and that noise is the price of making the computation possible at all. This matters operationally — betweenness on a full transaction graph is a batch job, so the feature your real-time scorer reads is always slightly stale, and how stale is a design decision you should be able to defend.

Interview point

"Fraud motifs are structural — collectors, distributors, peeling chains — and different centralities catch different ones: degree finds the stars, betweenness finds the chain intermediaries, clustering coefficient finds tight rings. So I compute several as features and let the booster combine them, rather than picking one. Betweenness is O(V·E), so at graph scale it's a sampled batch feature, which means the real-time model reads a stale value and that lag has to be part of the design."

The trap

Exchange and mixer addresses have enormous degree and betweenness by construction, and they are not fraud — they are infrastructure. A model trained on raw centrality will learn "high degree = risky" and flag every exchange deposit address in the dataset. The standard fixes are an entity list that excludes known services, degree-normalised versions of each metric, and features computed on the graph with those hubs removed. Say that unprompted: it is the first thing anyone who has actually built on-chain features discovers, usually the hard way.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Name three fraud motifs in a transaction graph.

Collector (fan-in from mules), distributor (fan-out), and peeling chain (long low-degree path moving value in hops).

Which metric catches a peeling chain?

Betweenness — every chain node lies on many shortest paths. Degree cannot, since each node has degree 2.

What does clustering coefficient measure?

The fraction of a node's neighbours that are connected to each other — high in tight rings, zero in stars and chains.

Why is betweenness rarely computed exactly?

O(V·E) — at graph scale you sample source nodes and accept a noisy estimate.

How do graph features usually enter a fraud model?

As columns in a tabular gradient-boosted model, not as a graph algorithm making the decision.

Why do exchange addresses break centrality features?

They are hubs by design, so raw centrality conflates infrastructure with risk. Exclude or degree-normalise them.

What is the operational consequence of expensive graph features?

They are batch-computed, so the serving model reads a stale value — the staleness window is a design decision.

Track X · Graph ML for fraud · Module X2

PageRank & Risk PropagationYou know a handful of bad wallets. Guilt by association, done properly, turns them into a risk score for everything else.

Fraud labels are scarce and structural evidence is abundant — so the highest-leverage move in graph fraud work is propagation: start from confirmed bad wallets and let risk diffuse outward along the edges, decaying with distance. Personalised PageRank is the standard way to do that, it runs in O(E) per iteration, and it has exactly one failure mode you must handle.

Propagation bench
real power iteration
left: propagated risk, seeds ringed in teal · right: AUC against damping, and how far risk actually travels

The iteration

p ← α · Aᵀ p + (1 − α) · s s = the seed vector, not uniform α controls how far risk travels: expected walk length ≈ 1/(1 − α) α = 0.50 → ~2 hops α = 0.85 → ~7 hops α = 0.95 → ~20 hops (1 − α) is the restart probability — every walk keeps falling back to the known-bad set

Personalised PageRank differs from the classic algorithm in one place: the teleport vector points at your seeds rather than spreading uniformly, so the resulting score is "how reachable is this wallet from known fraud", not "how important is this wallet overall". Drag α and watch the AUC curve on the right: too low and risk never leaves the seeds' immediate neighbours, too high and it spreads until everything looks equally suspicious. There is a peak, and it depends on how clustered the fraud is.

The hub problem

Raise hub wallets from 0. These are exchanges — enormous degree, connected to everyone, entirely legitimate. Under raw propagation they absorb risk from every seed and then re-radiate it across the whole graph, so their neighbours (which is most wallets) all inherit a share. The AUC collapses, and the failure is not subtle: your risk score becomes a proxy for "has ever touched an exchange".

Switch to Degree-normalised, where each edge's contribution is divided by √deg of the receiving node. Hubs stop acting as risk superconductors, and the AUC recovers. The same idea appears again in X4 as the symmetric normalisation inside a graph convolution — it is not a coincidence, it is the same problem being solved twice.

Interview point

"Personalised PageRank propagates risk from known-bad seeds, with the teleport vector pointing at the seeds so the score means reachability-from-fraud rather than global importance. α sets how far it travels — expected walk length is 1/(1−α). The failure mode is hubs: exchanges absorb and re-radiate risk to everything, so I degree-normalise the edge weights or drop known service addresses entirely."

The trap

Propagation is guilt by association, and that phrase should make you uncomfortable in a regulated setting. A wallet two hops from a sanctioned address may be a victim, a counterparty, or an exchange's internal transfer — the score cannot distinguish them. Treat it as a triage feature that routes cases to review, never as an automated decision, and be ready to explain the path that produced the score. Also note the label leakage risk: if you train a supervised model on features computed from a graph that already contains your labels as seeds, the feature encodes the answer (A2), so seeds must come from a strictly earlier period than the labels you are predicting.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
How does personalised PageRank differ from standard PageRank?

The teleport vector points at a seed set instead of being uniform, so the score measures reachability from those seeds.

What does α control?

How far risk propagates; expected walk length is 1/(1−α).

Why do hubs break propagation?

High-degree legitimate nodes absorb risk from many seeds and re-radiate it to everything they touch.

Two fixes for the hub problem.

Degree-normalised edge weights, and excluding known service or exchange addresses.

Complexity per iteration?

O(E) — which is why it scales where betweenness does not.

What leakage risk does seeding create?

If the seeds are the same labels you are predicting, the feature encodes the answer; seeds must predate the label period.

Why is propagation a triage feature rather than a decision?

Proximity to fraud does not distinguish an accomplice from a victim or a counterparty, so it routes to review rather than deciding.

Track X · Graph ML for fraud · Module X3

Community DetectionFraud rings are communities. Finding them is easy; finding the small ones is the part that fails.

A fraud ring is a set of wallets that transact far more with each other than with the outside — which is the definition of a community. Modularity-based detection finds them without labels, which is exactly what you want when labels are scarce. It also has a documented, mathematically guaranteed resolution limit: below a certain size, communities get swallowed by their neighbours no matter how tightly connected they are.

Community bench
label propagation · real modularity
left: detected communities by colour, planted rings ringed in gold · right: ring recovery as ring size and leakage change

What modularity measures

Q = (1/2m) Σ_ij [ A_ij − k_i·k_j/(2m) ] · δ(c_i, c_j) A_ij is there an edge? k_i k_j/2m how many edges you'd EXPECT by chance given the degrees δ(c_i,c_j) only count pairs in the same community Q ≈ 0 no more structure than a random graph with the same degrees Q > 0.3 meaningful community structure

The bench uses label propagation — each node repeatedly adopts its neighbours' most common label — which is O(E) per round and the only community method that scales to a full transaction graph. Louvain and Leiden optimise Q directly and give better partitions, at more cost. All of them share the limitation below.

The resolution limit

Here is where the bench and the textbook part company, and the difference is worth knowing. Drag ring size down to 4: label propagation, which this bench uses, recovers the small rings perfectly well. The resolution limit is a property of modularity optimisation — Louvain, Leiden, greedy agglomeration — not of community detection in general. In those methods the expected-edges term k_i·k_j/2m scales with the size of the whole graph, so in a large network the expected number of edges between two small groups falls below one, and merging them always increases Q. Small communities therefore cannot be resolved, however dense they are internally, and the threshold grows as √m. Label propagation optimises nothing global — each node simply adopts its neighbours' majority label — so it has no such floor, which is a concrete reason to prefer it for fraud rings even though it produces messier partitions.

That is a direct problem if you reach for Louvain by default: a ring of six wallets inside a graph of ten million is exactly the case it cannot see. The practical responses are to run detection on subgraphs rather than the whole network, to use a resolution parameter, or to use a method without the limitation — label propagation and clique percolation both qualify.

Now raise leakage. Real rings are not isolated: they touch exchanges, victims and ordinary counterparties. Past roughly half the edges pointing outward, the ring stops being a community in any measurable sense, and the recovery curve tells you where that boundary sits.

Interview point

"A fraud ring is a community — more internal edges than chance predicts given the degrees, which is what modularity measures. The catch is the resolution limit: because the null model scales with total graph size, small communities get absorbed no matter how dense they are, and that threshold grows with √m. So on a large transaction graph I run detection on neighbourhood subgraphs around flagged wallets rather than globally, or use a resolution parameter."

The trap

Community detection has no labels, so it will always return communities — including on a random graph, where it happily reports a partition with positive modularity. Before believing a partition, compare its Q against the same algorithm run on a degree-preserving random rewiring of your graph. If the real Q is not clearly higher, you have found nothing, and the neat clusters on your slide are an artefact of the algorithm's optimisation rather than a property of the data. This is M4's problem wearing different clothes: an unsupervised method with no evaluation is a method you cannot defend.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does modularity compare against?

A null model — the edges you would expect between nodes given their degrees in a random graph.

What is the resolution limit?

Modularity optimisation cannot resolve communities below a size scaling with √m, because merging small groups increases Q. Label propagation, which optimises nothing global, does not share it.

Why does that matter for fraud?

Rings are small and the graph is huge — precisely the case the limit hides.

Two ways around it.

Run detection on neighbourhood subgraphs, or use a resolution parameter / a method without the limitation.

Why label propagation over Louvain at scale?

O(E) per round and trivially parallel; Louvain optimises Q better but costs more.

How do you know a partition means anything?

Compare its modularity against a degree-preserving random rewiring of the same graph.

What happens as a ring leaks edges outward?

Its internal edge share falls toward chance and it stops being detectable as a community.

Track X · Graph ML for fraud · Module X4

GNN IntuitionA graph neural network is feature averaging over neighbours, repeated. Understanding that explains both why it works and why deep ones fail.

Strip away the framework and a graph convolution is one line: each node's new representation is a function of its own features and the average of its neighbours'. Stack k layers and information travels k hops. That is the whole mechanism — and it immediately predicts the two things that matter: a GNN beats a tabular model exactly when the neighbourhood carries signal the node itself lacks, and stacking too many layers destroys the model.

Message-passing bench
real aggregation · real logistic head
left: AUC by number of layers — the rise and then the collapse · right: how similar node representations become as layers stack (over-smoothing, measured)

One layer, written out

h_v^(k+1) = σ( W · [ (1−β)·mean_{u ∈ N(v)} h_u^(k) + β·h_v^(k) ] ) ^ aggregate ^ self / skip term GCN normalises by 1/√(deg_u · deg_v) — the same hub fix as X2 GraphSAGE samples a fixed number of neighbours, so the cost per node is bounded GAT learns attention weights over neighbours instead of averaging uniformly

This bench does the aggregation for real and fits a logistic head on the result, so the AUC readouts are honest — what it does not do is learn the weight matrix W, which is the part a framework contributes. Everything structural about a GNN's behaviour is visible without it.

Two results, both mechanical

With signal in the neighbourhood — a wallet's risk determined by who it transacts with rather than by its own attributes — zero layers is just a tabular model on node features and scores 0.500, exactly chance, because the tags are assigned independently of structure. One layer jumps to 0.782. That gap is the case for graph learning. Switch to signal in the node itself and the sign reverses: the tabular model scores 0.909 and two layers of message passing drag it down to 0.713, because averaging with neighbours who know nothing dilutes a feature that already had the answer. If your data looks like that, a GNN is an expensive way to underperform gradient boosting.

Now set the self-weight to zero and push layers to eight: AUC falls back to 0.536 while representation similarity climbs from 1% to 32%. Each layer averages a node with a wider neighbourhood, so after enough rounds every node's representation converges to the graph average and nodes become indistinguishable. This is over-smoothing, it is why production GNNs are two or three layers deep when convolutional nets are a hundred, and the self-weight slider is the standard mitigation. Set it to 0.7 at the same eight layers and the AUC returns to 0.771 with similarity back down to 9% — a skip connection preserving each node's own identity through the averaging, measured rather than asserted.

Interview point

"A GNN layer is aggregate-then-update: each node's representation becomes a function of its own features and its neighbours', so k layers means a k-hop receptive field. That's why they're shallow — stack too many and every representation converges to the graph mean, which is over-smoothing, and skip connections are the standard fix. I'd only reach for one when the neighbourhood carries signal the node's own features don't, because otherwise boosted trees on graph features like the ones in X1 and X2 are cheaper and usually better."

The trap

Transductive versus inductive is the question that decides whether a GNN can ship. The original GCN is transductive: it learns representations for the graph it was trained on, and a brand-new wallet appearing at 3am is not in it. GraphSAGE is inductive precisely because it learns an aggregation function that can be applied to unseen nodes — which is the only variant that works for a live fraud stream. And the neighbourhood explosion is real: two hops from a wallet that touched an exchange can be most of the graph, which is why neighbour sampling exists and why the latency budget, not the accuracy, usually decides the architecture.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does one GNN layer do?

Aggregates neighbour representations, combines them with the node's own, and transforms the result.

What does the number of layers control?

The receptive field — k layers means information from k hops away.

What is over-smoothing?

Repeated averaging drives all node representations toward the same value, so nodes become indistinguishable.

Standard mitigations?

Few layers, skip or residual connections, and normalisation.

Transductive vs inductive?

Transductive models only score nodes present at training; inductive ones like GraphSAGE learn a function applicable to new nodes.

Why does GCN normalise by 1/√(deg·deg)?

To stop high-degree hubs dominating the aggregation — the same hub problem as PageRank propagation.

When is a GNN not worth it?

When node features already carry the signal — boosted trees on graph-derived features are cheaper and usually stronger.

Track V · Governance & the arms race · Module V1

Fairness & Bias MetricsThree reasonable definitions of "fair". When base rates differ, you can satisfy at most one.

Fairness is not one metric with a threshold. It is a family of mutually incompatible definitions, and the incompatibility is a theorem, not a tuning problem. This bench computes every standard metric on the same model and lets you try to equalise them, so you can watch fixing one break another — which is the conversation you will actually have with a model-risk committee.

Fairness bench
calibrated scores, two groups
left: score distributions by group with the applied cut(s) · right: every fairness gap at once — you are trying to get all four bars to zero

The definitions

CriterionEqualises across groupsAlso called
Demographic parityFlag rate — P(flag)Statistical parity, the "four-fifths rule" in US employment law
Equal opportunityRecall — P(flag | actually fraud)TPR parity
Equalised oddsRecall and false-positive rateThe strict version of the above
Predictive parityPrecision — P(fraud | flagged)Outcome test, PPV parity
Calibration by groupA 0.2 means 20% in every groupTest fairness, sufficiency

The impossibility

If two groups have different base rates, and the model is calibrated, then equal false-positive AND false-negative rates are mathematically impossible. (Kleinberg–Mullainathan–Raghavan; Chouldechova)

Set the base-rate ratio to 3 and press each policy in turn. Equalise recall and the flag-rate gap and precision gap open up. Equalise flag rate and recall diverges — the higher-base-rate group loses coverage of real fraud. There is no slider position that zeroes all four bars, and the bench will not let you find one, because none exists.

This is why "is the model fair?" is not answerable as posed. The answerable question is which error do we distribute equally, and who bears the remainder — and that is a policy decision requiring a documented rationale, not a threshold you tune. Being able to say that sentence, and then name which criterion your use case implies, is the whole skill.

Proxies

Raise proxy feature strength. No protected attribute is in the model — the bench does not have one — but a correlated feature is, and every gap widens. Removing the protected attribute does not remove the disparity; it removes your ability to measure it. This is why fairness work requires collecting the attribute you are forbidden to use, a genuine tension that regulators handle explicitly and that catches people out.

Interview point

"Fairness definitions conflict by theorem: with different base rates, a calibrated model cannot have equal false-positive and false-negative rates across groups. So I don't ask whether a model is fair — I ask which criterion the use case implies, document why, and monitor the remainder. And I know that dropping the protected attribute doesn't remove disparity, because proxies carry it; it just removes my ability to measure it."

The trap

Group-specific thresholds are the obvious technical fix and are illegal in several jurisdictions for protected characteristics — US fair-lending rules in particular treat explicitly different cut-offs by race or sex as disparate treatment regardless of intent. So the levers you actually have are upstream: better features for the under-served group, more training data, a different objective, or a different operating point applied uniformly. Proposing per-group thresholds in a bank interview signals you have not met the legal constraint; naming that constraint yourself signals you have.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define demographic parity and equal opportunity.

Demographic parity equalises the flag rate; equal opportunity equalises recall among those who are actually positive.

State the impossibility result.

With unequal base rates, a calibrated model cannot simultaneously equalise false-positive and false-negative rates across groups.

What is predictive parity?

Equal precision across groups — of those flagged, the same fraction are truly positive.

Does removing the protected attribute make a model fair?

No — proxies carry the information. It removes measurability, not disparity.

Why are group-specific thresholds problematic?

They can constitute disparate treatment under fair-lending law, whatever their statistical justification.

What is the four-fifths rule?

A US guideline flagging adverse impact when a group's selection rate falls below 80% of the highest group's.

So what do you actually do?

Choose and document a criterion tied to the use case, fix it upstream in features and data, and monitor the disparity you accepted.

Track V · Governance & the arms race · Module V2

Model Risk Management & SR 11-7What a bank's validation function will ask for, and the evidence pack that answers it.

At Barclays or JPMorgan a model does not go live because its PR-AUC improved. It goes live because an independent validation team accepted an evidence pack. The governing framework — the Fed and OCC's SR 11-7 — defines model risk as the risk of loss from a model that is wrong or misused, and requires three things: sound development, independent validation, and ongoing monitoring. This bench computes the quantitative half of that pack.

Validation bench
champion vs challenger, out-of-time
performance view: in-time vs out-of-time for both models, with score PSI · sensitivity view: output response to a shock in each input

The three pillars, and what each demands of you

PillarValidation asksArtefact you supply
DevelopmentIs the design conceptually sound and documented?Design rationale, data lineage, feature justification, assumption log
Independent validationDoes someone who didn't build it agree?Out-of-time results, benchmark comparison, sensitivity analysis, limitations
Ongoing monitoringIs it still the model you approved?Drift dashboards (D7), performance tracking, override logs, breach thresholds

What the bench computes

Out-of-time degradation. Every validation pack contains a holdout from a later period, not a random split — D4's argument, now as a compliance requirement. Raise the drift slider and read both models' degradation. What the bench actually shows is worth more than the folk wisdom: at zero drift the tree ensemble does not beat the logistic challenger at all (uplift −0.018), so its complexity is buying nothing; under heavy drift both degrade, and the ensemble degrades less (0.119 against 0.172), so its uplift turns positive. Complexity that is unjustified in-sample can still buy robustness out-of-time — and a validation pack has to show both numbers, because either one alone tells the wrong story.

Benchmark comparison. A simple, well-understood challenger — here a logistic regression — is mandatory, not optional. If your gradient-boosted champion beats it by two points of AUC and is ten times harder to explain, validation will ask whether the two points justify the model risk. Sometimes the answer is no — as it is here at zero drift — and knowing that is a mark of maturity rather than defeat.

Sensitivity analysis. Switch views. Each input is shocked by a fixed percentage and the mean change in output is measured. A model whose output moves violently on a small shock to one feature is fragile in a way AUC cannot see, and that feature becomes a monitoring priority. This is also where implausible behaviour surfaces — a risk score that falls when a fraud-indicative feature rises will not pass, however good the AUC.

Stability. Score-distribution PSI between development and out-of-time is the standard stability statistic (D7). Above 0.25 you are explaining yourself; the thresholds are convention, so the defensible move is to state which convention you adopted and why.

Interview point

"Under SR 11-7 a model needs sound development, independent validation and ongoing monitoring — so I build the evidence pack alongside the model rather than afterwards: out-of-time performance, a simple challenger benchmark, sensitivity analysis per input, documented limitations, and monitoring thresholds with defined breach actions. In a regulated setting an unexplainable two-point AUC gain is often not worth the model risk, and being able to say that is part of the job."

The trap

SR 11-7's definition of model risk includes misuse, not just error. A model validated for one purpose and quietly reused for another is a finding even if it performs well — a fraud score repurposed as a creditworthiness signal, say, or a model approved on retail transactions applied to a commercial portfolio. Every model needs a documented scope of intended use, and every reuse needs its own approval. This is also the sharpest difference between shipping in a bank and shipping in a startup: the constraint is not "does it work" but "can an independent party reconstruct why we believed it works, from documents, after you have left".

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is SR 11-7?

US Federal Reserve and OCC supervisory guidance on model risk management, defining model risk and requiring development standards, independent validation and ongoing monitoring.

How does it define model risk?

The potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs.

What is a challenger model for?

Benchmarking — establishing that the champion's complexity buys enough performance to justify its model risk.

Why out-of-time rather than a random holdout?

It reproduces deployment: train on the past, validate on a later period, and expose degradation from drift.

What is sensitivity analysis?

Shocking each input and measuring the output response, to find fragility and implausible directional behaviour that AUC cannot show.

What does "scope of intended use" mean?

The documented purpose a model was validated for; applying it elsewhere is misuse and requires fresh approval.

Who performs validation?

A function independent of the developers, with authority to challenge and to block deployment.

Track V · Governance & the arms race · Module V3

Adversaries, Delayed Labels & Feedback LoopsThe model only learns about what it flagged, and the fraudster is watching what it flags. Both facts compound.

Every other module assumed a fixed data-generating process. Fraud does not have one — it has an opponent who observes your decisions and moves. Combine that with labels that only arrive for cases someone reviewed, and you get a system that can degrade badly while every dashboard it produces looks healthy. This bench runs the loop over many periods so you can watch that happen.

Closed-loop bench
retrain · adapt · repeat
left: what the dashboard shows (precision on reviewed cases) against what is actually happening (true recall) · right: where the fraud population has moved relative to the model's attention

The three mechanisms, and how they interact

Selective labelling

You only learn the outcome of cases you reviewed, and you reviewed them because the model ranked them highly. So the next training set is a sample of the current model's beliefs — the frauds it missed are absent, and it therefore has no gradient pointing toward them. The blind spot is self-sealing.

Delayed labels

Chargebacks arrive 30–90 days late, so the model you retrain today learns from a world one quarter old. Against a static process that is a minor cost; against an adversary it means you are always fitting the previous strategy.

Adaptation

Raise adversary adaptation and the fraud population drifts away from the region the model attends to. Note what happens to the two lines on the left: measured precision stays high — the cases the model flags really are fraud — while true recall collapses, because an increasing share of fraud now happens in a region the model neither flags nor samples. Every number on the dashboard is real and the system is failing.

measured precision = hits / reviewed computed from the labels you have true recall = hits / all fraud requires labels you don't have the gap between them is the thing you cannot see and must estimate anyway

The measurement that looks wasteful

Press Add a random quota. A slice of review capacity is spent on cases sampled at random rather than by rank. Precision on that slice is terrible by construction, which is exactly why it gets cut in every efficiency review. It is also the only unbiased estimate of what you are missing, and the only training signal from outside the model's current beliefs.

Now read the recall line carefully, because the bench does something more useful than confirming the obvious: recall does not recover, even at a 50% quota. In this configuration the adapting share has moved toward ordinary behaviour in both observed features, so labelling more of it changes nothing — there is no boundary left to learn. The quota bought visibility, not performance: it turned an invisible failure into a measured one, and that measurement is the diagnosis. The answer is a feature the adversary cannot cheaply move — account age, historical graph position (X1) — not more sampling.

This is the same argument as M4's evaluation problem and D7's blind spot, arriving as an operational policy: you must deliberately spend scarce capacity on cases the model thinks are boring, and you must be honest that what it buys is measurement rather than a fix. Being able to make that distinction — this is a feature problem, not a threshold problem, and here is the number that proves it — is a genuinely senior conversation.

Interview point

"Fraud models sit in a closed loop: you only get labels for what you reviewed, you reviewed what the model ranked highly, and the adversary moves away from wherever you're looking. So measured precision can stay flat while true recall collapses — the dashboard looks fine because it's computed on a biased sample. I hold back 10–20% of review capacity for randomly sampled cases, which is the only unbiased measure of what we're missing and the only training signal from outside the model's beliefs."

The trap

Do not describe this as "concept drift" and move on. Drift (D7) is a passive process you can monitor and retrain against; an adversary is an optimiser responding to your decisions, which means your model changes the distribution it is trying to predict. The practical consequences differ: against drift you retrain on a schedule, against an adversary you also need feature diversity so that evading one signal does not evade all of them, features expensive for the attacker to change (account age, historical graph position from X1) rather than cheap ones (transaction amount, device string), and a deliberate degree of unpredictability in what gets reviewed. A model that is perfectly predictable is a model that has been solved.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is selective labelling?

Only reviewed cases get labels, and cases are reviewed because the model flagged them — so the labelled sample reflects the model's beliefs.

Why can precision look healthy while the system fails?

Precision is measured on flagged cases only; fraud moving outside the flagged region never enters the calculation.

What does a random review quota buy?

An unbiased estimate of what is being missed, and training signal from outside the model's beliefs — but only recovery if the missed population is still separable in your features. Otherwise it buys the diagnosis, not the fix.

How does adversarial adaptation differ from drift?

Drift is passive; an adversary optimises against your decisions, so your model alters the distribution it predicts.

What kinds of features resist adaptation?

Ones expensive for the attacker to change — account age, historical behaviour, graph position — rather than cheap surface attributes.

Why does label delay matter here?

Retraining always fits a strategy the adversary has already moved on from.

What breaks the doom loop?

Random sampling in review, feature diversity, unpredictability in enforcement, and monitoring recall proxies rather than only precision.

Track F · Dimensionality reduction · Module F1

Principal Component AnalysisRotate the axes onto the directions of greatest variance. Everything else about PCA follows from that one sentence.

PCA finds the orthogonal directions along which your data varies most, and lets you keep the first few. It is the decorrelation step that fixes Isolation Forest's axis-alignment problem (M1), the compression that makes distance methods survivable (A6), and the most commonly misapplied technique in this bench — because variance is not the same thing as information.

PCA bench
exact Jacobi eigendecomposition
left: the data with its principal axes drawn to scale · right: explained variance per component, cumulative

The mechanics

1. centre the data X − μ 2. covariance matrix C = XᵀX / (n−1) 3. eigendecomposition C = V Λ Vᵀ eigenvectors V = the principal directions, orthogonal by construction eigenvalues Λ = variance along each one 4. project Z = (X − μ) · V[:, :k] explained variance ratio of component i = λᵢ / Σλ

The bench draws the eigenvectors scaled by √λ, so you can see the axes lengthening as correlation rises. At ρ = 0 the components are arbitrary directions of equal length; at ρ = 0.95 the first component carries almost everything and the second is nearly noise. That collapse is exactly why correlated features compress well and why B3's collinearity has a geometric interpretation: the data lives near a line.

The scaling trap, made visible

Switch to Raw features and push unit mismatch to ×1000. The first component now points almost entirely along the large-unit feature, and its explained-variance share approaches 100% — not because that feature matters but because it is measured in smaller units. PCA maximises variance, and variance has units. Standardise first and the components re-align to the actual correlation structure.

This is the same lesson as A3, with a sharper consequence: an unscaled PCA does not merely perform worse, it produces a decomposition of your unit choices. Anyone who has run PCA on a table containing both transaction counts and rupee amounts has seen PC1 turn out to be "amount, in rupees".

Use PCA whenDon't when
Features are correlated and you want decorrelation (M1's axis-alignment fix)You need interpretable features — components are linear mixtures of everything
Reducing dimension before a distance-based method (A6, M2)The signal lives in a low-variance direction — see F2
Visualising structure in two dimensionsThe structure is non-linear — see F3 and F4
Compressing correlated sensor or price seriesFeatures are already independent; there is nothing to remove

Interview point

"PCA is the eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix: components are the orthogonal directions of maximum variance, and the eigenvalues are the variance along each. That makes it scale-dependent, so I standardise first or I'm just decomposing my unit choices. And it's unsupervised — it has no idea which directions carry the label, so a low-variance direction that happens to separate the classes gets discarded first."

The trap

PCA must be fitted on training data only and applied to test data as a fixed transform — it is a learned transform and leaks exactly like a scaler (A2). Two more that catch people: the components have no inherent sign, so PC1 can flip between refits on the same data and any interpretation of its direction is unstable; and choosing k by "95% of variance" is a convention, not an optimisation — the honest approach is to cross-validate k against the downstream task, since the whole point is what happens after the projection.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What are the principal components mathematically?

The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by their eigenvalues.

What does an eigenvalue represent?

The variance of the data along that component.

Why standardise before PCA?

Variance has units, so an unscaled decomposition reflects unit choices rather than structure.

Is PCA supervised?

No — it maximises variance and knows nothing about the target, so it can discard a discriminative low-variance direction.

Are components interpretable?

Only as linear mixtures of all original features, and their sign is arbitrary.

How do you choose the number of components?

Cumulative explained variance is the convention; cross-validating against the downstream task is the defensible version.

Relationship to SVD?

PCA is the SVD of the centred data matrix; libraries compute it that way for numerical stability.

Track F · Dimensionality reduction · Module F2

Linear Discriminant AnalysisPCA asks where the data varies. LDA asks where the classes separate. Those are frequently different directions.

F1 ended on the sharpest limitation of PCA: it is unsupervised, so it keeps the directions with the most variance whether or not they carry the label. LDA uses the labels — it maximises between-class scatter relative to within-class scatter — and this bench builds data where the two methods point almost perpendicular to each other.

Discriminant bench
real scatter matrices · exact eigen
left: the data with the PCA and LDA directions drawn · right: the two 1-D projections — which one separates the classes?

The objective

S_W = Σ_classes Σ_i (x − μ_c)(x − μ_c)ᵀ within-class scatter S_B = Σ_classes n_c (μ_c − μ)(μ_c − μ)ᵀ between-class scatter maximise J(w) = (wᵀ S_B w) / (wᵀ S_W w) → eigenvectors of S_W⁻¹ S_B two classes: w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₀) the closed form worth remembering

Read that last line carefully: LDA does not simply point from one class mean to the other. It points along the mean difference after whitening by the within-class covariance. That correction is the whole method — it discounts directions in which both classes are already spread out, because spread there is nuisance rather than signal.

The comparison the bench makes

Select Signal in a low-variance direction and raise the nuisance variance. PCA's first component locks onto the high-variance nuisance axis and the projected classes overlap almost completely; LDA finds the narrow direction in which they separate. The AUC readouts for the two 1-D projections diverge, often dramatically — one number is the case for supervision in a sentence.

Then select Equal means, different spread. Now the classes have identical means and differ only in covariance. LDA's between-class scatter is zero by construction, so it has nothing to maximise and fails completely, while the classes are still perfectly distinguishable to anything that looks at second moments — QDA, or a tree. This is the limitation to know: LDA is a mean-difference method.

PCALDA
Uses labelsNoYes
MaximisesTotal varianceBetween/within scatter ratio
Max componentsmin(n, p)C − 1 — two classes give you exactly one
AssumesNothingRoughly Gaussian classes with shared covariance
Fails whenSignal has low varianceClasses differ in spread rather than mean

Interview point

"PCA maximises variance and ignores the label; LDA maximises between-class scatter over within-class scatter, so it finds the direction that separates classes even when that direction carries very little total variance. For two classes the solution is w ∝ S_W⁻¹(μ₁−μ₀) — the mean difference whitened by the within-class covariance — and you only ever get C−1 components, which is a real constraint in binary problems."

The trap

S_W must be invertible, and with more features than rows it is not — LDA breaks exactly where you most want dimensionality reduction. The standard remedies are shrinkage (regularised LDA, the same ridge idea as B5) or running PCA first and LDA on the result, which is a common pipeline and worth naming. Also: LDA is both a projection and a classifier, and people conflate them. As a classifier it assumes shared covariance across classes; drop that assumption and you have QDA, which handles the equal-means case this bench shows LDA failing on.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does LDA maximise?

The ratio of between-class scatter to within-class scatter.

Give the two-class solution.

w ∝ S_W⁻¹(μ₁ − μ₀) — the mean difference whitened by within-class covariance.

How many components can LDA produce?

At most C − 1, so exactly one for a binary problem.

When does PCA beat LDA?

When you have no labels, or when LDA's assumptions fail — and PCA can never overfit the labels because it never sees them.

When does LDA fail outright?

Equal class means with different covariances: between-class scatter is zero and there is nothing to maximise.

What breaks when p > n?

S_W is singular; use shrinkage or run PCA first.

LDA vs QDA?

LDA assumes a shared covariance across classes and gives linear boundaries; QDA estimates one per class and gives quadratic ones.

Track F · Dimensionality reduction · Module F3

Kernel PCAPCA can only rotate. When the structure is a circle, no rotation will straighten it — so do the PCA somewhere else.

Linear PCA finds the best linear subspace, which means concentric rings, spirals and any manifold with curvature are beyond it. Kernel PCA applies the same trick as C4: run the eigendecomposition on a kernel matrix rather than a covariance matrix, and you have implicitly done PCA in a space where the structure is linear.

Kernel PCA bench
centred kernel matrix · power iteration
left: linear PCA's first two components · right: kernel PCA's — the same data, a different space

What changes

linear PCA eigendecompose C = XᵀX/(n−1) a p × p covariance matrix kernel PCA eigendecompose K̃, where K_ij = k(xᵢ, xⱼ) an n × n kernel matrix K̃ = K − 1ₙK − K1ₙ + 1ₙK1ₙ centring, done in kernel space because you cannot centre points you never computed projection of point i onto component m = √λ_m · v_m[i]

Two consequences follow immediately. The cost flips from p to n: kernel PCA on a million rows means a million-by-million matrix, which is why it is an analysis tool rather than a pipeline stage at fraud scale. And there is no straightforward inverse transform — the pre-image problem — so you cannot reconstruct the original features from the components the way linear PCA lets you.

Reading the panels

On Concentric rings, linear PCA produces two components that are simply a rotation of the original circle: the inner and outer rings remain entangled and the separation readout stays near chance. Kernel PCA at a sensible γ unfolds them completely — a single threshold separates the rings perfectly.

But read the separating component readout, because it carries a lesson the textbook figures skip: it is a later component, not component 1 — with the default settings, the fourth. The data is rotationally symmetric, so the leading kernel components encode that symmetry — they are essentially the angle around the circle — and the radial structure that actually distinguishes the rings sits behind them. The habit of plotting the first two components and concluding "no structure" would have missed it entirely. The bench therefore plots whichever component separates, and names it.

Now try Two Gaussian blobs — a case linear PCA handles fine. Kernel PCA offers little and costs enormously more. That comparison is the honest framing: kernel methods buy you curvature, and you should only pay when the structure has some. And γ carries the same failure as C4: too large and each point becomes its own island, so the components describe individual points rather than structure.

Interview point

"Kernel PCA eigendecomposes the centred kernel matrix instead of the covariance matrix, so you get principal components in an implicit high-dimensional space and can capture curved structure that linear PCA can't. The costs are real: it's O(n²) memory and O(n³) to decompose, and there's no clean inverse transform because of the pre-image problem — so I use it to understand data, not as a production feature step."

The trap

Kernel PCA is unsupervised, and unsupervised non-linear methods will always produce a picture. Given a large γ it will happily "discover" structure in pure noise, because at that setting the kernel matrix approaches the identity and every point becomes its own component. Before believing a kernel PCA plot, run it on a shuffled or resampled version of your data and check that the structure disappears — the same defence as X3's random-rewiring test, and for the same reason.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does kernel PCA decompose?

The centred n × n kernel matrix, rather than the p × p covariance matrix.

Why centre in kernel space?

The feature-space points are never computed, so centring must be expressed purely through the kernel matrix.

What is the pre-image problem?

There is no exact way to map a point in feature space back to the input space, so reconstruction is approximate at best.

How does the cost compare to linear PCA?

It scales with the number of rows, not features — O(n²) memory and roughly O(n³) time.

What does γ control?

Kernel locality; too large and every point becomes its own component, which is memorisation.

When is linear PCA the better choice?

Whenever the structure is linear — it is cheaper, invertible and interpretable.
