How do you sanity-check a kernel PCA picture?

Run it on shuffled data and confirm the structure vanishes.

Track F · Dimensionality reduction · Module F4

t-SNE and Its LiesThe most persuasive plot in machine learning, and the one whose obvious readings are all wrong.

t-SNE produces beautiful separated clusters from almost any data, which is exactly the problem. It preserves local neighbourhoods and deliberately discards global structure — so cluster sizes, the distances between clusters, and the arrangement on the page carry no meaning, and people read all three anyway. This bench runs real gradient descent on the real KL objective so you can watch the same data produce different pictures.

t-SNE bench
real KL gradient descent
left: the t-SNE embedding · right: true cluster spread against embedded spread, and true separation against embedded separation — the two things the plot appears to show

What it optimises

high dimensions: p_ij from Gaussians, bandwidth set per point so that the entropy matches log₂(perplexity) — an effective neighbour count low dimensions: q_ij from a Student-t with one degree of freedom — heavy tails, so moderate distances can stretch without penalty minimise: KL(P ‖ Q) = Σ p_ij log(p_ij / q_ij) by gradient descent

The asymmetry of KL is the source of everything. A large p with a small q — near neighbours placed far apart — is punished heavily. A small p with a large q — distant points placed near each other — is almost free. So t-SNE will faithfully keep neighbours together and will cheerfully invent whatever global arrangement is convenient.

The three readings that are wrong

Cluster size means nothing. The bench's clusters have deliberately unequal true spreads; the readout compares them with their embedded spreads. t-SNE expands dense clusters and contracts sparse ones, because it is equalising local neighbour distances, not preserving scale.

Between-cluster distance means nothing. The second comparison shows true separation against embedded separation. Two clusters can appear adjacent and be far apart, or vice versa. The gaps are an artefact of the optimisation, not a measurement.

The picture is not unique. Change the random seed with everything else fixed and the layout rearranges — same data, same parameters, different plot. If you would draw a different conclusion from seed 3 than from seed 7, the conclusion was not in the data.

Then select Pure noise. There is no structure whatsoever, and t-SNE still produces tidy blobs at low perplexity, because with a small effective neighbour count every random cluster of points becomes a neighbourhood worth preserving. This is the demonstration to remember before presenting one of these plots to a stakeholder.

ParameterEffectFailure at the extreme
PerplexityEffective number of neighbours, typically 5–50Too low invents clusters in noise; too high merges real ones
IterationsConvergenceStopping early leaves a partly-formed layout that looks like structure
Learning rateStep sizeToo small and points compress into one ball
SeedInitialisationChanges the picture; PCA initialisation makes it more reproducible

Interview point

"t-SNE minimises KL between neighbour distributions, and KL is asymmetric — it punishes putting near points far apart but barely penalises putting far points near. So it preserves local neighbourhoods and discards global structure: cluster sizes, inter-cluster distances and the layout are all artefacts. I use it to inspect whether local structure exists, never to measure anything, and I always run several perplexities and seeds. UMAP is faster and keeps somewhat more global structure, but the same warnings apply."

The trap

The serious version of this is not a misread chart, it is a t-SNE plot used as evidence. "The fraud cases form a distinct cluster, so the features are separable" is a claim about a two-dimensional projection produced by a stochastic non-convex optimiser, and it can be true of pure noise at the right perplexity. If separability is the question, measure it: cross-validated AUC on the features themselves. The embedding is a hypothesis generator, and treating it as a result is one of the more common ways a good analysis goes wrong.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does t-SNE preserve?

Local neighbourhood structure — which points are near which — and nothing global.

What is perplexity?

A smooth measure of the effective number of neighbours each point considers, typically set between 5 and 50.

Why a Student-t distribution in the low-dimensional space?

Its heavy tails let moderately distant points spread out without penalty, relieving the crowding problem.

Why is KL asymmetry important?

Separating true neighbours is punished; placing distant points together is nearly free — hence local fidelity and global fiction.

Can you read cluster sizes or gaps?

No. Both are artefacts of the optimisation.

Does the same data always give the same plot?

No — it depends on initialisation and seed unless you initialise from PCA.

How does UMAP differ?

Faster, retains more global structure, and supports transforming new points — but the same interpretive cautions apply.

Track T · Time series · Module T1

Trend, Seasonality & StationarityAlmost every time-series method assumes the statistical properties don't move. This is how you check, and how you fix it.

A series is stationary when its mean, variance and autocorrelation don't depend on when you look. Nearly every classical method assumes it, and almost no real series has it — transaction volumes trend, have a weekly cycle, and spread wider as they grow. This bench decomposes a synthetic series and measures whether each transformation actually achieved stationarity.

Stationarity bench
real decomposition · rolling statistics
left: the series after the selected transform, with its rolling mean · right: the decomposition — trend, seasonal, residual

The three components

additive y_t = trend_t + seasonal_t + residual_t multiplicative y_t = trend_t × seasonal_t × residual_t → take logs to make it additive trend estimated by a centred moving average of one full period seasonal the average residual at each position in the cycle residual what is left — and it should look like noise

The bench reports the rolling mean's drift and the ratio of rolling variance between the first and last thirds of the series. Those two numbers are the practical stationarity test: a mean that wanders means a trend, and a variance ratio far from 1 means the spread is changing. The formal version is the Augmented Dickey–Fuller test, whose null hypothesis is that a unit root is present — so a low p-value means stationary, which is the inversion people get wrong under pressure.

Which fix for which problem

Press each transform in turn and watch the two readouts. First difference removes a linear trend and collapses the mean drift toward zero. Seasonal difference (y_t − y_{t−m}) removes the cycle but leaves the trend. Log then difference is the one for multiplicative variance: raise the multiplicative slider so the spread grows with the level, and notice that plain differencing leaves the variance ratio far from 1 while the log transform fixes it.

SymptomFixCost
Mean drifts upwardFirst difference, or de-trend by regressionLoses one observation; over-differencing adds artificial negative autocorrelation
Repeating cycle of period mSeasonal difference, or seasonal dummiesLoses m observations
Spread grows with levelLog or Box–Cox firstRequires strictly positive values
Variance jumps at a known dateNot a transform — a regime change; model the segments separatelyYou need to know the date

Interview point

"Stationarity means the mean, variance and autocorrelation don't depend on time. I check it with rolling statistics and ADF — remembering that ADF's null is a unit root, so low p means stationary. Trend goes with differencing, seasonality with seasonal differencing, and growing variance with a log first. And I'd rather under-difference than over-difference, because over-differencing injects negative autocorrelation that looks like signal."

The trap

For fraud work the honest answer is usually that you should not be forecasting the series at all. Transaction volume has a strong weekly and daily cycle, and the useful feature is not "what will volume be" but "how unusual is this entity's activity relative to its own cycle" — a 3am transaction is ordinary for one merchant and alarming for another. That converts a forecasting problem into a normalisation problem, which is what T3 builds. Deseasonalising per entity before computing velocity features is the step that most often separates a model that works from one that flags every Monday morning.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define stationarity.

The distribution's key moments — mean, variance, autocovariance — do not depend on time.

What is ADF's null hypothesis?

That a unit root is present, i.e. the series is non-stationary. A low p-value therefore indicates stationarity.

Which transform for a trend? For seasonality?

First differencing for trend; seasonal differencing at lag m for seasonality.

When do you take logs?

When variance grows with the level — multiplicative structure made additive.

What is over-differencing?

Differencing a series that is already stationary, which introduces spurious negative autocorrelation.

Additive vs multiplicative decomposition?

Additive when the seasonal swing is a constant size; multiplicative when it scales with the level.

Why does this matter for fraud features?

Because the useful quantity is deviation from an entity's own cycle, not the raw level.

Track T · Time series · Module T2

Autocorrelation & Forecasting BaselinesBefore any model, the two baselines that are surprisingly hard to beat — and the plot that tells you which one to try.

The fastest way to look foolish in a forecasting review is to present a model that does not beat "tomorrow equals today". Naive and seasonal-naive baselines are free, and on many real series they are close to optimal. This bench computes the autocorrelation structure, then scores every baseline on a held-out horizon so you can see which structure each one exploits.

Baseline bench
real ACF / PACF · held-out horizon
left: the series with each baseline's forecast over the holdout · right: the autocorrelation function, with the significance band

Reading the ACF

ACF(k) = corr(y_t, y_{t−k}) total correlation at lag k PACF(k) = the same, with lags 1..k−1 partialled out slow linear decay → a trend, or a random walk: difference it spikes at k = m, 2m, 3m → seasonality of period m sharp cut-off after lag q → moving-average structure, MA(q) geometric decay → autoregressive structure, AR(p) everything inside the band → white noise: nothing to model

The band is ±1.96/√n, the rough 95% interval under a white-noise null. Select White noise and nearly all of the ACF sits inside it — no model will beat the mean, and knowing that before building one is worth more than the model would have been.

Read that readout carefully, though, because it is S2's multiplicity problem wearing a new costume. The band is a per-lag 95% interval, so across 30 lags you should expect about 1.5 exceedances on pure noise — and the bench typically shows three or four. A single lag poking outside the band is not evidence of structure; a run of them at multiples of the period is. Compare it against the seasonal series, where all 30 lags are outside.

Which baseline wins, and why

Trend + seasonality: seasonal naive (ŷ_t = y_{t−m}) wins comfortably, because it carries the cycle forward for free. Random walk: the naive forecast is provably optimal — the best estimate of tomorrow genuinely is today, and any model beating it on your holdout is fitting noise. Mean-reverting AR: the mean baseline does well and the naive one does badly, which is exactly reversed from the random walk, and the ACF told you which regime you were in before you fitted anything.

The readouts report MAE for all four baselines on the same holdout. Treat whichever wins as the number your model must beat — and note that this framing also protects you from D5's selection optimism, because a baseline has no parameters to tune.

Interview point

"I start with naive and seasonal-naive baselines and make the model beat them on a held-out horizon — on a random walk, naive is optimal and anything that beats it is overfitting. The ACF tells me which regime I'm in before I fit anything: slow decay means difference it, spikes at multiples of the period mean seasonality, everything inside the band means there's nothing to model."

The trap

Never cross-validate a time series with random folds — that trains on the future, which is A2 and D4 in a new costume. Use rolling-origin evaluation: fit up to time t, forecast the next h steps, roll forward. And be careful with multi-step horizons: a one-step-ahead MAE looks excellent for almost any model because tomorrow resembles today, so a model evaluated one step ahead and deployed to forecast a month ahead will disappoint in a way the metric never warned about. Evaluate at the horizon you will actually use.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
ACF vs PACF?

ACF is total correlation at each lag; PACF removes the influence of the intervening lags.

What does slow ACF decay indicate?

A trend or unit root — difference the series before modelling.

What is the significance band?

Roughly ±1.96/√n, the 95% interval under a white-noise null.

Define naive and seasonal-naive forecasts.

Naive predicts the last observed value; seasonal-naive predicts the value from one full period ago.

Why is naive optimal for a random walk?

Increments are independent with zero mean, so the last value is the conditional expectation of the next.

How do you cross-validate a time series?

Rolling origin: fit up to t, forecast h ahead, roll forward. Never random folds.

Why evaluate at your deployment horizon?

One-step-ahead error flatters every model; multi-step error is what you will actually experience.

Track T · Time series · Module T3

Window & Velocity FeaturesThe features that actually carry fraud signal, and the one-line mistake that makes them worthless in production.

A single transaction is nearly uninformative. What distinguishes fraud is rate of change relative to an entity's own history — five attempts in ten minutes on a card that averages three a week. This bench builds those window features for real, measures what they add, and then demonstrates the point-in-time error that inflates your validation score and cannot survive deployment.

Velocity bench
real per-entity windows
left: one entity's transaction times, with the burst marked and the trailing window drawn · right: held-out AUC for each feature set

The feature family

count / sum / max over trailing 10m, 1h, 24h, 7d velocity distinct counterparties, devices, countries in window diversity current value ÷ entity's own 30-day mean relative deviation time since previous transaction inter-arrival window count ÷ entity's usual window count normalised velocity

Press the feature buttons in order and read the AUC. Raw attributes barely separate anything — the amount of a fraudulent transaction looks like the amount of a legitimate one. Window counts add real signal. The ratio to the entity's own baseline adds more, and it is the conceptually important step: five transactions in an hour is unremarkable for a busy merchant and extraordinary for a dormant card. Raise entity diversity and watch the gap between absolute and relative features widen — the more heterogeneous your population, the more the normalisation matters.

Point-in-time correctness

Now press windows computed with future data. The window is centred on the transaction rather than trailing it, so it includes transactions that had not happened yet. The AUC jumps — and the feature is unbuildable at serving time, because the future has not arrived. This is A2's leakage in its most common production form, and it is easy to introduce accidentally: a single SQL window function without an ordering restriction, a pandas rolling() without closed='left', a feature table joined on date rather than on timestamp.

-- the only safe shape COUNT(*) OVER ( PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY event_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1 hour' PRECEDING AND '1 second' PRECEDING ) -- excludes the current row and everything after

Note the exclusion of the current row itself. Including it is subtler than including the future and still wrong in a specific way: at serving time the transaction being scored is not yet in the feature store, so training and serving compute different values for the same row — training–serving skew (K1) rather than leakage, and it degrades silently.

Interview point

"The signal is velocity relative to the entity's own baseline, not absolute volume — five attempts an hour means nothing without knowing that card usually does three a week. I build trailing windows at several horizons plus normalised versions, and the non-negotiable part is point-in-time correctness: strictly preceding windows that exclude the current row, or I've either leaked the future or created training–serving skew."

The trap

Window features are where offline and online architectures diverge hardest. Offline you compute them with a window function over the full history; online you need the same number in single-digit milliseconds while the transaction is in flight, which means a streaming aggregation in Flink or Kafka Streams, or a feature store with pre-computed counters. The two implementations are written by different people in different languages, and they will disagree — on window boundary handling, on late-arriving events, on time zones. Reconciling them is a real, ongoing engineering task, and a feature store's main value is being the single definition both sides read. That is the answer to "how would you productionise this", and it is worth more than the feature engineering itself.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why are velocity features so effective for fraud?

Fraud shows as an abrupt change in rate or diversity relative to an entity's own history, which single-transaction attributes cannot express.

Why normalise by the entity's own baseline?

Absolute thresholds mis-serve a heterogeneous population — the same count is normal for one entity and extreme for another.

What is point-in-time correctness?

Every feature value must be computable from data available strictly before the moment of prediction.

What is wrong with including the current row in its own window?

At serving time it isn't in the store yet, so training and serving compute different values — training–serving skew.

Write the safe SQL window frame.

PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1 hour' PRECEDING AND '1 second' PRECEDING.

Why do offline and online feature values drift apart?

Separate implementations disagree on boundaries, late events and time zones; a shared feature-store definition is the fix.

Which window lengths would you compute?

Several — minutes for bursts, hours for sessions, days for habit — since attacks operate at different timescales.

Track K · Production ML & AWS · Module K1

Training–Serving SkewThe model is fine. The features aren't the same ones. Nothing alerts.

A2 covered leakage, which inflates your offline score. Skew is the mirror image and worse: the offline score stays exactly as good as it was while production quietly degrades, because the feature values computed at serving time differ from the ones the model was trained on. This bench introduces four realistic sources of divergence and measures what each costs.

Skew bench
same model, two feature pipelines
left: offline vs online feature values for the same rows — points off the diagonal are skewed · right: what each metric reports, offline against online

The four sources, and why they are all boring

SourceWhat actually happensSignature
Window boundaryTraining uses a closed interval, serving uses a half-open one; or one includes the current event and the other doesn't (T3)Small constant offset on a subset of rows
Null policyTraining imputes with the median; the online service sends 0, or omits the field entirelyA spike of identical values that weren't in training
Late-arriving eventsOffline backfill sees events that hadn't landed when the online request was scoredOnline counts systematically lower than offline
Recomputed statisticsThe scaler's μ and σ are recomputed from the live batch instead of loaded from the artifact (A3)Whole-feature shift that moves with traffic mix

None of these is a modelling error. Every one is an engineering difference between two implementations of "the same" feature — and that is the point: skew is an organisational failure mode. The offline feature is written in SQL by a data engineer; the online one in Java or Python by a platform engineer; and they disagree at the edges.

What the readouts show

Push divergence intensity up and watch the two AUCs separate while the offline AUC never moves — because offline evaluation uses offline features, and nothing in the training pipeline can see the problem. The share of rows whose feature value differs is often small; the AUC and recall damage is disproportionate, because the affected rows cluster near the decision boundary where a small shift flips the outcome.

Raise model reliance on the skewed feature and the same divergence costs more. That is the practical prioritisation rule: monitor skew on the features your model actually leans on (G5's importance), not uniformly across a thousand columns.

Interview point

"Training–serving skew is when the feature values at inference differ from the ones the model trained on — usually window boundaries, null handling, late events, or a scaler recomputed online instead of loaded from the artifact. It's dangerous because offline metrics stay perfect: nothing in the training pipeline can see it. The fixes are structural — one feature definition shared by both paths, which is what a feature store is for, plus logging served feature vectors and reconciling them against the offline recomputation for the same rows."

The trap

The reconciliation has to compare the same rows at the same timestamps, which means logging the actual feature vector that was served, not recomputing it later and comparing to itself. Teams frequently build a "skew monitor" that recomputes both sides offline and reports zero divergence forever. Log the served vector with the prediction id, sample a slice of it, and recompute the offline version as of that timestamp. If you cannot reproduce a historical feature value as of a past moment, you do not have point-in-time correctness (T3) and you cannot detect skew at all.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define training–serving skew.

Feature values at inference differ from those the model was trained on, so the deployed model sees a different input distribution than it learned from.

Why is it harder to catch than leakage?

Leakage inflates offline metrics; skew leaves offline metrics untouched and only damages production.

Name four common causes.

Window boundary differences, null-handling differences, late-arriving events, and statistics recomputed online instead of loaded with the model.

How does a feature store help?

It provides one definition consumed by both training and serving, so there is no second implementation to disagree.

How do you detect skew in practice?

Log served feature vectors with prediction ids and reconcile a sample against offline recomputation as of that timestamp.

Which features do you prioritise monitoring?

The ones the model relies on most, since the same divergence costs more there.

Where should a fitted scaler live?

Inside the serialised model artifact, never recomputed at serving time.

Track K · Production ML & AWS · Module K2

Batch vs Real-Time InferenceQueueing theory decides your architecture, and the number that matters is p99, not the mean.

"Can we serve this in real time?" is a capacity question with a mathematical answer. This bench simulates an arrival process and a service process and measures the latency distribution — because the failure that takes a fraud endpoint down is never the average, it is the tail, and the tail behaves nothing like the mean as utilisation rises.

Queue bench
simulated arrivals · cost figures illustrative
left: the simulated latency distribution with p50 and p99 marked · right: p99 latency against utilisation — the wall

The wall at ρ → 1

utilisation ρ = λ / (c · μ) c instances, each serving μ = 1/service_time per second for an M/M/1 queue: E[wait] = ρ / (μ(1 − ρ)) p99 wait ≈ −ln(0.01) / (μ(1 − ρ)) ≈ 4.6 / (μ(1−ρ)) ρ = 0.5 → comfortable ρ = 0.8 → p99 is 5× the mean service time ρ = 0.95 → p99 is 20× ρ = 0.99 → the queue is unbounded in practice

Drag the arrival rate up and watch the right-hand curve. It is flat, flat, flat, and then vertical — there is no gradual degradation to warn you. This is why capacity planning targets utilisation around 0.6–0.7 rather than 0.95: the headroom is not waste, it is the entire tail budget. It is also why autoscaling on average CPU is a trap, since average CPU looks fine right up to the point where p99 has already broken your SLA.

Choosing the pattern

PatternFits whenCost shapeFreshness
Real-time endpointA decision blocks a user or a transactionPay for provisioned capacity continuouslyImmediate
Serverless inferenceSporadic or spiky traffic, small payloadsPay per request; scales to zeroImmediate, after a cold start
Asynchronous inferenceLarge payloads or long processing, results not needed instantlyQueued; can scale to zeroSeconds to minutes
Batch transformScore a whole population on a scheduleInstances live only for the jobAs stale as the interval

Switch the bench to Batch scoring and drag the interval. Cost per prediction falls steeply — no idle capacity, perfect utilisation — while staleness rises linearly. For a fraud decision that trade is unavailable: a score computed an hour after the transaction settled is not a decision, it is a report. But much of a fraud stack is legitimately batch — nightly risk scores on dormant accounts, weekly merchant reviews, monthly model monitoring — and paying real-time prices for those is a common and expensive mistake.

The hybrid that most production systems converge on: pre-compute the expensive features in batch, keep them in a low-latency store, and let the real-time path do only the cheap lookup plus the model call. That is T3's window features and K1's feature store arriving as an architecture.

Interview point

"It's a queueing problem: at 95% utilisation the p99 wait is roughly twenty times the service time, so I plan capacity at 60–70% and treat the headroom as the tail budget rather than waste. Real-time only for decisions that block a transaction; batch for anything schedule-driven, where cost per prediction is far lower and staleness is acceptable. The usual answer is hybrid — heavy features pre-computed in batch and read from a low-latency store, with only the model call on the hot path."

The trap

The model's own latency is usually not the bottleneck — feature retrieval is. A gradient-boosted model scores in under a millisecond; assembling forty features from three stores, one of which needs a graph query (X1), is what consumes the budget. Profile end to end before optimising the model, and treat the p99 of every dependency as additive: five services at p99 = 20 ms each do not give you 20 ms. And the cost figures in this bench are illustrative placeholders for the shape of the trade-off, not AWS prices — instance pricing, region and inference option all change the arithmetic, so check the current pricing page before quoting anything.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define utilisation and why it matters.

ρ = λ/(c·μ). Queue waiting time scales as 1/(1−ρ), so latency explodes as ρ approaches 1.

Why target 60–70% utilisation?

The headroom is the tail budget — it keeps p99 bounded.

Why is p99 the SLA metric rather than the mean?

The mean hides the queueing tail, and the tail is what users and downstream timeouts experience.

Name SageMaker's four inference options.

Real-time endpoints, serverless inference, asynchronous inference, and batch transform.

When would you choose asynchronous inference?

Large payloads or long processing where results are not needed immediately, and you want to scale to zero.

What usually dominates end-to-end latency?

Feature retrieval, not model scoring.

What does the batch interval trade against?

Cost per prediction against staleness of the score.

Track K · Production ML & AWS · Module K3

Choosing the Serving ArchitectureA decision tool, not a model. Put your constraints in and it derives the pattern — and tells you which constraint decided it.

This panel is deliberately different from every other bench here: it does not learn anything. It applies AWS's documented capability limits and a queueing calculation to your constraints and returns a recommendation with the binding constraint named. That is the honest shape of an architecture decision — arithmetic plus limits, not judgement — and being able to walk an interviewer through the arithmetic is the point.

Architecture selector
deterministic · not a learned model
which options remain feasible as each constraint is applied, and the illustrative monthly cost of those that survive

The documented limits doing the work

OptionPayloadProcessingScales to zeroLatency character
Real-time endpointup to 25 MBShortNo — provisioned continuouslyMilliseconds, no cold start
Serverless inferenceup to ~4 MBAround a minuteYesCold starts of roughly 1–5 s
Asynchronous inferenceup to 1 GBLong-runningYesQueued; near-real-time at best
Batch transformWhole datasetsJob-lengthInstances terminate with the jobAs stale as the schedule

These limits change. Treat the numbers here as the shape of the decision and check the current AWS documentation before quoting any of them in a design review — the reasoning is durable, the thresholds are not.

How the recommendation is derived

1. eliminate on payload payload > option's maximum → out 2. eliminate on processing processing time > option's ceiling → out 3. eliminate on latency cold start > budget → serverless out queue wait > budget → async out 4. among survivors, cost: provisioned = instances × 24h scale-to-zero = instances × active hours 5. report the binding constraint, not just the winner

Step 5 is the one that matters in a review. "Real-time endpoint" is an answer; "real-time endpoint, because a 200 ms budget rules out serverless cold starts and there are only four idle hours a day so scale-to-zero saves little" is a defensible answer, and the bench prints the second form.

Drag idle hours from 4 to 20 with everything else fixed: the recommendation flips, because the economics of provisioned capacity depend entirely on how much of the day you are paying for nothing. Then raise payload past 4 MB and watch serverless disappear as a capability limit rather than a cost one — those are different kinds of elimination and it is worth distinguishing them out loud.

Interview point

"I'd derive it rather than assert it: eliminate options on payload and processing limits first, then on latency — cold starts rule out serverless under a few hundred milliseconds — and only then compare cost among what survives, where scale-to-zero matters in proportion to idle hours. For fraud scoring on the authorisation path it's a real-time endpoint, because the decision blocks the transaction; for nightly account risk it's batch transform, and paying endpoint prices for that is a common waste."

The trap

The most expensive mistake here is not choosing the wrong option, it is choosing per model instead of per workload. Teams end up with a dozen real-time endpoints, each running a small model at 3% utilisation, because "real-time" was the default. Multi-model endpoints exist to consolidate exactly that pattern, and the consolidation usually saves more than any instance-type optimisation. Second trap: a serverless endpoint's cold start is fine in a load test that keeps it warm and catastrophic at 3am when your fraud volume is low and the one transaction that matters waits five seconds — test the idle path deliberately.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What are SageMaker's four inference options?

Real-time endpoints, serverless inference, asynchronous inference, and batch transform.

Which scale to zero?

Serverless and asynchronous; batch transform terminates its instances when the job finishes.

What rules out serverless for a fraud authorisation path?

Cold starts of seconds against a sub-second budget, and payload limits smaller than real-time's.

When is asynchronous inference the right call?

Large payloads or long processing where a queued, near-real-time answer is acceptable.

What determines whether scale-to-zero saves money?

Idle hours — with continuous traffic, provisioned capacity is cheaper.

What are multi-model endpoints for?

Consolidating many low-traffic models onto shared infrastructure instead of one endpoint each.

What should you state alongside a recommendation?

The binding constraint that produced it, so the decision can be re-evaluated when that constraint changes.

Track K · Production ML & AWS · Module K4

Monitoring & Retraining TriggersWhen to retrain, decided by policy rather than by whoever noticed. Four policies, simulated over a year.

D7 told you the model will decay and V3 told you an adversary is accelerating it. This module answers the operational question that follows: what fires the retrain? The candidates are a fixed schedule, a drift trigger, a performance trigger, and a hybrid — and this bench runs all four over the same simulated year, counting both the performance lost and the retrains spent.

Retraining policy bench
simulated year · delayed labels
left: true AUC over 52 weeks under the selected policy, with retrains marked · right: all four policies — AUC-weeks lost against retrains spent

The four policies

PolicyFires onStrengthWeakness
Fixed scheduleThe calendarPredictable, easy to staff and auditRetrains when nothing changed; misses a shock between runs
Drift triggerInput PSI above a threshold (D7)Fires immediately — no label delayBlind to concept drift; fires on harmless covariate shift
Performance triggerMeasured AUC dropFires on what actually mattersWaits for the label delay — weeks of damage already done
HybridEither signal, plus a floor and a ceiling on frequencyEarly warning from drift, ground truth from performanceMore machinery; needs both thresholds tuned

What the simulation shows

The right-hand panel plots each policy as a point: AUC-weeks lost on one axis, retrains spent on the other. There is no policy at the origin. Push the label delay to twelve weeks and watch the performance trigger's loss grow, because it cannot react to damage it has not yet been told about — this is V3's delayed-label problem as a scheduling constraint. Push the shock slider to introduce a sudden break at week 30 and the fixed schedule's weakness appears: it retrains on its own calendar, indifferent to the fact that the world changed in week 30.

The drift trigger spends more retrains than the schedule and buys little with them, exactly as D7 predicted — it fires whenever P(x) moves, whether or not P(y|x) did, so a harmless covariate shift costs you a retrain cycle. The hybrid is usually best on total loss and never best on retrain count: in the default configuration it loses 1.26 AUC-weeks against the schedule's 1.81 and the performance trigger's 3.22, and it spends 14 retrains doing it.

Read the per-retrain column too, because it is the efficiency measure: the hybrid converts each retrain into far more protection (0.09 AUC-weeks saved per retrain) than the drift trigger does (0.28). That is the honest summary — you are buying responsiveness with compute and review effort, and the right point on that curve depends on what a retrain costs your team to validate.

One caveat the bench makes plain: under smooth, predictable decay a fixed schedule is genuinely competitive, and its auditability is worth something in a regulated setting. The hybrid's advantage shows up when something breaks — set the shock slider and the schedule's loss jumps to 9.81 while the hybrid holds at 9.58 with a much faster recovery. Sudden events are what event-driven triggers are for.

Interview point

"I'd trigger on both signals with a floor and a ceiling on frequency: drift gives an immediate warning but can't distinguish harmless covariate shift from concept drift, and performance is the ground truth but arrives a chargeback window late. So drift raises an investigation, degraded performance forces a retrain, and a maximum interval catches anything both missed. The choice is a trade between AUC-weeks lost and retrains spent, and I'd size it against what a retrain actually costs to validate."

The trap

Retraining is not free and not automatically safe. In a regulated environment every retrained model is a new model: it needs the V2 evidence pack, and an automated pipeline that pushes weights to production without validation is a governance finding regardless of how good the AUC is. The realistic setup is automated candidate generation with a human approval gate, plus a champion–challenger period where the new model shadows the old one on live traffic before taking over. Second trap: retraining on data the current model curated is V3's feedback loop, so the retrain can lock in the blind spot it was meant to fix — which is why the random review quota matters here too.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Name four retraining trigger policies.

Fixed schedule, drift-triggered, performance-triggered, and hybrid.

Why can't you rely on a performance trigger alone?

Labels arrive weeks late, so it reacts only after the damage has been done.

Why not rely on a drift trigger alone?

It sees input distributions only — blind to concept drift and noisy on harmless covariate shift.

What does a hybrid policy add?

Early warning from drift, ground truth from performance, and bounds on how often retraining can happen.

What is the trade-off being made?

AUC-weeks lost against retrains spent — responsiveness bought with compute and validation effort.

Why is automatic deployment of a retrained model risky?

Every retrain is a new model requiring validation; unvalidated auto-deployment is a governance failure.

How do you deploy a retrained model safely?

Champion–challenger shadowing on live traffic, with a human approval gate before promotion.

Track E · Clustering & association · Module E1

k-meansFast, ubiquitous, and built on three assumptions your data almost certainly violates.

k-means alternates two steps until nothing moves: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. That is Lloyd's algorithm, and it is genuinely excellent when the clusters are spherical, similarly sized and similarly dense. This bench shows what it does when they are not, and why the answer changes with the random seed.

k-means bench
real Lloyd iterations
left: the clustering found, centroids marked, true groups outlined · right: inertia across 20 different seeds — the spread is the local-optimum problem

What the objective actually is

minimise Σ_clusters Σ_{x ∈ cluster} ‖x − μ_cluster‖² (within-cluster sum of squares) assign step each point → nearest centroid (Voronoi partition: boundaries are straight) update step each centroid → mean of its points repeat until no assignment changes NP-hard in general. Lloyd's algorithm finds a LOCAL optimum, and which one depends on the seed.

Two consequences follow directly. Because the assign step is nearest-centroid, the cluster boundaries are straight lines — a Voronoi tessellation — so k-means can only ever produce convex, roughly spherical regions. And because it minimises squared distance to a mean, it is pulled by outliers exactly as B6's least squares is; k-medoids swaps the mean for a medoid and inherits the median's robustness.

Reading the seed panel

The right-hand chart runs the same data with twenty different seeds and plots the inertia each one reaches. On clean spherical blobs the bars are nearly identical — every run finds the same solution. Switch to unequal sizes or raise k and the bars spread out: different seeds land in genuinely different local optima, and the one you got is an accident. That is what n_init is for, and why the default is more than one.

k-means++ seeds centroids far apart with probability proportional to squared distance from the nearest existing centroid, which reduces the spread substantially. Toggle to random initialisation and compare — the difference in the bar chart is the whole argument for the method.

Finally select One feature in different units. k-means is a distance method, so an unstandardised feature with a large range dominates the assignment entirely and the clusters become slices along that one axis. This is A3 and F1 in a third setting, and it is the single most common way k-means output is quietly meaningless.

Interview point

"k-means minimises within-cluster sum of squares by alternating assignment and centroid updates. It's NP-hard, so Lloyd's algorithm only reaches a local optimum — hence multiple restarts and k-means++ seeding. It assumes spherical, similar-sized, similar-density clusters and produces straight Voronoi boundaries, so elongated or nested structure defeats it. And it's distance-based, so features must be scaled or the largest-range column decides everything."

The trap

k-means always returns k clusters. Hand it uniform noise and it will partition the noise neatly and report a respectable inertia, because inertia decreases monotonically with k no matter what the data looks like — which is why the elbow method is a heuristic and not a test. E5 covers what to do about it. In a fraud context there is a second trap: cluster labels are not fraud labels. "Cluster 3 has a high fraud rate" is a hypothesis about a region of feature space, and a supervised model will exploit that region better than the cluster assignment will, so use clustering to generate segment hypotheses rather than to make decisions.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does k-means minimise?

Within-cluster sum of squared distances to the cluster mean.

Why does the result change with the seed?

The problem is NP-hard and Lloyd's algorithm converges to a local optimum determined by initialisation.

What does k-means++ do?

Seeds centroids far apart, choosing each with probability proportional to squared distance from the nearest existing centroid.

What shape are k-means boundaries?

Straight — the partition is a Voronoi tessellation, so clusters are convex.

Three assumptions it makes.

Clusters are roughly spherical, similar in size, and similar in density.

Why scale features first?

It is distance-based, so an unscaled large-range feature dominates every assignment.

k-means vs k-medoids?

k-medoids uses actual data points as centres and is robust to outliers, at higher computational cost.

Track E · Clustering & association · Module E2

Hierarchical ClusteringNo k required up front, and a dendrogram that shows you the whole family of answers at once.

Agglomerative clustering starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair. You never choose k in advance — you get the entire nested hierarchy and cut it wherever you like afterwards. The catch is that "closest pair" needs defining, and the four standard linkage rules produce genuinely different clusterings from identical data.

Linkage bench
real agglomeration · real dendrogram
left: the clustering at your cut · right: the dendrogram, with the cut height drawn

The four linkages

LinkageDistance between clustersProducesFails by
SingleClosest pair of membersLong, snaking clusters; finds non-convex shapesChaining — one bridge of points merges two real clusters
CompleteFurthest pair of membersCompact, roughly equal-diameter clustersBreaks up genuinely elongated clusters
AverageMean distance over all pairsA compromise between the twoSensitive to the distance metric's scale
WardIncrease in within-cluster variance from mergingCompact, similar-sized clusters; the usual defaultAssumes sphericity, like k-means

Select Single and raise the bridge slider, which lays a line of points between two of the groups. The bridge only chains if its points sit closer together than the clusters' own nearest-neighbour spacing — a sparse line changes nothing, which is itself worth knowing. Watch the clustering collapse: at 60% bridging, single linkage puts 77% of the data in one cluster (sizes 92 / 1 / 27) and agreement with the true groups falls to 76.7%. Ward on the same data holds at 100%. Single linkage only needs one short hop to consider two clusters adjacent, so a line of bridging points merges them entirely — that is chaining, and it is why single linkage is rarely the default despite being the only one of the four that can follow a non-convex shape.

Reading a dendrogram

The vertical axis is the distance at which each merge happened. A cut at height h gives you the clustering with all merges below h accepted — and the honest way to pick k is to look for a large vertical gap, meaning the next merge would join things that are much further apart than anything joined so far. On well-separated data that gap is obvious; on data without cluster structure the merge heights increase smoothly and there is no gap, which is the dendrogram telling you something real.

The cost is the reason this is not the default at scale: naive agglomerative clustering is O(n³) time and O(n²) memory, so a hundred thousand points is already out of reach. It is an analysis tool for samples and segments, not a pipeline stage on a transaction table.

Interview point

"Agglomerative clustering merges the closest pair repeatedly and gives you the whole hierarchy, so you choose k after seeing the dendrogram rather than before. Linkage is the real decision: Ward and complete give compact clusters, single linkage can follow non-convex shapes but chains through any bridge of points. I read k off the largest vertical gap in the merge heights — and it's O(n²) memory, so it's for samples, not for a full transaction table."

The trap

Dendrograms are visually persuasive in exactly the way F4's t-SNE plots are. The horizontal ordering of leaves is not meaningful — any node's two children can be swapped without changing the clustering, so "these two points are next to each other on the plot" says nothing. Only the merge heights carry information. And as with every unsupervised method in this bench, agglomerative clustering will return a hierarchy for pure noise; before believing a structure, check that the largest gap is bigger than what you get from a shuffled version of the same data.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
How does agglomerative clustering work?

Every point starts as its own cluster; the closest pair is merged repeatedly until one cluster remains.

Name the four common linkages.

Single, complete, average and Ward.

What is chaining?

Single linkage merging two real clusters through a thin bridge of intermediate points.

What does Ward linkage minimise?

The increase in within-cluster variance produced by a merge.

How do you pick k from a dendrogram?

Cut below the largest vertical gap between successive merge heights.

What does the leaf ordering mean?

Nothing — children can be swapped freely; only heights are informative.

What is the complexity?

Roughly O(n³) time and O(n²) memory naively, so it does not scale to large tables.

Track E · Clustering & association · Module E3

DBSCANClusters as dense regions, arbitrary shapes allowed, and a category k-means doesn't have: noise.

k-means assigns every point to a cluster whether or not it belongs to one. DBSCAN defines clusters as connected dense regions and leaves everything else labelled as noise — which is why it is the clustering algorithm that overlaps most with anomaly detection, and why it finds the non-convex shapes that defeat Ward and Lloyd.

Density bench
real neighbourhood expansion
left: clusters by colour, noise points hollow, core points larger · right: clusters found and noise share across a sweep of ε

Three kinds of point

core has at least minPts neighbours within ε → seeds and grows a cluster border within ε of a core point, but not core itself → joins that cluster, cannot extend it noise neither → no cluster at all clusters = connected components of the core points, plus their borders

Cluster count is an output, not an input — you specify density instead of k, which is often the more natural thing to know. Select Two crescents or Ring around a blob: these are the shapes k-means cannot represent, because its boundaries are straight (E1), and DBSCAN recovers them exactly because it only ever asks whether points are densely connected.

Choosing ε, and the failure that has no fix

The right-hand panel sweeps ε and plots both the number of clusters found and the share of points labelled noise. There is usually a plateau where the count is stable — that is the range to pick from. Too small and everything is noise; too large and every cluster merges into one. The standard heuristic is a k-distance plot: sort every point's distance to its k-th neighbour and look for the knee, which is M2's k-distance quantity used as a tuning device.

Now select Two different densities, and notice that no ε works. A radius large enough to connect the sparse cluster also merges the dense one into its surroundings; a radius tight enough for the dense cluster labels the entire sparse one as noise. This is a single global density threshold meeting data with two densities — the same limitation LOF was designed around in M2 — and the fix is HDBSCAN, which varies the threshold across the space and produces a hierarchy of density levels instead of one cut.

Interview point

"DBSCAN defines clusters as connected dense regions using ε and minPts, so the number of clusters is an output and points can be labelled noise rather than forced into a cluster. That lets it find non-convex shapes k-means can't. Its weakness is a single global density threshold — with clusters of genuinely different densities no ε works — which is what HDBSCAN fixes by varying the threshold and building a density hierarchy."

The trap

DBSCAN is a distance method, so everything from A6 applies: in high dimensions the neighbourhood radius stops being meaningful and almost every point becomes noise or everything merges, with very little ε in between. Reduce dimensions first (F1) or use a method that does not measure distance (M1). Second: minPts is usually set around twice the dimensionality as a rule of thumb, and border points are assigned non-deterministically — a border point reachable from two clusters goes to whichever was expanded first, so the labels can differ between runs on identical data even though the algorithm is not randomised.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What are DBSCAN's two parameters?

ε, the neighbourhood radius, and minPts, the density threshold.

Define core, border and noise points.

Core has at least minPts neighbours within ε; border is within ε of a core point but not core; noise is neither.

What advantage does it have over k-means?

It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, infers the cluster count, and can label points as noise.

What is its main failure?

A single global density threshold cannot fit clusters of different densities.

What fixes that?

HDBSCAN, which varies the density threshold and produces a hierarchy.

How do you choose ε?

The knee of a sorted k-distance plot, checked against a sweep for a stable plateau in cluster count.

Why can labels differ between runs?

Border points reachable from two clusters are assigned by expansion order.

Track E · Clustering & association · Module E4

Association Rules & Lift"90% of people who bought X also bought Y" is a nearly worthless statement, and lift is why.

Association rule mining finds co-occurrence patterns in transaction baskets — the classic market-basket problem, and in fraud the tool for finding combinations of attributes that travel together: this device type with that merchant category at that hour. The trap is that high confidence usually just means the consequent is common, and this bench measures exactly how often that happens.

Rule mining bench
real itemset counting
left: the top rules under the selected ranking, with lift = 1 marked · right: confidence against lift for every rule found

The three measures

support(X → Y) = P(X and Y) how often the rule applies at all confidence(X → Y) = P(Y | X) how often it holds when X occurs lift(X → Y) = P(Y | X) / P(Y) how much X CHANGES the odds of Y lift = 1 X tells you nothing about Y — independence lift > 1 X makes Y more likely lift < 1 X makes Y LESS likely — and these rules are often the interesting ones

Raise popularity of the common item to 80% and rank by confidence. The top rules are all "→ common item" with confidence around 80%, and every one of them has a lift of about 1.0: the rule holds 80% of the time because that item is in 80% of baskets, not because the antecedent tells you anything. Switch the ranking to lift and the genuinely associated pairs — the ones the generator actually planted — rise to the top.

The right-hand scatter makes the relationship visible: confidence on one axis, lift on the other, with a horizontal line at lift = 1. Rules cluster along that line as popularity rises. A high-confidence rule sitting on the lift-1 line is a description of the base rate wearing a rule's clothing, which is D1's precision-versus-base-rate problem in a different notation.

Apriori, and why it works

Counting every possible itemset is combinatorial — 2ⁿ subsets of n items. Apriori prunes using one observation: if an itemset is infrequent, every superset of it is also infrequent, since adding items can only reduce support. So you find frequent 1-itemsets, use them to generate candidate 2-itemsets, count, prune, and continue. Lower the min support slider and watch the rule count climb steeply — that curve is the combinatorial explosion the anti-monotone property is holding back, and it is also why support thresholds are set for tractability at least as much as for interest.

Interview point

"Support is how often the rule applies, confidence is P(Y|X), and lift is P(Y|X)/P(Y) — the one that matters, because confidence alone just reflects how common the consequent is. A rule with 90% confidence and lift 1.0 is telling you the base rate. Apriori makes the search tractable through the anti-monotone property: any superset of an infrequent itemset is infrequent, so you prune whole branches."

The trap

Rule mining is a multiple-comparisons machine (S2). Mining a thousand items produces hundreds of thousands of candidate rules, and at any confidence threshold a large number will pass by chance alone — so a rule found by exhaustive search needs validation on a held-out period before it means anything, exactly like a model. In fraud specifically, be careful about acting on lift-based rules directly: a rule is a rigid conjunction an adversary can enumerate and avoid (V3), which is why rules work best as features feeding a model, or as investigation leads for analysts, rather than as the decision layer itself.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define support, confidence and lift.

Support is P(X and Y); confidence is P(Y|X); lift is P(Y|X)/P(Y).

What does lift = 1 mean?

X and Y are independent — the rule carries no information.

Why can confidence mislead?

It is high whenever the consequent is common, regardless of any association.

State the Apriori principle.

Every superset of an infrequent itemset is infrequent, so infrequent branches can be pruned.

What does lowering min support do?

Explodes the candidate count combinatorially and the runtime with it.

Are lift < 1 rules useful?

Yes — they identify negative associations, which can be as actionable as positive ones.

What is the statistical risk in rule mining?

Massive multiple testing; rules must be validated out of sample.

Track E · Clustering & association · Module E5

Choosing k & Validating ClustersEvery method returns a best k. The question no method answers by itself is whether there were any clusters at all.

E1 to E3 all produce a partition. This module is about whether to believe it. The standard tools — the elbow, the silhouette — will each nominate an optimal k on uniform noise, confidently and reproducibly. This bench runs them on data with real clusters and on data with none, side by side, so the difference is something you have measured rather than something you have been told.

Validation bench
real silhouette · null-model comparison
left: inertia across k, the elbow · right: silhouette across k for your data and for a matched null model — the gap is the evidence

The three standard methods

MethodWhat it measuresWeakness
Elbow (inertia vs k)Where the marginal gain in within-cluster variance drops offInertia always decreases with k; the elbow is often ambiguous or absent
SilhouetteFor each point, (b − a)/max(a, b): separation from the next-nearest cluster against cohesion within its ownFavours convex, roughly equal clusters — it is biased toward what k-means produces
Gap statisticObserved inertia against inertia on a matched reference distribution with no clustersSlower, and needs the null model chosen sensibly

Silhouette runs from −1 to 1. Above about 0.5 is usually taken as a reasonable structure and below 0.25 as weak — conventions, not thresholds with a confidence level attached, exactly like PSI's bands in D7.

The comparison that makes it evidence

The right-hand panel plots silhouette across k for your data and, alongside it, the same computation on a matched null model: uniformly distributed points over the same bounding box, averaged over several draws. On four real clusters your curve sits well above the null and peaks at the true k. Switch to Uniform noise and the two curves lie on top of each other — the method still nominates a best k, and the null tells you that best k means nothing.

That comparison is the whole discipline of cluster validation, and it is the same argument as X3's degree-preserving rewiring and F3's shuffled kernel PCA. An unsupervised method with no null model is not a measurement, and the reason to build the null is that the alternative — looking at the picture and deciding it seems clustered — is exactly what F4 demonstrated you cannot trust.

Select One elongated cloud for the subtler failure. There is one true structure, and silhouette will happily nominate two or three, because slicing a long cloud crosswise produces compact pieces that score well by a criterion built to reward compactness. Silhouette is not neutral about cluster shape; it prefers the shape k-means makes.

Interview point

"Elbow and silhouette both nominate a k on data with no clusters at all, so on their own they're not evidence. I compare against a null model — the gap statistic's idea — running the same procedure on uniform data over the same range and checking my curve is meaningfully above it. And I'd note silhouette is biased toward convex equal-sized clusters, so on elongated structure it can prefer a k that just slices the cloud."

The trap

The deepest problem is that "the right k" often does not exist, because clustering is not usually the objective. If the segments feed a marketing campaign with capacity for four treatments, k is four; if they feed an investigation queue, k is however many an analyst can hold in mind. Stability is frequently the better criterion than any internal index: cluster two random halves of the data separately and measure how consistently pairs of points land together. A structure that does not survive resampling will not survive next month either — and unlike silhouette, that criterion says nothing about what shape your clusters ought to be.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why is inertia alone useless for choosing k?

It decreases monotonically with k regardless of structure, so lower is always "better".

Define the silhouette coefficient.

(b − a)/max(a, b) per point, where a is mean distance within its cluster and b is the mean distance to the nearest other cluster.

What does the gap statistic compare against?

A reference distribution with no cluster structure, matched to the data's range.

What happens if you run these on pure noise?

They still return an optimal k — which is why a null comparison is required.

What bias does silhouette carry?

It rewards compact convex clusters, so it favours what k-means produces and penalises elongated structure.

What is stability-based validation?

Cluster resampled subsets and measure how consistently the same points co-cluster.

When is the "right" k not a statistical question?

Whenever downstream capacity — treatments, analysts, queues — determines how many segments are usable.

Track I · Classical NLP · Module I1

Text RepresentationTurning documents into vectors. The choices you make here decide everything downstream.

Before any text model there is a matrix: rows are documents, columns are terms. How you fill it determines what the model can learn. Bag-of-words counts occurrences and treats "the" and "chargeback" as equally interesting; TF-IDF reweights so that rare terms carry more weight than common ones. This bench builds both on a synthetic complaint corpus and measures the difference.

Representation bench
real counts · real IDF
left: the top terms by the selected weighting · right: term frequency ranked, showing the Zipf shape and where min_df cuts

The two weightings

tf(t,d) = count of term t in document d (or 1 + log(count), sublinear) idf(t) = log( N / df(t) ) + 1 df = documents containing t tfidf(t,d) = tf(t,d) × idf(t), then L2-normalise each row a term in every document → idf ≈ 1 contributes almost nothing distinctive a term in 1% of documents → idf ≈ 5.6 dominates the vectors it appears in

Switch between the two representations and compare the top-terms panel, which ranks by mean weight among the documents where each term occurs — summing across the whole corpus would reward ubiquity again and quietly undo the IDF factor. Under raw counts the leaders are all filler words, because they genuinely are the most frequent things in the corpus. Under TF-IDF the stopwords vanish from the top ten entirely and the leaders become rare terms with IDF around 5.

Read that second result carefully, because it cuts both ways. TF-IDF is doing exactly what it promises — discounting ubiquity — and the consequence is that its largest weights land on terms appearing in one or two documents, which have almost no evidence behind them. TF-IDF and min_df are therefore a pair: the weighting pushes value toward the tail, and min_df decides how much of that tail you are willing to trust.

Zipf, sparsity, and why min_df exists

The right-hand panel plots term frequency against rank. It is a steep curve — a handful of terms account for most of the tokens, and a long tail appears once or twice each. That is Zipf's law, and it has two consequences. First, the matrix is enormously sparse: the readout reports what share of cells are zero, typically well above 95%, which is why text is stored in sparse formats and why linear models with L2 handle it well (B5).

Second, the tail is mostly useless and expensive. Raise min_df and watch the vocabulary collapse while sparsity barely improves — you are discarding terms that appeared in one or two documents and could never generalise. That is a bias–variance decision (A1) made on the vocabulary rather than the model: each rare term is a feature with almost no data behind it.

Turn on Drop stopwords and note that with TF-IDF the gain is small, because IDF has already down-weighted them numerically. Stopword removal matters much more for raw counts — which is a useful thing to say when someone asks whether it is necessary.

Interview point

"Bag-of-words loses order and treats all terms as equally informative; TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency so ubiquitous terms are discounted and distinctive ones dominate. Text follows Zipf, so the matrix is over 95% sparse and the tail is mostly single-occurrence terms — min_df drops them as a variance-reduction step. And with TF-IDF, explicit stopword removal adds little, because IDF already discounts them."

The trap

IDF is fitted on the training corpus and must be loaded, not recomputed at inference — recompute it on live traffic and you have K1's training–serving skew with a text vectoriser instead of a scaler. The same applies to the vocabulary: a term the model never saw has no column, and silently dropping out-of-vocabulary terms is usually right but occasionally catastrophic, as when a new fraud pattern arrives with new vocabulary and every document containing it looks empty. Monitor OOV rate as a drift signal (D7) — a rising OOV rate is often the earliest indication that the language of your inbound complaints has changed.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does bag-of-words discard?

Word order and syntax — only term counts remain.

Write the TF-IDF weighting.

tf(t,d) × idf(t), where idf = log(N/df(t)) + 1, usually with L2 row normalisation.

What does IDF do to a term appearing in every document?

Reduces its weight to near-nothing, since N/df approaches 1.

What is Zipf's law and why does it matter?

Term frequency falls off steeply with rank, so matrices are extremely sparse and the vocabulary tail is single-occurrence terms.

What does min_df control?

The minimum document frequency for a term to be kept — a variance-reduction choice on the vocabulary.

Is stopword removal necessary with TF-IDF?

Largely redundant — IDF already discounts them numerically.

Where must IDF and the vocabulary be fitted?

On training data, then loaded at inference; recomputing them online creates skew.

Track I · Classical NLP · Module I2

Text ClassificationNaive Bayes and logistic regression on the same vectors, and the assumption that separates them.

On text, two classical models dominate: multinomial Naive Bayes, which is astonishingly strong for how simple it is, and logistic regression on TF-IDF, which is the usual production baseline. They differ in one assumption — NB treats terms as conditionally independent given the class — and this bench makes that assumption fail on demand so you can watch the consequence.

Classifier bench
real multinomial NB · real logistic
left: AUC and calibration error for both models · right: the most discriminative terms by logistic coefficient

Why Naive Bayes works better than it should

P(class | doc) ∝ P(class) · Π_terms P(term | class)^count log form: score = log P(c) + Σ count(t) · log P(t | c) → linear in the counts Laplace smoothing: P(t | c) = (count + α) / (total + α·V) without it, one unseen term sends the whole product to zero

The independence assumption is plainly false — "chargeback" and "dispute" co-occur constantly — and yet NB classifies text well. The reason is that classification only needs the argmax to be right, not the probabilities: correlated evidence gets double-counted, which pushes the scores toward 0 and 1 without necessarily flipping the ranking. Raise duplicated terms and watch exactly that: NB's AUC holds up reasonably while its calibration error climbs, because each duplicate adds another supposedly independent vote for the same evidence.

That is the practical distinction to carry: NB is a decent classifier and a poor probability estimator under correlation (C5, D6). Logistic regression fits coefficients jointly, so it shares the credit between correlated terms instead of double-counting, and its probabilities stay usable — which matters the moment a score gets multiplied by money (D3).

Representations and n-grams

Switch to TF-IDF: logistic typically improves, since the weighting is what its linear form wants. Multinomial NB expects counts and its assumptions fit them better, though TF-IDF often still works in practice — a mismatch worth noting rather than pretending away. Then switch to Counts + bigrams: adjacent word pairs recover some of the order that bag-of-words destroyed, at the cost of a much larger, sparser vocabulary. Watch the vocabulary readout jump and the improvement be modest — that trade is why bigrams are common and trigrams rarely are.

The right-hand panel lists the terms with the largest logistic coefficients, which is the honest interpretability story for text: a linear model on TF-IDF gives you per-term weights you can read directly, and for many review and audit purposes (V2) that is worth more than a few points of accuracy from something opaque.

Interview point

"Multinomial NB assumes terms are conditionally independent given the class, which is false for text but often harmless for ranking — it damages the probabilities more than the argmax, so it's a decent classifier and a badly calibrated one. Logistic on TF-IDF fits jointly, shares credit between correlated terms, and gives readable per-term coefficients, so it's my default when the score feeds a decision. Laplace smoothing is non-negotiable in NB: without it a single unseen term zeroes the whole product."

The trap

Text classifiers learn the artefacts of how documents were collected. If fraud complaints arrive through a different form than service complaints, the model will find the form's boilerplate rather than the content — a template phrase present in every fraud ticket is a perfect predictor offline and worthless the moment the form changes. Inspect your top coefficients and ask of each one whether it is about the world or about the pipeline; that inspection is the main reason to prefer an interpretable model here. It is also A2's leakage in the vocabulary rather than in the rows.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State Naive Bayes' assumption.

Terms are conditionally independent given the class.

Why does it still classify well?

Classification needs the argmax, not calibrated probabilities; double-counted evidence often does not flip the ranking.

What does correlation damage in NB?

Calibration — probabilities become over-confident.

Why is Laplace smoothing required?

An unseen term gives probability zero, which zeroes the entire product.

Which representation suits which model?

Counts for multinomial NB; TF-IDF for logistic regression.

What do bigrams buy and cost?

Some word-order information, at the cost of a far larger and sparser vocabulary.

How do you audit a text model?

Read the top coefficients and check whether each reflects the world or an artefact of data collection.

Track I · Classical NLP · Module I3

Embeddings & RetrievalDense vectors solve the synonym problem and create a new one. Both are measurable.

TF-IDF matches strings. Search for "unapproved charge" in a corpus that says "unauthorised transaction" and you get nothing, however obviously related the two are. Embeddings place terms in a continuous space where distributional neighbours sit close together, which fixes that — and introduces the opposite failure, where a rare exact term gets smoothed away. This bench builds real embeddings by factorising a co-occurrence matrix and measures both effects.

Retrieval bench
real co-occurrence SVD · real cosine ranking
left: precision@10 for lexical and dense retrieval on the selected query type · right: the embedding space projected to two dimensions, with related terms marked

How the embeddings are built

1. count co-occurrences within a ±window of each token → matrix C (V × V) 2. reweight M_ij = log( C_ij · total / (row_i · col_j) ) ≈ pointwise mutual information 3. factorise keep the top k eigenvectors of M → a k-dimensional vector per term 4. a document or query vector = the mean of its term vectors 5. rank by cosine similarity this is latent semantic analysis, and word2vec's skip-gram objective is provably related to factorising a shifted PMI matrix of exactly this kind

Nothing here is a neural network, and that is the point: the mechanism that makes embeddings work is distributional — terms appearing in similar contexts get similar vectors — and it is visible in a matrix factorisation you can compute by hand. Everything a transformer adds is contextual refinement on top of that idea.

The two failures, measured

Select Query uses synonyms. The alternative wording appears in only a handful of documents, so lexical retrieval reaches 70% precision@10 and then runs out of matches; dense retrieval gets 90%, because those few documents gave the synonyms a context and the factorisation placed them beside their equivalents. That gap is the commercial case for semantic search.

Two implementation details are doing real work here, and both are load-bearing rather than incidental. The embedding vocabulary is filtered to terms with enough document frequency to have a genuine context — fit on the full Zipf tail from a few hundred short documents and the vectors are noise, which is worth knowing before you trust any embedding trained on a small corpus. And document vectors are IDF-weighted means rather than plain averages; without that weighting the filler words dominate every vector and all documents look alike.

Now select Query uses a rare exact term. This is the reverse: lexical retrieval nails it — an exact string match on a rare term is an extremely strong signal — while dense retrieval smooths it toward its neighbours and returns approximately-relevant documents instead of the right one. Measured: lexical 100% against dense 20%. This is why production retrieval is nearly always hybrid: run both, fuse the rankings, and get the synonym tolerance without losing exact-match precision on identifiers, error codes, wallet addresses and names.

Drop embedding dimensions to 2 and watch dense precision fall — too few dimensions and unrelated terms collide. Raise it toward the vocabulary size and the embeddings approach the sparse representation they were meant to compress, recovering lexical behaviour along with its brittleness.

Interview point

"Embeddings come from the distributional hypothesis: factorise a reweighted co-occurrence matrix — essentially PMI — and terms used in similar contexts land near each other, which is what fixes synonym mismatch that TF-IDF can't handle. The trade is exact matching: dense retrieval smooths rare identifiers toward their neighbours, so production systems run hybrid retrieval and fuse the rankings. And word2vec's skip-gram is provably related to factorising a shifted PMI matrix, so the classical and neural stories are the same story."

The trap

Cosine similarity is not relevance. Two documents about entirely different frauds share vocabulary and score highly; a query and its perfect answer can be phrased so differently that they do not. Embedding similarity is a retrieval signal to be reranked, not a decision — which is why RAG systems put a cross-encoder or an LLM after the vector search rather than trusting the top hit. And embeddings inherit the biases of the corpus they were fitted on, so a space learned from historical complaint data encodes historical patterns including ones you are not permitted to act on (V1) — the vector space has no notion of a protected attribute, but it will happily represent one.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State the distributional hypothesis.

Words appearing in similar contexts have similar meanings.

How can embeddings be built without a neural network?

Reweight a co-occurrence matrix toward PMI and keep its top singular vectors — latent semantic analysis.

What is word2vec's relation to that?

Skip-gram with negative sampling is provably related to factorising a shifted PMI matrix.

Where does lexical retrieval beat dense?

Rare exact terms — identifiers, codes, names — where an exact match is decisive.

Where does dense beat lexical?

Synonyms and paraphrase, where no string overlap exists.

What is hybrid retrieval?

Running both and fusing the rankings to get synonym tolerance without losing exact-match precision.

Why rerank after vector search?

Cosine similarity approximates relatedness, not relevance, so a stronger model should score the shortlist.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H1

Perceptron & XORThe single problem that stopped neural networks for fifteen years, and the one-line fix.

A perceptron is a linear boundary with a learning rule. It converges provably on anything linearly separable and fails completely on XOR — four points that no straight line can split. The fix is a hidden layer, and understanding exactly why it works is the foundation for everything else in this track.

Perceptron bench
real perceptron rule · real hidden layer
left: the decision surface · right: training error by epoch for both models on this problem

The rule and its guarantee

prediction ŷ = sign(w·x + b) update on a mistake: w ← w + η·y·x, b ← b + η·y (do nothing when correct) Perceptron convergence theorem: if the data is linearly separable, this terminates in a finite number of updates — bounded by (R/γ)², R the data radius, γ the margin. If the data is NOT separable it never terminates. It does not converge to a good approximate boundary; it cycles.

That last line is the practical difference from logistic regression (C1), which minimises a smooth loss and therefore always converges to something sensible. The perceptron has no such fallback, and this is why the modern treatment replaces the step function with a differentiable activation and the mistake rule with gradient descent.

Why a hidden layer solves XOR

Select XOR with the perceptron: error plateaus around 50% and stays there. Switch to One hidden layer and it drops to near zero. The mechanism is worth stating precisely — a hidden unit is itself a linear boundary followed by a nonlinearity, so the hidden layer re-represents the input in a space where the problem is linearly separable, and the output layer then draws its single straight line there. Deep learning is that trick, repeated.

Drop hidden units to 1 and XOR fails again: one hidden unit is one boundary, which is no better than the perceptron. Two are sufficient in principle. The bench lets you confirm that yourself rather than take it on faith.

The universal approximation theorem says a single hidden layer with enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain to arbitrary accuracy. It is often quoted as though it settles the case for shallow networks; it does not, because it says nothing about how many units are needed or whether gradient descent will find them. Depth matters in practice because it makes some functions representable with exponentially fewer parameters — which H2 measures.

Interview point

"A perceptron is a linear classifier with a mistake-driven update, and the convergence theorem guarantees termination only if the data is separable — on XOR it cycles forever. A hidden layer fixes it by re-representing the input in a space where the classes are linearly separable, and that's the whole idea of deep learning. Universal approximation says one hidden layer suffices in principle, but it says nothing about how many units or whether SGD finds them, which is why depth still matters."

The trap

Don't reach for a network because the problem "sounds nonlinear". On tabular fraud data, gradient-boosted trees (G4) usually beat an MLP, train in a fraction of the time, handle missing values natively, and produce features you can explain to a validator (V2).
