Neural networks earn their place where the input has structure a network can exploit — sequence, image, graph (X4), or text — or where you need a learned representation rather than a prediction. Being able to say when not to use one is a stronger signal than knowing the architectures.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
State the perceptron update rule.

On a misclassified point, w ← w + η·y·x and b ← b + η·y; nothing changes when the prediction is correct.

What does the convergence theorem guarantee?

Termination in finitely many updates if the data is linearly separable, bounded by (R/γ)².

What happens on non-separable data?

It never terminates and does not settle on a good approximation — it cycles.

Why can't a perceptron learn XOR?

XOR is not linearly separable and a perceptron can only draw one hyperplane.

How does a hidden layer fix it?

Hidden units re-represent the input in a space where the classes become linearly separable.

What does universal approximation actually say?

One hidden layer of sufficient width can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain — with no bound on width and no guarantee of trainability.

When would you not use a neural network?

On tabular data, where boosted trees are usually faster, stronger and easier to validate.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H2

The Forward PassWhat a network computes, and why depth buys more than width for the same parameter budget.

A forward pass is a chain of affine transforms with a nonlinearity between them. With ReLU that composition has a precise geometric meaning: the network is a piecewise-linear function, and its capacity is roughly the number of linear pieces it can produce. This bench counts those pieces so you can watch width and depth buy them at different rates.

Forward-pass bench
real fitting · real piece counting
left: the fitted function against the target, with detected kinks marked · right: linear pieces produced, width against depth at a matched parameter budget

The computation

a⁽⁰⁾ = x a⁽ˡ⁾ = σ( W⁽ˡ⁾ a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾ ) for each hidden layer ŷ = W⁽ᴸ⁾ a⁽ᴸ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ᴸ⁾ linear output for regression parameters = Σ (in × out + out) the readout computes this exactly with ReLU every unit is either on or off, so the network is linear within each region of input space and the boundaries between regions are where units flip.

The left panel marks the kinks it detects in the fitted function. Those are precisely the points where some hidden unit crosses zero, and counting them is a direct measurement of the model's expressive capacity on this input.

Width versus depth

The right-hand panel is the experiment worth running: it holds the parameter budget roughly fixed and reallocates it between width and depth, plotting the pieces each configuration produces. Width adds pieces additively — each new unit contributes one more possible kink. Depth composes, so pieces multiply across layers, and the count grows far faster for the same parameters.

That is the theoretical case for depth, and the bench shows its limit too: raise depth to five and the fit often gets worse despite more available pieces, because deeper networks are harder to optimise (H4). Capacity you cannot train is not capacity. This is the honest version of "deeper is better" and it is the version worth saying.

More widthMore depth
Pieces gainedAdditiveMultiplicative
Parameters per unit addedGrows with neighbouring layer sizesSame
OptimisationEasy, stableHarder — vanishing gradients, needs care
ParallelismExcellent — one big matrix multiplySequential; layers must run in order

Interview point

"A forward pass is repeated affine transform plus nonlinearity. With ReLU the network is piecewise-linear, so its capacity is essentially how many linear pieces it can form — width adds pieces additively, depth composes so they multiply, which is the formal case for depth at a fixed parameter count. The catch is trainability: past a few layers, optimisation degrades faster than capacity helps, which is what residual connections and normalisation exist to fix."

The trap

Parameter count is a poor proxy for capacity and an even worse proxy for cost. Two networks with identical parameter counts can differ by an order of magnitude in FLOPs and in latency, because a deep narrow network runs its layers sequentially while a wide shallow one is one large matrix multiply the hardware loves. If a model is going on the fraud authorisation path (K2), profile the actual forward-pass latency rather than reasoning from parameter count — and remember that on that path, feature retrieval usually costs more than the network does anyway.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write the forward pass for one layer.

a⁽ˡ⁾ = σ(W⁽ˡ⁾a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾).

How many parameters does a layer have?

in × out weights plus out biases.

What kind of function does a ReLU network compute?

A piecewise-linear one; regions are defined by which units are active.

How do width and depth differ in expressiveness?

Width adds linear pieces additively; depth multiplies them through composition.

Why isn't deeper always better?

Optimisation degrades with depth, so untrainable capacity is useless.

Why is a linear output used for regression?

A bounded activation would cap the range of predictions.

Is parameter count a good cost proxy?

No — depth, memory layout and parallelism dominate real latency.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H3

BackpropagationThe chain rule applied in reverse, and the gradient check that proves you got it right.

Backprop is not an algorithm for computing gradients so much as the efficient ordering of the chain rule — one backward sweep gets every parameter's gradient for roughly the cost of one forward pass. This bench computes gradients both ways, analytically and by finite differences, and reports the relative error between them. That comparison is the gradient check, and it is how you know an implementation is correct.

Gradient bench
analytic vs numerical, computed live
left: analytic against numerical gradient for sampled parameters — the diagonal is agreement · right: relative error as ε varies, showing both failure modes

The backward pass

forward: z⁽ˡ⁾ = W⁽ˡ⁾a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾, a⁽ˡ⁾ = σ(z⁽ˡ⁾) output: δ⁽ᴸ⁾ = ∂L/∂ŷ (ŷ − y for squared or logistic loss) recurse: δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ᵀ δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ σ′(z⁽ˡ⁾) gradients: ∂L/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾ (a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾)ᵀ, ∂L/∂b⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾ cost: one backward sweep ≈ one forward pass, for ALL parameters naive finite differences would need one forward pass PER parameter

That cost comparison is the entire reason deep learning is feasible. A network with a million parameters would need a million forward passes per step to estimate gradients numerically; backprop gets all of them in one. It also explains why the forward activations must be cached — a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ appears in the gradient — which is why training memory scales with depth and batch size while inference memory does not.

The gradient check, and how ε betrays you

numerical: ∂L/∂θ ≈ ( L(θ + ε) − L(θ − ε) ) / 2ε central difference, O(ε²) error relative error = |analytic − numerical| / max(|analytic|, |numerical|) below 1e-7 → correct · around 1e-5 → suspicious · above 1e-3 → a bug

The right-hand panel sweeps ε across nine orders of magnitude, and the curve is U-shaped for a reason worth knowing. Large ε carries truncation error — the difference quotient is a poor approximation of the derivative. Small ε carries floating-point cancellation — subtracting two nearly identical numbers destroys precision. The minimum sits near 1e-5, and someone who picks 1e-12 expecting more accuracy gets a failed gradient check on correct code.

Raise training steps taken first and re-check. The agreement holds, which is the point: backprop is exact, not approximate, so a correct implementation matches finite differences at any point in parameter space. If the error grows as training proceeds, the bug is usually in a layer that only activates once weights leave their initial range — a ReLU never firing at initialisation, for instance.

Interview point

"Backprop is the chain rule ordered to reuse work: δ propagates backwards as Wᵀδ elementwise-times the activation derivative, and one backward sweep gives every parameter's gradient for about the cost of a forward pass — versus one forward pass per parameter numerically. It needs cached forward activations, which is why training memory scales with depth and batch size. I verify an implementation with a central-difference gradient check at ε around 1e-5, where truncation and floating-point cancellation are balanced."

The trap

Gradient checking must be done in double precision and with any stochastic component disabled — dropout (H6) resamples its mask between the two forward passes, so the numerical gradient is computed on a different function and the check fails on correct code. The same applies to batch norm in training mode, to data augmentation, and to any sampling inside the forward pass. Fix the seed, disable the randomness, check a random subset of parameters rather than all of them, and remember that non-differentiable points — ReLU exactly at zero — will legitimately disagree.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write the backprop recursion.

δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ᵀδ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ σ′(z⁽ˡ⁾), with ∂L/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾(a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾)ᵀ.

Why is backprop efficient?

One backward sweep yields all gradients at roughly the cost of one forward pass.

Why must activations be cached?

They appear directly in the weight gradients, so training memory scales with depth and batch size.

What is a gradient check?

Comparing analytic gradients against central finite differences and requiring a tiny relative error.

Why is the error U-shaped in ε?

Large ε suffers truncation error; small ε suffers floating-point cancellation.

What ε is typical?

Around 1e-5 in double precision.

What breaks a gradient check on correct code?

Any randomness in the forward pass — dropout, augmentation, batch-norm statistics — or non-differentiable points.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H4

Activations & Vanishing GradientsWhy sigmoid stopped being the default, measured layer by layer.

The backprop recursion multiplies by σ′(z) at every layer. If that derivative is reliably smaller than one, gradients shrink geometrically as they travel backwards, and the early layers stop learning — the vanishing gradient problem, which is the single reason deep networks were impractical before ReLU. This bench measures the gradient norm at each layer so you can watch it happen.

Gradient-flow bench
real per-layer gradient norms
left: gradient norm by layer on a log scale — the slope is the problem · right: the activation and its derivative

Where the factor comes from

δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ᵀ δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ σ′(z⁽ˡ⁾) one multiplication by σ′ per layer sigmoid σ′ = a(1−a) maximum 0.25, and far smaller once saturated tanh σ′ = 1 − a² maximum 1.0 at zero, but saturates just as hard ReLU σ′ = 1 or 0 no shrinkage where active — the reason it won after L layers of sigmoid at its BEST case: 0.25^L L=6 → 2.4e-4 · L=10 → 1e-6

Select Sigmoid and set depth to 10. The left panel plots gradient norm per layer on a log axis, and the line falls off a cliff toward the input — the first layers receive gradients orders of magnitude smaller than the last, so they barely move. The network trains its final layers and leaves the early ones near their initialisation.

Switch to ReLU. The line flattens, because σ′ is exactly 1 wherever the unit is active, and there is no per-layer shrinkage at all. That single property is why ReLU replaced sigmoid as the default hidden activation, and it is a better answer than "ReLU is faster to compute".

The costs of ReLU, and the initialisation that matters

ReLU's derivative is zero for negative inputs, so a unit pushed firmly negative stops receiving gradient permanently — a dead unit. The bench reports the share of hidden units that never activate. Push the init scale up and watch that share climb: too-large weights saturate units into the dead region before training begins. Leaky ReLU passes a small slope for negative inputs specifically so the gradient never reaches exactly zero.

Init scale also controls the opposite failure. Below 1.0 the gradients shrink even with ReLU; well above it they explode. That is what He initialisation (variance 2/fan_in, the default here) and Xavier/Glorot (2/(fan_in+fan_out), for tanh) exist to set — they choose the scale that keeps activation variance roughly constant across layers, which is the same problem as gradient flow seen from the forward direction.

Interview point

"Backprop multiplies by σ′ at every layer, and sigmoid's derivative peaks at 0.25, so gradients shrink at least fourfold per layer — 0.25¹⁰ is about 1e-6, and the early layers stop learning. ReLU's derivative is exactly 1 where active, so there's no shrinkage, which is why it became the default. Its cost is dead units, which leaky ReLU addresses, and the scale still has to be set properly — He initialisation for ReLU, Xavier for tanh."

The trap

ReLU does not solve vanishing gradients on its own; it removes one of the causes. The other is the repeated multiplication by Wᵀ, which shrinks or explodes depending on the weight spectrum — which is why very deep networks still need residual connections, giving the gradient an identity path that bypasses the layers entirely, and normalisation to keep activation scales in range. If someone says "we use ReLU so gradients are fine at 50 layers", that is the gap in the reasoning. And exploding gradients are the mirror failure: usually handled by gradient clipping, and much easier to spot because the loss goes to NaN rather than quietly not improving.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Why do gradients vanish?

Backprop multiplies by σ′ at each layer; if σ′ < 1 the product shrinks geometrically with depth.

What is sigmoid's maximum derivative?

0.25, at z = 0 — and far less once saturated.

Why does ReLU help?

Its derivative is exactly 1 wherever the unit is active, so there is no per-layer shrinkage.

What is a dead ReLU?

A unit whose input is always negative, so its gradient is permanently zero and it never recovers.

What does leaky ReLU change?

A small negative slope keeps the gradient non-zero, preventing permanent death.

He vs Xavier initialisation?

He uses variance 2/fan_in for ReLU; Xavier uses 2/(fan_in+fan_out) for tanh and sigmoid.

What else is needed at real depth?

Residual connections for an identity gradient path, normalisation, and clipping for the exploding direction.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H5

OptimisersSGD, momentum, RMSprop and Adam on the same surface — and why Adam isn't automatically the answer.

B2 showed plain gradient descent zig-zagging down a ravine because a single learning rate has to serve directions with very different curvature. Every optimiser since is an attempt to fix that: momentum accumulates velocity, RMSprop rescales per parameter, and Adam does both. This bench runs all four on the same surfaces and counts the steps.

Optimiser bench
real update rules, step by step
left: each optimiser's path across the surface · right: loss by step, log scale

The four update rules

SGD θ ← θ − η·g momentum v ← βv − η·g, θ ← θ + v β ≈ 0.9 accumulates velocity along consistent directions, cancels oscillation RMSprop s ← ρs + (1−ρ)g², θ ← θ − η·g/(√s + ε) per-parameter step size: large where gradients have been small Adam m ← β₁m + (1−β₁)g first moment (momentum) v ← β₂v + (1−β₂)g² second moment (RMSprop) bias-correct both, then θ ← θ − η·m̂/(√v̂ + ε)

Adam's bias correction is the part people forget and interviewers ask about. Both moments start at zero, so early estimates are biased toward zero; dividing by (1 − βᵗ) corrects this. Without it the first steps are far too small, and since β₂ = 0.999 the second-moment bias persists for hundreds of steps.

What each surface shows

Ravine. Raise the condition number and watch SGD oscillate across the narrow direction while creeping along the flat one. Momentum damps the oscillation because the crosswise components alternate in sign and cancel while the along-valley components accumulate. RMSprop attacks it differently — it normalises by the gradient's recent magnitude, so the steep direction gets small steps and the flat direction large ones, which is exactly the per-direction scaling a single η cannot provide.

Saddle. The gradient is near zero at the saddle, so SGD nearly stalls. Momentum carries through on accumulated velocity. In high dimensions saddles vastly outnumber local minima, which is why this case matters more than the textbook picture of getting stuck in a local minimum suggests.

Well-conditioned bowl. The honest case: everything works, and plain SGD is competitive. Adaptive methods buy the most where conditioning is worst, and nothing where it is fine.

Interview point

"Momentum accumulates velocity so oscillations across a ravine cancel while progress along it accumulates. RMSprop divides by a running root-mean-square of the gradient, giving per-parameter step sizes. Adam combines both with bias correction, since the moment estimates start at zero and would otherwise be far too small early on. I'd start with Adam for fast convergence, but note that well-tuned SGD with momentum often generalises better, which is why vision models are still trained with it."

The trap

Adam converging faster in training loss does not mean a better model. There is a well-documented tendency for adaptive methods to find sharper minima that generalise slightly worse, which is why SGD with momentum and a learning-rate schedule remains standard in vision. Two other practical points: Adam's default weight decay is not L2 regularisation once the adaptive scaling is applied — AdamW decouples them and that distinction is a common interview question — and the learning-rate schedule usually matters more than the choice of optimiser, with warmup plus cosine decay being the current default for large models.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does momentum do?

Accumulates a velocity vector so consistent gradient directions reinforce and oscillations cancel.

What does RMSprop divide by?

The square root of a running average of squared gradients, giving per-parameter step sizes.

What are Adam's two moments?

A first moment (momentum) and a second moment (squared gradients), both bias-corrected.

Why is bias correction needed?

The moment estimates start at zero, so early values are biased small — especially with β₂ = 0.999.

Why do saddles matter more than local minima?

In high dimensions saddle points vastly outnumber local minima.

When is plain SGD preferable?

Well-conditioned problems, and settings where its generalisation edge matters more than convergence speed.

What is AdamW?

Adam with weight decay decoupled from the gradient, so decay isn't scaled by the adaptive term.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H6

Dropout, Early Stopping & Batch NormThree techniques that all reduce overfitting, for three completely different reasons.

A network with more parameters than data will fit the noise (A1). Deep learning's answer is not a single regulariser but a stack of them, and they are frequently confused because they share a symptom. This bench trains the same over-parameterised network with each one switched on so you can compare what the validation curve does.

Regularisation bench
real dropout masks · real running statistics
left: training and validation loss by epoch, with the early-stopping point marked · right: the fitted function against the truth

Three different mechanisms

TechniqueWhat it actually doesTrain / inference behaviour
DropoutRandomly zeroes units each step, so no unit can rely on any other — approximately an ensemble over subnetworksDifferent: active in training, disabled at inference with weights scaled
Weight decay / L2Penalises large weights, shrinking the function toward smoothness (B5)Same
Early stoppingStops at the validation minimum — limits how far optimisation travels rather than where it can goSame; needs a validation split
Batch normNormalises activations per mini-batch, stabilising scale so higher learning rates work; regularises as a side effect via batch noiseDifferent: batch statistics in training, running averages at inference

The train/inference column is where bugs live. Dropout and batch norm behave differently in the two modes, which is why frameworks have an explicit train/eval switch and why forgetting to flip it is among the most common production errors in deep learning — the model appears to work and its outputs are subtly wrong. It is also, as H3 noted, what breaks a gradient check on correct code.

What the curves show

Set training rows to 20 with width at 40 and no regularisation: training loss drives toward zero while validation loss bottoms out early and then climbs. That divergence is overfitting drawn precisely, and the marked minimum is what early stopping captures — note it is free, requires no hyperparameter beyond patience, and is the first thing to reach for.

Now switch on dropout and watch the validation curve flatten rather than rise. Push the rate to 0.8 and the model underfits instead: dropout is a capacity control, and too much of it is as damaging as none. Rates of 0.2–0.5 are conventional for exactly this reason.

Interview point

"They fix different things. Dropout randomly zeroes units so no unit can co-adapt on another, which approximates ensembling over subnetworks. Weight decay shrinks weights toward a smoother function. Early stopping bounds how far optimisation travels and costs nothing but a validation split. Batch norm is primarily an optimisation aid — it stabilises activation scale so you can use higher learning rates — and regularises only incidentally through batch noise. Dropout and batch norm behave differently at train and inference time, which is where the bugs come from."

The trap

Batch norm's dependence on the mini-batch is a real architectural constraint, not a detail. At batch size 1 — common in online fraud scoring — the batch statistics are meaningless, which is why layer norm is used in transformers and in anything served per-request. The running averages it keeps for inference are also fitted on training data, so they drift when the input distribution moves (D7) and can silently degrade a model whose weights are unchanged. And combining dropout with batch norm often hurts, because the variance shift dropout introduces interacts badly with the normalisation statistics — an effect documented well enough that most modern architectures use one or the other, not both.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What does dropout do and why?

Randomly zeroes units during training so units cannot co-adapt; it approximates an ensemble over subnetworks.

How does dropout behave at inference?

Disabled, with activations scaled so expected outputs match training.

What is early stopping's advantage?

It costs nothing but a validation split and has no hyperparameter beyond patience.

What is batch norm's primary purpose?

Stabilising activation scale so higher learning rates and deeper networks train; regularisation is a side effect.

Why does batch norm fail at batch size 1?

Batch statistics are undefined or meaningless — use layer norm instead.

What is the risk of a high dropout rate?

Underfitting — dropout is capacity control, and too much removes needed capacity.

Why avoid combining dropout with batch norm?

Dropout's variance shift interferes with the normalisation statistics.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H7

Convolution & PoolingWeight sharing as a structural assumption, and what it buys in parameters.

A convolution is a small filter slid across the input, reusing the same weights at every position. That single change encodes a strong assumption — a pattern is worth detecting regardless of where it occurs — and it collapses the parameter count by orders of magnitude. This bench applies real filters to a real signal and counts the parameters both ways.

Convolution bench
real filters · real pooling
left: the input signal, the convolved response, and the pooled output · right: parameters needed by a convolution against a dense layer, by input size

The two structural priors

convolution y[i] = Σ_k w[k] · x[i·stride + k] + b the same w at every position parameters conv: kernel_size × channels_in × channels_out + channels_out dense: input_size × output_size + output_size ← grows with INPUT size output size floor( (n − k + 2·pad) / stride ) + 1 pooling max or mean over a window: shrinks the map and makes the response insensitive to small shifts in position

Parameter sharing is the first prior: a feature detector useful at one position is useful at another, so one set of weights serves the whole input. Locality is the second: each output depends only on a small neighbourhood, and long-range structure is built up by stacking layers, so the receptive field grows with depth rather than with width.

The right-hand panel plots the parameter counts against input size. The convolution's line is flat — a 5-tap filter has five weights whether the input is 100 samples or 100,000 — while the dense layer's line climbs linearly. That gap is why convolutions made large inputs tractable at all.

Invariance, tested rather than assumed

Drag signal shift and watch the two readouts. The convolved response translates with the input — it is equivariant, not invariant — while the pooled output changes much less, because max-pooling over a window discards precisely the positional detail that shifted. The readout measures the change in each, which is the honest way to state the property: convolution gives equivariance; pooling converts some of it into invariance, and the amount depends on the pooling window.

Raise the pooling window and the invariance improves while resolution is lost. That is the trade in one slider, and it is why classification networks pool aggressively — position does not matter for "is this a cat" — while segmentation networks avoid it, because position is the answer.

Interview point

"A convolution shares one small filter across all positions, which encodes the prior that a useful pattern is worth detecting anywhere and makes the parameter count independent of input size. Convolution is translation-equivariant — shift the input and the feature map shifts — and pooling turns some of that into invariance by discarding positional detail. So classification networks pool heavily and segmentation networks don't, because there the position is the output."

The trap

The convolutional prior is an assumption about your data, and on tabular fraud features it is false — column 7 next to column 8 means nothing, so sliding a filter across them is meaningless. Convolutions apply where the axis has genuine structure: time (a transaction sequence, T3), or a genuine spatial or sequential ordering. For a fraud stack that means 1-D convolutions over event sequences are reasonable and 2-D convolutions over a feature table are not. A related caution: pooling's invariance is only to small shifts, and modern architectures have largely replaced aggressive pooling with strided convolutions and, in transformers, attention — which learns which positions matter instead of assuming locality.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What are convolution's two structural priors?

Parameter sharing across positions and locality of each response.

How many parameters does a conv layer have?

kernel × channels_in × channels_out + biases — independent of input size.

Give the output-size formula.

floor((n − k + 2·pad)/stride) + 1.

Equivariance vs invariance?

Convolution is equivariant — the feature map shifts with the input; pooling converts some of that into invariance by discarding position.

Why do segmentation networks avoid pooling?

Position is the output, so discarding it is discarding the answer.

How does the receptive field grow?

With depth — stacking layers, or dilating them, rather than widening.

Why are convolutions wrong for tabular data?

Adjacent columns have no ordering relationship, so the sharing prior is false.

Track H · Deep learning · Module H8

Autoencoder Anomaly DetectionTrain it to rebuild normal data, then score by what it fails to rebuild. And know when that logic breaks.

This is the module where Track H meets your capstone. An autoencoder compresses input through a bottleneck and reconstructs it; trained only on normal transactions it learns the manifold normal data lives on, and anomalies — which lie off it — reconstruct badly. Reconstruction error becomes the anomaly score. The bench builds one for real, benchmarks it against Isolation Forest from M1, and then demonstrates the case where the whole argument fails.

Autoencoder bench
real training · scored against M1
left: reconstruction error for normal and anomalous rows · right: AUC against bottleneck size, with the Isolation Forest baseline

The construction

encoder z = f(x) compress to a bottleneck of dimension k ≪ input dimension decoder x̂ = g(z) reconstruct train minimise ‖x − x̂‖² on normal data only score anomaly(x) = ‖x − x̂‖² the bottleneck is the whole mechanism: with k too large the network learns the identity function and reconstructs anomalies perfectly too

Drag bottleneck size toward the input dimension and watch the AUC fall. That is the identity-function failure, and it is the same lesson as C4's memorising kernel and F3's over-large γ: a model with enough capacity to reproduce anything cannot distinguish anything. The right-hand panel sweeps the bottleneck so the optimum is visible rather than asserted.

The two failures that matter operationally

Select Anomalies inside the manifold. These are transactions whose individual features all look ordinary — the fraud is in the combination, or in the timing relative to the account's history (T3). The autoencoder reconstructs them fine, because they lie exactly where normal data lies, and the AUC collapses toward chance. This is the honest boundary of reconstruction-based detection, and it is a large share of real fraud.

Then select Contaminated training data and raise the slider. "Train on normal data only" assumes you can identify normal data, and in fraud you cannot — your unlabelled history contains undetected fraud (M3). The autoencoder learns to reconstruct those too, and its error on similar future cases drops accordingly, which is a self-inflicted blind spot that no metric on the training set will reveal.

Against the Isolation Forest baseline, the useful summary is: the autoencoder wins when the manifold is genuinely nonlinear and you have enough clean data to learn it; Isolation Forest wins on cost, on training time, on tolerance to contamination, and on not requiring a GPU. For a first fraud anomaly layer, start with M1 and reach for this when you can show the manifold argument holds.

Interview point

"You train an autoencoder to reconstruct normal data and score by reconstruction error, since anomalies lie off the learned manifold. The bottleneck is doing the work — make it too wide and the network learns the identity and reconstructs anomalies perfectly too. It fails on anomalies that sit inside the manifold, where each feature is individually ordinary and only the combination is wrong, and it degrades when the training data is contaminated, which in fraud it always is. So I'd benchmark it against Isolation Forest rather than assume the deep model wins."

The trap

Reconstruction error is not calibrated and is not comparable across feature types — a large error on a high-variance column outweighs a large error on a tightly-distributed one, so the score is dominated by whichever features happen to be noisiest. Standardise per feature, or weight the reconstruction loss by the inverse variance, or the detector silently becomes a "which row had an unusual amount" detector. And the whole score still needs D6's calibration and D3's threshold before it can drive a decision — an anomaly score is a ranking, and everything Track D said about turning rankings into decisions applies unchanged.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
How does an autoencoder detect anomalies?

Trained to reconstruct normal data, it reconstructs off-manifold points badly; the reconstruction error is the score.

What does the bottleneck do?

Forces compression — without it the network learns the identity and reconstructs anomalies just as well.

When does it fail?

When anomalies lie inside the normal manifold, and when the training data is contaminated with undetected anomalies.

Why standardise the features first?

Reconstruction error is dominated by high-variance columns otherwise.

How does it compare to Isolation Forest?

Better on genuinely nonlinear manifolds with clean data; worse on cost, training time and contamination tolerance.

Is the reconstruction error a probability?

No — it needs calibration and a cost-based threshold before it can drive a decision.

What is a variational autoencoder's difference?

It learns a distribution over the latent space with a KL term, giving a generative model and a likelihood-based score.

Track A · Data & features · Module A7

Outliers & Robust StatisticsThe estimators you use to find outliers are themselves destroyed by outliers. And in fraud, the outliers are the point.

The standard outlier rule — flag anything beyond three standard deviations — has a circularity problem: the outliers inflate the standard deviation they are being measured against, so they hide themselves. This bench measures that masking effect, contrasts it with median-and-MAD alternatives, and then asks the question that actually matters for fraud: whether you should be removing them at all.

Robustness bench
real breakdown behaviour
left: the data with each method's fences drawn · right: estimates as contamination rises — the breakdown point, measured

Masking, and the breakdown point

z-score (x − mean) / SD breakdown point 0% modified z 0.6745·(x − median) / MAD breakdown point 50% IQR fence below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR breakdown point 25% MAD = median( |xᵢ − median(x)| ), scaled by 1/0.6745 ≈ 1.4826 to match σ for Gaussians

The breakdown point is the fraction of contamination an estimator tolerates before it can be made arbitrarily wrong. For the mean it is zero — one sufficiently extreme value moves it anywhere you like. For the median it is 50%, the highest achievable. The right-hand panel plots both as contamination rises, and the mean's line diverges immediately while the median's stays flat until half the data is contaminated and then jumps.

Now watch masking, which behaves in a way most people find counter-intuitive once they see it measured. Drag outlier distance from ×8 to ×40 with the z-score selected: detection barely improves, from 33% to 44%. The outliers inflate the SD they are measured against, so the fence travels outward with them — being more extreme does not make them easier to find, because the ruler is made of the thing being measured.

The collapse comes from the other direction. Hold the distance and raise contamination from 3% to 30%: detection falls from 67% to 6%. Thirty percent of the data is now dragging the mean to 435 (median: 55) and the SD to 719 (MAD-scaled: 45), and almost nothing clears the fence. That is a breakdown point of zero, drawn. Switch to modified z at the same setting and detection is complete, because the median and MAD never noticed them.

The fraud-specific question

The readout labelled downstream AUC after clipping is the one that matters here. The bench trains a fraud model on the raw feature and on a version clipped at whichever fence the selected detector drew — "remove what the detector flagged", the action people actually take — and compares. With modified z at ×40 the cost is 0.900 → 0.893: small, consistent, and entirely self-inflicted. In most contexts clipping extreme values is sensible hygiene. In fraud it frequently destroys the signal, because an unusually large amount at an unusual hour is the fraud — the outliers are not measurement error, they are the positive class.

SituationReasonable response
Sensor glitch, impossible value, obvious data errorRemove or repair — it is not data
Heavy-tailed but genuine (amounts, velocities)Transform (log) or use a robust model, don't clip
The extreme values are the target classKeep them. Clipping deletes your signal
Extreme values destabilise a linear modelRobust loss (S5), or a tree model that is indifferent to monotone scale

Interview point

"The three-sigma rule has a breakdown point of zero — outliers inflate the SD they're measured against, so extreme ones mask themselves, and detection actually gets worse as they get further out. Median and MAD have a 50% breakdown point, so I use a modified z-score or an IQR fence. But in fraud the prior question is whether to remove them at all: the extreme values are usually the positive class, so I'd rather log-transform or use a tree model than clip away the signal."

The trap

Any clipping or winsorising is a learned transform and belongs inside the pipeline fitted on training data (A2, K1) — clip bounds recomputed on live traffic are training–serving skew with a different name. Two more: outlier detection per column misses multivariate outliers entirely, since a point can be unremarkable on every axis and impossible in combination, which is what robust Mahalanobis distance and M3's elliptic envelope are for. And "remove the outliers" applied before a train/test split leaks, because the removal decision used the test rows' values.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What is a breakdown point?

The fraction of contaminated data an estimator tolerates before it can be made arbitrarily wrong.

Breakdown point of the mean, median and IQR fence?

0%, 50% and 25% respectively.

What is masking?

Outliers inflate the standard deviation used to detect them, so extreme ones fall inside the fence and hide.

Define MAD and its scaling.

Median absolute deviation from the median, scaled by about 1.4826 to match σ under normality.

When should outliers be removed?

When they are genuine data errors — not when they are extreme but real, and never when they are the class you are predicting.

What does per-column detection miss?

Multivariate outliers, ordinary on every axis but impossible in combination.

Why must clip bounds be fitted on training data?

Recomputing them at serving time creates training–serving skew, and computing them before splitting leaks test information.

Track J · Reinforcement learning · Module J1

Multi-Armed BanditsThe explore–exploit trade in its purest form, and the three algorithms worth being able to name.

You have k options with unknown payoffs. Every pull is both a chance to earn and a chance to learn, and those goals conflict. This is the simplest reinforcement-learning problem — no state, no transitions, just regret — and it is the one that actually shows up in fraud work, as rule selection, treatment assignment and review routing.

Bandit bench
real pulls · real regret
left: cumulative regret for all four policies on the same arms · right: how often each arm was pulled under the selected policy

The four policies

ε-greedy with probability ε pull at random, otherwise pull the current best simple; explores forever, so regret grows linearly decaying ε ε_t = min(1, k / t) explores hard early, then commits — logarithmic regret UCB1 pull argmax [ x̄_i + √(2 ln t / n_i) ] "optimism under uncertainty": the bonus shrinks as an arm is sampled Thompson sample θ_i ~ Beta(successes+1, failures+1), pull the argmax Bayesian; usually the strongest in practice and trivial to implement

Regret is the gap between what you earned and what an oracle pulling the best arm every time would have earned. The right frame is that a fixed ε has linear regret — it keeps spending ε of every round on arms it already knows are worse — while decaying ε, UCB and Thompson achieve logarithmic regret, meaning the cost of learning stops growing. At 8000 pulls with six arms: fixed ε 198, decaying ε 140, Thompson 78.

And one result the bench produces that the textbook ordering does not predict: UCB1 comes last, at 261. That is not a bug. UCB1's guarantee is asymptotic, and its exploration bonus √(2 ln t / n) carries a deliberately conservative constant — with gaps as small as 0.08 it keeps sampling arms long after the evidence is clear. Tune that constant down, or lengthen the horizon far enough, and the ordering reverts. The transferable lesson is that a regret bound is an asymptotic statement, and at the horizon you actually run, constants decide the winner — which is why Thompson sampling, with no constant to tune, tends to be the production default.

What the sliders show

Narrow the gap to 0.02 and everything degrades: when arms are nearly identical it takes enormous samples to tell them apart, and regret per pull is small precisely because the mistake is cheap. Widen it to 0.3 and the adaptive policies identify the best arm almost immediately while fixed ε keeps paying its exploration tax forever — the same total regret arriving through two completely different mechanisms.

Raise arms to 20 and watch every policy suffer. Exploration cost scales with the number of options, which is the practical argument against testing dozens of variants at once: with a fixed traffic budget, more arms means less evidence per arm and a longer period of paying for it.

Interview point

"A bandit is the explore–exploit trade with no state. Fixed ε-greedy has linear regret because it explores forever; UCB1 adds an optimism bonus that shrinks as an arm is sampled, and Thompson sampling draws from the posterior — both get logarithmic regret and Thompson usually wins in practice. Where it matters for fraud is rule and treatment selection: routing a fraction of traffic to alternative thresholds and letting the bandit converge, rather than running a fixed A/B test to completion."

The trap

Bandits assume payoffs are stationary and feedback is immediate. Fraud violates both: an adversary makes rewards non-stationary (V3), and outcomes arrive weeks later (K4). A standard bandit converges on the arm that was best last quarter and then stops exploring, which is exactly wrong against an opponent. The adaptations are sliding-window or discounted estimates so old evidence decays, and a floor on exploration so no arm is abandoned permanently — the same argument as V3's random review quota, arriving from a different direction. Also: bandits optimise a single scalar reward, so if the true objective is a trade between fraud loss, customer friction and analyst cost, that trade must be baked into the reward before you start.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Define regret.

The cumulative difference between the reward obtained and the reward an oracle always pulling the best arm would have obtained.

Why does fixed ε-greedy have linear regret?

It spends a constant fraction of every round exploring arms already known to be worse.

State the UCB1 rule.

Pull the arm maximising its mean plus √(2 ln t / n_i) — optimism in the face of uncertainty.

How does Thompson sampling choose?

It samples a value from each arm's posterior and pulls the argmax of the samples.

What happens as the number of arms grows?

Exploration cost grows with it — less evidence per arm for a fixed budget.

Why are bandits fragile in fraud?

Rewards are non-stationary because of an adversary, and feedback is delayed.

Two adaptations for non-stationarity?

Discounted or sliding-window reward estimates, and a permanent floor on exploration.

Track J · Reinforcement learning · Module J2

Q-Learning & the MDPAdd state and consequences to a bandit and you have the full problem. One update rule solves it.

A bandit's choices don't change the world. A Markov decision process adds state and transitions: actions move you somewhere, and where you end up determines what you can do next. Q-learning learns the value of each action in each state from experience alone — no model of the environment — through a single update that is worth being able to write from memory.

Gridworld bench
real Q-learning · compared against value iteration
left: the grid with the learned policy as arrows, goal in teal and pit in red · right: reward per episode, smoothed

The update

Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α [ r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a') − Q(s,a) ] └────── TD target ──────┘ └ current estimate ┘ the bracket is the temporal-difference error α learning rate — how much of the new evidence to absorb γ discount — how much a future reward is worth now; effective horizon ≈ 1/(1−γ) γ = 0.5 → ~2 steps of foresight γ = 0.99 → ~100 steps

Q-learning is off-policy: the target uses max over next actions, so it learns the value of the greedy policy while behaving with exploration. SARSA uses the action actually taken instead, making it on-policy and more conservative near hazards — the distinction interviewers ask about, and the reason SARSA learns to walk further from a cliff than Q-learning does.

What each slider breaks

Drop γ to 0.3 and the agent becomes myopic. The effective horizon falls from 20 steps to 1.4, and the value of the start state goes from +5.21 to −1.43: at that discount the distant goal is genuinely almost worthless, so heading toward it is not a mistake the agent is making — it is the correct answer to a different question. This is why γ is a statement about the problem, not a tuning knob.

Set ε to 0 and something instructive happens: the agent still learns. Q starts at zero while every step costs −1, so every untried action looks optimistic; trying one makes it look worse, which pushes a purely greedy agent to try something else. Exploration falls out of the initialisation for free. That is the technique called optimistic initialisation, and it is why "greedy always fails" is too strong — it stops working the moment rewards are positive or the optimism is exhausted. Set ε to 0.9 instead and it fails the other way: plenty of exploration, almost no exploitation, and the reward curve stays low.

Raise α toward 1 and each update overwrites the estimate with a single noisy sample, so the policy oscillates instead of converging — the same instability as B2's learning rate, in a different setting.

Interview point

"Q-learning updates toward the TD target r + γ·max Q(s',a'), so it's model-free and off-policy — it learns the greedy policy's values while exploring. γ sets the effective horizon at roughly 1/(1−γ), so too small a discount makes distant rewards invisible and the agent myopic. SARSA is the on-policy version using the action actually taken, which makes it more cautious around hazards."

The trap

Tabular Q-learning needs to visit every state–action pair many times, and real problems have state spaces far too large for that — which is what function approximation, and eventually deep Q-networks, exist to solve. But the moment you approximate, the convergence guarantees vanish: bootstrapping from your own estimates while generalising across states is unstable, and the tricks that make DQN work (a replay buffer to break correlation between successive samples, a frozen target network to stop the target moving with the estimate) are patches for exactly that instability. Knowing why those two components exist is a much better answer than knowing that they do.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Write the Q-learning update.

Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ·max_a' Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)].

What is the TD error?

The bracketed difference between the bootstrapped target and the current estimate.

What does γ control?

How far ahead rewards matter — an effective horizon of roughly 1/(1−γ) steps.

On-policy vs off-policy?

SARSA uses the action actually taken; Q-learning uses the max, so it learns the greedy policy while exploring.

Why does ε = 0 fail?

The agent exploits initial estimates and never discovers better states.

Why does a large α destabilise learning?

Each update nearly replaces the estimate with one noisy sample.

Why do DQNs need replay and target networks?

To break sample correlation and stop the bootstrapped target moving with the estimate — both instabilities introduced by function approximation.

Track J · Reinforcement learning · Module J3

Contextual Bandits & Off-Policy EvaluationThe RL that actually fits a fraud system — and the question of how you'd ever know it worked.

Full RL is rarely the right tool for fraud, but the contextual bandit is: for each transaction you observe features, choose an action — approve, review, decline, step up authentication — and receive a reward, with no state transitions to worry about. The hard part is not learning the policy. It is answering "would this new policy have done better?" using only logs generated by the old one.

Off-policy bench
real IPS estimator · true value known
left: the IPS estimate against the true value of the new policy, with the estimator's spread across resamples · right: the distribution of importance weights — the tail is the problem

Inverse propensity scoring

V̂(π_new) = (1/n) Σ [ π_new(a_i | x_i) / π_log(a_i | x_i) ] · r_i └──── importance weight ────┘ unbiased IF every action the new policy might take had positive probability under the logging policy — the support / overlap condition π_log(a|x) → 0 ⇒ the weight explodes ⇒ variance explodes π_log(a|x) = 0 ⇒ the estimate is undefined, and no amount of data fixes it

Press the three logging modes in order while watching the two panels. With ε = 0.2 the IPS estimate tracks the true value closely and its spread across resamples is modest. At ε = 0.02 it is still unbiased — the average across many resamples is right — but any single estimate can be far off, because a handful of rare actions carry enormous weights. Look at the right-hand histogram: a long tail of large weights is exactly what high variance looks like before it bites you.

With a deterministic logging policy, off-policy evaluation is not hard, it is impossible. The logs contain no information about what would have happened under any other action, and no estimator can recover it. This is the single most important operational consequence in the module: if you ever want to evaluate a new policy from logs, the current policy must randomise a little. That is the same argument as V3's random review quota and M4's label budget, arriving for a third time from a third direction — and it is the reason mature decision systems deliberately log propensities alongside actions.

Practical estimators

EstimatorIdeaTrade
IPSReweight logged rewards by the propensity ratioUnbiased; variance explodes with small propensities
Clipped / capped IPSCap the weights at some MIntroduces bias, removes the worst variance — usually the right call
Direct methodFit a reward model and evaluate the new policy against itLow variance, biased by whatever the reward model gets wrong
Doubly robustReward model plus IPS correction on its residualsConsistent if either the model or the propensities are right

Interview point

"For fraud I'd use a contextual bandit rather than full RL — there's no meaningful state transition, just context, action and reward. The hard part is off-policy evaluation: IPS reweights logged rewards by the propensity ratio and is unbiased, but variance explodes when the logging policy assigned tiny probabilities, and it's undefined where it assigned zero. So the production requirement is that the live policy randomises and logs its propensities, otherwise no new policy can ever be evaluated offline. In practice I'd use clipped IPS or a doubly robust estimator."

The trap

The reward is not observed for actions you did not take, and in fraud it is often not observed at all: decline a transaction and you never learn whether it was fraudulent. That is censored feedback on top of the bandit problem, and it biases the reward estimate for exactly the action you most want to evaluate. The partial remedies are a small holdout that approves cases the policy wanted to decline — expensive, and the only clean source of counterfactual evidence — plus proxies like re-attempt behaviour. Anyone proposing to "let RL optimise the decline policy" without a plan for censored feedback and a safety floor has not thought about what happens during the exploration phase, and in a regulated setting that exploration is itself the thing that needs approval (V2).

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
How does a contextual bandit differ from full RL?

There are no state transitions — each round is context, action, reward, independent of the last.

Write the IPS estimator.

Mean over logged rounds of (π_new(a|x)/π_log(a|x))·r.

When is IPS unbiased?

When the logging policy gave positive probability to every action the new policy might take.

What happens with small propensities?

Importance weights explode and the variance becomes unusable, even though the estimator stays unbiased.

Why can't you evaluate off-policy from deterministic logs?

They contain no counterfactual information; the estimator is undefined and more data cannot help.

What is doubly robust estimation?

A reward model corrected by IPS on its residuals, consistent if either component is correct.

What is censored feedback in fraud?

Declining a transaction means never learning its true label, biasing the estimate for that action.

Evaluation & imbalance · Module D1

ROC-AUC vs PR-AUCSame model, same predictions. One curve flatters it, the other tells you the truth.

A fraud model reporting 0.96 ROC-AUC sounds finished. The same model may have a precision of 4% at usable recall — and the ROC curve will never show you that, because its x-axis is diluted by a class that outnumbers fraud three hundred to one. This bench draws both curves from the same scores while you change the base rate.

Curve Bench — ROC and PR from identical scores
real curves, real areas
left: ROC with chance diagonal · right: precision–recall with the prevalence baseline

Why one curve moves and the other does not

ROC plots recall against false-positive rate. Both axes are normalised within a class: TPR divides by all positives, FPR divides by all negatives. Change the mix between classes and neither axis notices — ROC-AUC is invariant to prevalence, which is a genuinely useful property when you want to compare a model across populations with different base rates.

The precision–recall curve plots precision against recall. Precision is TP/(TP+FP), and TP comes from the positive class while FP comes from the negative one. It is the only common metric that mixes the two, so it is directly sensitive to their ratio. Hit Drop to 0.2% prevalence: ROC-AUC barely twitches while average precision falls off a cliff, because at that base rate every threshold that catches real fraud also sweeps up a crowd of legitimate transactions.

ROC baseline (chance) = 0.5 always, regardless of imbalance PR baseline (chance) = prevalence 0.002 at a 0.2% fraud rate so PR-AUC 0.28 with a 0.002 baseline is a 140× lift while ROC-AUC 0.94 with a 0.5 baseline is less impressive than it sounds

Which to report

SituationReportReason
Rare positive class you actually care aboutPR-AUC / average precisionSensitive to the false positives that will drown your review queue
Comparing one model across populations with different base ratesROC-AUCPrevalence-invariant, so the comparison is about the model rather than the mix
Roughly balanced classesEither — they broadly agreeThe dilution effect is small
A specific operating point is already fixedPrecision and recall at that threshold, plus expected costCurves summarise all thresholds; the business runs at one

Both are threshold-free summaries — they rank models rather than telling you where to cut. That question is the next module's job.

One numeric footnote worth knowing: ROC-AUC has a clean probabilistic reading — it is the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative. Average precision has no such interpretation, which is precisely why it cannot be gamed by a class ratio.

Interview point

"ROC-AUC is invariant to class balance because both of its axes are normalised within a class. Precision isn't — it mixes true and false positives — so on a 0.3% fraud rate I report PR-AUC against a baseline equal to the prevalence. An ROC-AUC of 0.95 can coexist with 4% precision, and the review team feels the second number, not the first."

The trap

Do not compare PR-AUC across datasets with different prevalence — the baseline moves, so the numbers are not on the same scale. Compare the lift over baseline instead. And be careful with the interpolation: scikit-learn's average_precision_score is a step-wise sum, while auc(recall, precision) applies trapezoidal interpolation that is optimistically wrong on sparse positive classes. They can disagree by several points on the same predictions. Use average precision and say so.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
What are the axes of each curve?

ROC: TPR vs FPR. PR: precision vs recall.

Why is ROC-AUC insensitive to imbalance?

TPR and FPR are each normalised within their own class, so changing the ratio between classes doesn't move either axis.

What is the PR chance baseline?

The positive prevalence — 0.002 for a 0.2% fraud rate.

Interpret ROC-AUC probabilistically.

The probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative.

Which curve for a needle-in-haystack problem?

Precision–recall, quoted against its prevalence baseline.

Is a PR-AUC of 0.30 good?

Unanswerable without the baseline. Against a 0.002 prevalence it is a 150× lift; against a 0.4 prevalence it is worse than chance.

Do these metrics tell you where to threshold?

No — both average over all thresholds. Choosing the cut is a cost decision.

Evaluation & imbalance · Module D2

Class Imbalance: Resampling, SMOTE & Class WeightsMost of what resampling buys you is a moved threshold. This bench separates the part that is real from the part that is theatre.

The standard advice is to balance the classes and move on. What actually happens is subtler: undersampling throws away information, oversampling duplicates it, SMOTE invents points in regions where no fraud has ever occurred, and class weights change the loss without touching the data. This bench runs all four on the same imbalanced set and reports the metric that is hard to fool.

Resampling Bench — real SMOTE, real logistic fit
PR-AUC is the referee
majority · minority · gold = synthetic points created by SMOTE · line = fitted boundary at threshold 0.5

What each method actually does

MethodMechanismReal cost
Random undersamplingDrop majority rows until balancedDiscards genuine information; at 1:200 you throw away 99.5% of your legitimate transactions and with them the boundary detail
Random oversamplingDuplicate minority rowsNo new information. Encourages memorising individual fraud rows; equivalent to weighting for a linear model
SMOTENew points on the segment between a minority point and one of its k minority neighboursInterpolates in feature space. Fine on a convex cluster, wrong across a gap, and fatal on a mislabelled outlier
Class weightsMultiply the loss of minority errors by wNo data fabricated, no data discarded. Usually the first thing to try, and it composes with everything
Threshold moveLeave training alone, choose the cut from costCosts nothing and often achieves most of what the others do

The result that surprises people

Watch PR-AUC as you switch methods. Recall at threshold 0.5 leaps when you balance the classes — which is what makes resampling feel effective — but PR-AUC, which is threshold-free, usually moves far less. The reason is mechanical: balancing shifts the intercept of the fitted model, which is the same thing as moving the threshold. The ranking of transactions by risk, which is what a fraud queue consumes, barely changes.

That is why threshold selection is not an afterthought to resampling — for many problems it is the alternative to it. Resampling earns its place when it changes the shape of the boundary rather than merely its offset: severe imbalance combined with a decision-tree learner whose split criterion cannot see a class it almost never encounters.

SMOTE, honestly

for each minority point x: pick a random neighbour x_nn from its k minority neighbours λ ~ U(0,1) x_new = x + λ · (x_nn − x) # a point on the segment between them

Press Add noisy minority points — a few mislabelled fraud rows dropped inside the majority cloud. SMOTE now interpolates between a legitimate-looking outlier and a real fraud point, manufacturing synthetic fraud in a region that is overwhelmingly legitimate, and the boundary bends to accommodate it. Precision falls. This is why the practical variants — Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, SMOTE-ENN — all exist to control where synthesis is allowed to happen.

Interview point

"I start with class weights and a cost-chosen threshold, because both are free and neither fabricates data. Resampling only earns its place when it changes the boundary's shape rather than its offset — and I judge that on PR-AUC, since recall at a fixed 0.5 cut improves for trivial reasons. And SMOTE never touches the validation fold: synthetic points belong in training only."

The trap

Two ways teams break this. First, resampling before the split — synthetic or duplicated points end up on both sides, and the validation score becomes fiction. Resample inside the training fold only, every fold, always. Second, forgetting that resampling destroys calibration: a model trained on artificially balanced data outputs probabilities calibrated to the balanced prior, not the real 0.3% one. If anything downstream consumes those numbers as probabilities — expected-loss calculations, regulatory reporting — you must recalibrate or correct the intercept back to the true prevalence.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Describe SMOTE in one sentence.

It creates synthetic minority points by interpolating between a minority sample and one of its k minority nearest neighbours.

Why is undersampling risky at extreme imbalance?

You discard the overwhelming majority of real data, losing boundary detail and adding variance.

Where in the pipeline does resampling belong?

Inside the training fold, after the split, never on validation or test data.

Why might PR-AUC barely change after balancing?

Because balancing mostly shifts the decision offset, and PR-AUC is threshold-free — it measures the ranking, which is largely unchanged.

What does class_weight='balanced' compute?

Weights inversely proportional to class frequency, n/(k·n_c), applied to each class's loss contribution.

What does resampling do to calibration?

Breaks it — the output probabilities reflect the resampled prior, so they need correcting back to the true base rate.

Name two safer SMOTE variants and what they fix.

Borderline-SMOTE synthesises only near the decision boundary; SMOTE-ENN cleans noisy synthetic and majority points after generation.

Evaluation & imbalance · Module D3

Cost-Sensitive ThresholdsThe threshold is not a hyperparameter. It is a business decision with a closed-form answer.

Everything so far has produced a ranking. This module converts the ranking into a decision, and it is the module that sounds like it was written by someone who has worked in a bank rather than someone who has finished a course. Given the cost of a false positive and the cost of a missed fraud, the optimal cut is not tuned — it is derived.

Expected-Cost Bench
₹ per 10,000 transactions
expected cost per 10,000 transactions across all thresholds · teal = cost-optimal cut · gold = 0.5 default · violet = capacity limit

The derivation worth being able to write on a whiteboard

Flag a transaction when the expected cost of flagging is lower than the expected cost of not flagging. With calibrated probability p:

cost(flag) = (1 − p) · C_FP you review a legitimate transaction cost(don't flag)= p · C_FN you eat the loss on a real fraud flag when (1 − p)·C_FP < p·C_FN p* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN) C_FP = 200, C_FN = 12000 → p* = 200/12200 = 0.0164

The optimal threshold for realistic card-fraud costs is around 1.6%, not 50%. A default predict() is therefore not a neutral choice — it is an implicit claim that reviewing a good customer costs the same as losing the full transaction value, which is wrong by roughly two orders of magnitude. Press Equal costs and watch the optimum walk back to 0.5: that is the only assumption under which the library default is correct.

Capacity is the second constraint

The cost-optimal threshold assumes you can review everything it flags. You cannot. Push review capacity up from off and a second line appears: the threshold at which flagged volume equals the number of cases your analysts can actually clear. Whichever threshold is higher — stricter — is the one you can operate. This turns into a genuinely useful sentence in an interview, because it shows you know a model ships into a team, not into a vacuum.

RegimeGoverning ruleWhat you tune
Cost-boundp* = C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN)Nothing — you derive it and monitor calibration
Capacity-boundThreshold set so flagged volume ≤ analyst throughputAlert budget; then push recall by improving the model's ranking
Regulatory floorMinimum recall on a defined typology, regardless of costNothing. It is a constraint, not an objective

Costs are usually asymmetric and non-constant

C_FN often scales with transaction value, which means the right formulation is not a single threshold at all — it is per-transaction: flag when p · value > C_FP. That is expected-value ranking rather than probability ranking, and it is what mature fraud systems actually do. It also explains why calibration is not optional: the moment you multiply a score by money, the score has to be a probability rather than an arbitrary ranking.

Interview point

"I don't tune the threshold, I derive it: with calibrated probabilities the cost-optimal cut is C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN), which for card fraud lands near 1–2%, not 0.5. Then I check it against review capacity and take whichever is stricter. If costs scale with transaction value I rank on expected loss, p × value, instead of on p alone."

The trap

The formula assumes the scores are calibrated probabilities. Boosted trees and SVMs are not calibrated out of the box, and anything trained on resampled data is calibrated to the wrong prior. Plug an uncalibrated score into p* and you get a confidently wrong operating point that looks principled in the deck. Calibrate first — Platt or isotonic on a held-out set — then derive. Also note the cost figures in this bench are illustrative placeholders, not benchmarks: get the real numbers from the loss and operations teams, because they are the only inputs that matter.

Quick-fire · night-before sheet
Give the cost-optimal threshold formula.

p* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN), for calibrated probabilities.

Under what condition is 0.5 correct?

Only when the two error types cost the same and the model is calibrated.

What prerequisite does the formula have?

Calibration — the scores must behave like probabilities, or the derived cut is meaningless.

How does review capacity change the decision?

It imposes a volume ceiling; you take the stricter of the cost-optimal and capacity-feasible thresholds.

What if the cost of a miss scales with amount?

Rank on expected loss, p × value, and flag above a fixed expected-loss cut rather than a fixed probability.

Why not just maximise F1?

F1 implicitly assumes precision and recall matter equally, which is a cost assumption you never checked and almost certainly don't hold.

Where does the threshold live in production?

Versioned alongside the model artifact and monitored, since drift in prevalence or costs invalidates it even when the model is fine.
